records.patched_text: "Well, Prince, so Genoa and Lucca are now nothing more than estates belonging to the Bonaparte family. But I'm warning you — if you don't tell me this means war, if you keep on defending the atrocities committed by that Antichrist — and I truly believe he is the Antichrist — then I'm done with you. You are no longer my friend, no longer my 'faithful slave,' as you like to call yourself! But how are you? I can see I've frightened you — sit down and tell me all the news." (in French)

"If you have nothing better to do, Count (or Prince), and if the prospect of spending an evening with a poor invalid isn't too terrible, I would be delighted to see you tonight between seven and ten. — Annette Scherer." (in French)

"First of all, dear friend, tell me how you are. Put your friend's mind at rest," he said (in French), his tone unchanged — beneath the politeness and the show of sympathy, one could detect indifference, even irony.

"In a moment. By the way," she added (in French), growing calm again, "I'm expecting two very interesting men tonight: the Vicomte de Mortemart, who is connected to the Montmorencys through the Rohans — one of the finest French families. He is one of the true émigrés, the genuine ones. And also the Abbé Morio. Do you know that brilliant thinker? He has been received by the Emperor. Had you heard?"

"Wait," said Anna Pavlovna (in French), thinking it over. "I'll speak to Lise — young Bolkonski's wife — this very evening, and perhaps the thing can be arranged. It will be on your family's behalf that I begin my apprenticeship as an old maid."

Anna Pavlovna's drawing room was gradually filling up. The highest society of Petersburg was gathered there: people who differed widely in age and temperament but who all belonged to the same social world. Prince Vasili's daughter, the beautiful Helene, came to collect her father for the ambassador's party; she wore a ball gown and her badge as lady-in-waiting. The youthful little Princess Bolkonskaya, known as the most captivating woman in Petersburg (in French), was also there. She had married the previous winter and, being pregnant, no longer attended large gatherings — only small receptions. Prince Vasili's son Hippolyte had arrived with Mortemart, whom he introduced. The Abbé Morio and many others had come as well.
* La femme la plus séduisante de Pétersbourg.

The little princess circled the table with quick, short, swaying steps, her workbag on her arm, and cheerfully spreading out her skirts, sat down on a sofa near the silver samovar as though everything she did was a pleasure to herself and to everyone around her. "I've brought my work," she said (in French), showing her bag and addressing the whole room. "Mind you, Annette, I hope you haven't played a trick on me," she added, turning to her hostess. "You wrote that it would be just a small gathering — and look how badly I'm dressed." And she spread her arms wide to show off her short-waisted, lace-trimmed, elegant gray dress, cinched with a broad ribbon just below the bust.
"Don't worry, Lise — you will always be prettier than anyone else," replied Anna Pavlovna (in French).

"You know," said the princess in the same tone of voice, still in French, turning to a general, "my husband is abandoning me? He's going off to get himself killed. Tell me — what is this awful war even for?" she added, turning to Prince Vasili, and without waiting for an answer she turned to speak to his daughter, the beautiful Helene.
"It is so good of you, Monsieur Pierre, to come visit a poor invalid," said Anna Pavlovna (in French), exchanging an anxious look with her aunt as she led him over.
"Ah, yes! Do tell us all about it, Vicomte," said Anna Pavlovna (in French), pleased that the phrase had a certain Louis XV ring to it: "Contez nous çela, Vicomte" — tell us the story, Vicomte.
"Madame, I doubt my abilities before such an audience," he said (in French), smiling and inclining his head.

"I am so enchanted by the brilliance of the wit and culture in this society — especially the feminine society — in which I have had the honor of being received, that I have not yet had time to think about the climate," he said (in French).
"General Kutuzov" — said Bolkonski, speaking French and stressing the last syllable of the general's name in the French manner — "has been kind enough to take me on as an aide-de-camp..."

"André," said his wife (in French), addressing her husband in the same flirtatious way she spoke to other men, "the vicomte has been telling us the most wonderful story about Mademoiselle George and Bonaparte!"

"You must excuse me, dear Vicomte," said Prince Vasili to the Frenchman (in French), holding him by the sleeve in a friendly way to keep him from getting up. "This wretched party at the ambassador's is robbing me of a pleasure and forcing me to cut you short. I'm truly sorry to leave your delightful gathering," he said, turning to Anna Pavlovna.
"Papa, we're going to be late," said Princess Helene (in French), turning her beautiful head and glancing back over her sculpted shoulder as she waited by the door.

"My dear Anna Mikhaylovna," he said (in French) with his usual familiar, weary tone, "it's nearly impossible for me to do what you're asking. But to prove my devotion to you and my respect for your father's memory, I will do the impossible. Your son will be transferred to the Guards. Here is my hand on it. Are you satisfied?"
"Papa," said his beautiful daughter (in French) in the same tone as before, "we're going to be late."
"Well, goodbye then! Goodbye! You hear her?" (in French)

"Do promise, do promise, Vasili!" cried Anna Mikhaylovna (in French) as he left, wearing the smile of a flirtatious girl — which had probably once come naturally to her but was now very poorly suited to her careworn face.
"'God has given it to me — let anyone who touches it beware!'" he said (in French), then repeated the words in Italian: "'Dio mi l'ha dato. Guai a chi la tocchi!'"
* Dieu me la donne, gare à qui la touche!

"The sovereigns? I'm not speaking of Russia," said the vicomte (in French), politely but without hope. "The sovereigns, madame — what have they done for Louis XVII, for the Queen, for Madame Elizabeth? Nothing!" He grew more animated. "And believe me, they are reaping what they sowed when they betrayed the Bourbon cause. The sovereigns! They're sending ambassadors to congratulate the usurper."
"A red baton, engrailed, on an azure field — the house of Condé," he said (in French).
"God! My God!" murmured Anna Pavlovna (in French) in a horrified whisper.
"Rousseau's Social Contract," said the vicomte (in French) with a condescending smile.
"But my dear Monsieur Pierre," she said (in French), "how do you explain the fact that a great man would execute a duke — or even an ordinary person — who is innocent and has not been tried?"
"Go inside, Annette, or you'll catch cold," said the little princess (in French), taking leave of Anna Pavlovna. "It's settled," she added in a low voice.
"Princess, goodbye!" he cried (in French), stumbling over his words as much as his feet.

"Well, my friend," said the vicomte (in French), settling himself beside Hippolyte in the carriage, "your little princess is very charming, very charming indeed — quite French." And he kissed his fingertips. Hippolyte burst out laughing.

"How is it," she began, as usual in French, settling quickly and fussily into the armchair as she always did, "how is it that Annette never got married? How foolish you men all are for not marrying her! Forgive me for saying so, but you have no understanding of women whatsoever. What a debater you are, Monsieur Pierre!"
"My God, my God!" she murmured (in French), and gathering up her skirt with one hand, she went to her husband and kissed him on the forehead.

"I'm so very grateful to you, my dear" (in French) — he called absolutely everyone "my dear," whether they were above or below him in rank, without the slightest change in tone — "I thank you on my own behalf and on behalf of our two dear ones whose name day we're celebrating. But you must come to dinner — I'll be offended if you don't, my dear! On behalf of the whole family, I insist — please come, my dear!" He repeated these words to every single guest without exception or variation, wearing the same expression on his full, cheerful, clean-shaven face, giving the same firm handshake and the same quick, repeated bows. As soon as he had seen one visitor out, he returned to whoever was still in the drawing room, pulled a chair up close, and with his legs spread out comfortably and his hands on his knees — the posture of a man who enjoys life and knows how to live it — he swayed back and forth with easy dignity, made small talk about the weather or asked after someone's health, switching between Russian and very poor but thoroughly confident French. Then, like a man weary but committed to his duties, he would get up to see the next visitor off, smooth his sparse gray hair over his bald spot, and invite them to dinner too. Sometimes, on his way back from the entrance hall, he would pass through the conservatory and pantry into the great marble dining room, where tables were being laid for eighty guests. He would watch the footmen carrying in silver and china, rearranging tables, and unfolding damask tablecloths, and call over Dmitri Vasilyevich — a man of good family who managed all his affairs — and say with evident pleasure at the sight of the enormous table: "Well, Dmitri, make sure everything is just right? Good! The important thing is the service — that's what matters." And with a satisfied sigh, he would head back to the drawing room.

"How plainly all these young people wear their hearts on their sleeves!" said Anna Mikhaylovna, gesturing toward Nicholas as he left. "Cousinage—dangereux voisinage — cousinhood is a dangerous neighborhood," she added.
* Cousinhood is a dangerous neighborhood.
"We might as well go back," said the son in French.
"Prince, humanum est errare — to err is human — but..." replied the doctor, swallowing his r's and pronouncing the Latin words with a French accent.
"Goodbye, my dear," answered Prince Vasili (in French), turning away from her.

"Well then, old boy, my most honorable Alphonse Karlovich," said Shinshin, laughing ironically and mixing the most common Russian expressions with the choicest French phrases—a quirk of his speech. "You plan to make your fortune off the government (in French)—you want to turn a profit from your company?"
* Vous comptez vous faire des rentes sur l'état;
"That balances the books... A German can skin a flint, as the proverb goes," Shinshin remarked (in French), shifting his pipe to the other side of his mouth and winking at the count.
* La balance y est...
"Yes, madame," he replied (in French), looking around.
"No, madame." (in French) He smiled quite inappropriately.

"Do you know the proverb: 'Jerome, Jerome, don't roam—stay home and turn your spindles'?" said Shinshin, wrinkling his brow and smiling. "That suits us perfectly. Suvorov, now—he knew what he was doing, and even he was beaten to a pulp. And where are we going to find a Suvorov today? I ask you." He kept switching between French and Russian.
* Connaissez-vous le Proverbe:
* (2) Cela nous convient à merveille.
* (3) à plate couture
* (4) Je vous demande un peu
"That's how we used to dance in our day, my dear," said the count (in French).
"Do you think he can last until morning?" the German asked, addressing Lorrain in poorly pronounced French.
* Catherine.

"What next?" the princess interrupted with a sardonic smile, her eyes unchanged. "I am a woman, and you think we're all stupid. But I know this: an illegitimate son cannot inherit... un bâtard — a bastard!" she added, as though this French translation would conclusively prove the invalidity of his argument.

"Really, Catiche! Can't you understand? You're so intelligent—how can you not see that if the count has written to the Emperor asking him to recognize Pierre as legitimate, then Pierre will no longer be plain Pierre but Count Bezukhov, and he'll inherit everything under the will? And if the will and letter haven't been destroyed, you'll have nothing but the consolation of having been dutiful, and all that follows from that! That's certain." (in French)
* Et tout ce qui s'ensuit!

"I know, my dear, kind princess," Anna Mikhaylovna said (in French), gripping the portfolio so tightly it was obvious she would not let go easily. "Dear princess, I beg you, I implore you—have some pity on him! I beseech you..."

The third interruption came as Prince Andrew was wrapping up. The old man began singing in the cracked voice of old age: "Malbrook s'en va-t-en guerre. Dieu sait quand reviendra." — Marlborough is off to war. God knows when he'll return.
"Dieu sait quand reviendra — God knows when he'll return. Now go to the dining room."
"Dieu sait quand reviendra" — God knows when he'll return — the prince hummed, out of tune, and with a laugh even more so, he left the table.

"We should be patient with small weaknesses — who doesn't have them, Andrew? Don't forget she was raised in high society, so her position now is hardly an easy one. We should try to understand everyone's situation. Tout comprendre, c'est tout pardonner — to understand all is to forgive all. Think what it must be like for her, poor thing — after the life she was used to — to be separated from her husband and left alone in the country, and in her condition. It's very hard."
* Tout comprendre, c'est tout pardonner.
* Kutuzov.
"You asked me to remind you about the officer Dolokhov, reduced to the ranks in this regiment."
"Ah..." said Kutuzov, glancing at Bolkonski as though asking the adjutant to wait, and went on speaking in French.

"All I can say, General," he began (in French) with an elegant pleasantness of tone and delivery that made you want to listen to each carefully chosen word — it was clear Kutuzov enjoyed the sound of his own voice — "all I can say, General, is that if the matter depended solely on my personal wishes, His Majesty Emperor Francis's will would have been fulfilled long ago. I would have joined the Archduke without delay. And believe me, on my honor, it would be a genuine pleasure for me to hand over supreme command of the army to a more knowledgeable and capable general — of whom Austria has so many — and to lay down this heavy burden of responsibility. But circumstances are sometimes stronger than we are, General."

"But you know the wise maxim, Your Excellency — always prepare for the worst," said the Austrian general (in French), clearly wanting to move past the sarcasm and get down to business. He glanced involuntarily at the aide-de-camp.

"Excuse me, General," Kutuzov interrupted (in French), also turning to Prince Andrew. "Here's what I need, my dear fellow: get all the scout reports from Kozlovsky. Here are two letters from Count Nostitz, and here's one from His Highness Archduke Ferdinand, plus these" — he handed over several papers — "put together a clean memo in French summarizing everything we know about the Austrian army's movements, then deliver it to His Excellency."
"You see before you the unfortunate Mack," he said (in French), in a broken voice.
"Your Excellency," he said (in German), stepping forward and addressing the Austrian general, "I have the honor of congratulating you."
"God, how childish!" he muttered (in German) angrily after a few steps.
* Gott, wie naiv!

"What's gotten into me?" Prince Andrew burst out (in French), stopping in his tracks, his voice shaking with emotion. "Don't you understand? Either we are officers serving our Tsar and our country, who share in its victories and grieve at its misfortunes — or we are nothing but servants who couldn't care less about their master's business. Forty thousand men slaughtered and the army of our allies destroyed, and you find that amusing! That's fine for some worthless nobody like that creature you've made your friend, but not for you — not for you. Only a juvenile could find entertainment in this," he added in Russian, though he used the French-accented word for juvenile, noticing that Zherkov could still hear him.
* Quarante mille hommes massacrés et l'armée de nos alliés détruite, et vous trouvez là le mot pour rire.
* (2) C'est bien pour un garçon de rien comme cet individu dont vous avez fait un ami, mais pas pour vous, pas pour vous.

"Wonderful! He's going to be a superb horse," he thought, smiling, and with his saber at his side and spurs jingling, he ran up the porch steps. His German landlord, wearing a waistcoat and a pointed cap and holding a pitchfork, was shoveling manure from the cow shed. His face brightened the moment he saw Rostov. "Good morning! Very good morning!" he said (in German), winking with a cheerful smile, clearly pleased to see the young man.
* Schön gut Morgen! Schön gut Morgen!

"Busy already?" Rostov replied (in German) with that same bright, brotherly smile that never left his eager face. "Long live Austria! Long live Russia! Long live Emperor Alexander!" he added, repeating a phrase the German landlord used constantly.
* Schon fleissig?
* Hoch Oestreicher! Hoch Russen! Kaiser Alexander hoch!
"And long live the whole world!" (in German)
* Und die ganze Welt hoch!

Rostov waved his cap in the air just like the German and laughed (in German): "And long live the whole world!" Though neither the German shoveling his cow shed nor Rostov returning from hay-gathering duty had any particular reason to rejoice, they looked at each other with joyful delight and brotherly affection, wagged their heads as a sign of mutual goodwill, and parted smiling — the German going back to his cow shed, Rostov heading to the cottage he shared with Denisov.
"From Field Marshal Kutuzov?" he asked (in French). "Good news, I hope? An engagement with Mortier? A victory? It was about time!"
"Goodbye! Thank you very much. His Majesty will most likely wish to see you," he added (in French) with a bow.

"However, my dear fellow," he remarked (in French), examining his nails from a distance and puckering the skin above his left eye, "despite the deep respect I hold for the Orthodox Russian army, I must confess that your victory was not exactly the most victorious of victories."
* Cependant, mon cher, malgré la haute estime que je professe pour the Orthodox Russian army, j'avoue que votre victoire n'est pas des plus victorieuses.

"Buonaparte?" said Bilibin inquiringly, wrinkling his forehead to signal that a witticism was coming. "Buonaparte?" he repeated, stressing the 'u.' "I think, however, now that he's laying down the law for Austria at Schönbrunn, il faut lui faire grâce de l'u! — we really must drop the 'u.' I shall certainly adopt the innovation and simply call him Bonaparte!"
* "We must let him off the u!"
* beaux yeux
* les nôtres
"Woman is man's companion," announced Prince Hippolyte (in French), peering through a lorgnette at his own elevated legs.
* La femme est la compagne de l'homme.

"The Berlin cabinet cannot express a sentiment of alliance," Hippolyte began (in French), looking around importantly at the others, "without expressing... as in its last note... you understand... Besides, unless His Majesty the Emperor departs from the principle of our alliance..."
* messieurs les maréchaux
* tête-de-pont
* qu'il n'y voit que du feu, et oublie celui qu'il devait faire faire sur l'ennemi!

He remembered words from Bonaparte's address to his army at the beginning of the campaign: "That Russian army which English gold has transported from the ends of the earth—we shall make it share the same fate as the army at Ulm." (in French) These words awakened in him astonishment at his hero's genius, a sting of wounded pride, and a hope for glory. "And if all that's left is to die?" he thought. "Well, if it comes to that, I'll do it no worse than anyone else."
* Cette armée russe que l'or de l'Angleterre a transportée des extrémités de l'univers, nous allons lui faire éprouver le même sort—(le sort de l'armée d'Ulm).
"There you have the pleasures of camp life, Prince," said the staff officer (in French).
* Voilà l'agrément des camps, monsieur le prince.
"We'll make you dance the way we did under Suvorov," said Dolokhov (in French).
* On vous fera danser.
"What's he going on about?" asked one of the Frenchmen (in French).
* Qu'est-ce qu'il chante?
* "Daughter of Matthew" was the literal meaning of the name.
"I love you!" he said (in French), remembering what you're supposed to say at such moments. But his words sounded so feeble that he felt embarrassed.
* Je vous aime!
* Anna Pavlovna.

She asked if it had been long since Anatole left Paris and whether he had enjoyed it there. Anatole answered the Frenchwoman readily and, studying her with a smile, chatted with her about her homeland. When he noticed the pretty little Bourienne, Anatole decided that life at Bald Hills might not be boring after all. 'Not bad at all!' he thought (in French), looking her over. 'Not bad at all, that little companion! Hopefully she'll come along when we're married. She's quite charming.'
* la petite est gentille

"Ma foi, sire, nous ferons ce qui sera dans notre possibilité, sire" ("Indeed, Sire, we shall do everything it is possible to do, Sire,") he answered cheerfully, though his poor French drew ironic smiles from the gentlemen in the Tsar's entourage.
* Ma foi, sire, nous ferons ce qui sera dans notre possibilité, sire.
"Hang these Russians!" muttered a German (in German).
* Zum Henker diese Russen!
"Here he is... our own boy... Kolya, sweetheart... How he's changed!... Where are the candles?... Tea!..."

"I'll tell you the whole secret of dueling in two words. If you're going to fight a duel and you sit down to write your will and tender letters to your parents, thinking you might be killed — you're a fool and you're done for. But if you go with the firm intention of killing your opponent as quickly and surely as possible, then everything will be fine. That's what our bear hunter back in Kostroma used to tell me: 'Everyone's afraid of a bear,' he'd say, 'but once you see one, all your fear vanishes — your only thought is not to let him get away!' That's how it is with me. Until tomorrow, mon cher." (in French)
* À demain, mon cher.

"'I'm not that stupid.... Just you try.... You clear out of this,' she used to say (in French). Seeing how successful she was with young and old men and women, Pierre often couldn't understand why he didn't love her.
* Allez-vous promener

"It's all her fault," he told himself. "But what does that matter? Why did I tie myself to her? Why did I say 'I love you' (in French) to her — which was a lie, and worse than a lie? I'm guilty and must endure... what? A stain on my name? A lifelong misfortune? Oh, that's nonsense," he thought. "A stain on my name and honor — that's something separate from who I really am."
* Je vous aime

But the moment he imagined himself calmed by such thoughts, she suddenly came into his mind as she had been in those moments when he'd most strongly expressed his fake love for her, and he felt the blood rush to his heart and had to get up again and move around and smash and tear at whatever came to hand. "Why did I tell her 'I love you'?" he kept repeating to himself. And after saying it for the tenth time, Moliere's words came to him: "Mais que diable allait-il faire dans cette galère?" ("But what the devil was he doing in that galley?") — and he began to laugh at himself.
* Frühstück: breakfast.
"Nicholas, will you come to Iogel's? Please do!" said Natasha. "He invited you, and Vasili Dmitrich is coming too."

"Whatever the European sovereigns and commanders may do to appease Bonaparte, and to cause us annoyance and humiliation, our opinion of Bonaparte cannot change. We will not stop expressing our honest views on the matter, and can only say to the King of Prussia and the rest: 'So much the worse for you. Tu l'as voulu, George Dandin — you asked for it, George Dandin' — that's all we have to say about it!"

"Ah, my dear vicomte," Anna Pavlovna chimed in (in French), "L'Urope" — for some reason she pronounced it Urope, as if this were a specially refined French pronunciation she could permit herself when speaking with a Frenchman — "L'Urope ne sera jamais notre alliée sincère" ("Europe will never be our sincere ally").
* "Europe will never be our sincere ally."

"Oh, it's nothing. I only wanted to say..." — he had been trying all evening to work in a joke he'd heard in Vienna — "I only wanted to say that we are wrong to fight pour le Roi de Prusse — for the King of Prussia, that is, for nothing!"

"Delighted to see you. I'm very glad to see you," she said to Pierre (in French) as he kissed her hand. She had known him as a child, and now his friendship with Andrew, his marital troubles, and above all his kind, simple face inclined her warmly toward him. She looked at him with her beautiful, radiant eyes, and seemed to say: "I like you very much, but please don't make fun of my people." After the first greetings they sat down.
* Charmée de vous voir. Je suis très contente de vous voir.
"Andrew!" said Princess Mary imploringly. "You must know that this is a woman," Prince Andrew said to Pierre (in French).
"Andrew, for God's sake!" Princess Mary repeated (in French).
* Il faut que vous sachiez que c'est une femme.
* Andrew, au nom de Dieu!
"But, my dear friend," said Prince Andrew (in French), "on the contrary, you should be grateful that I'm explaining to Pierre your intimacy with this young man."
* Mais, ma bonne amie, vous devriez au contraire m'être reconnaissante de ce que j'explique à Pierre votre intimité avec ce jeune homme.

"Come, Pelageya, I was joking," said Pierre. "Princess, I give you my word, I didn't mean to offend her (in French). I meant nothing — I was only joking," he said, smiling shyly and trying to make amends. "It was all my fault, and Andrew was only joking."
* Princesse, ma parole, je n'ai pas voulu l'offenser.
"No — I only wonder how you got away from your regiment. I'll be with you in a moment," he said (in French), answering someone who called him.
* Dans un moment je suis à vous.

"I am an admirer of Montesquieu," replied Prince Andrew (in French), "and his idea that the principle of monarchies is honor strikes me as indisputable. Certain rights and privileges of the nobility seem to me a means of sustaining that sentiment."
* Le principe des monarchies est l'honneur me paraît incontestable. Certains droits et privilèges de la noblesse me paraissent être des moyens de soutenir ce sentiment.
* Si vous envisagez la question sous ce point de vue.
* The Illuminati sought to replace monarchical institutions with republican ones.

Helene had been at Erfurt during the famous meeting of the Emperors and had brought back from there her connections with Napoleonic dignitaries. At Erfurt her success had been brilliant. Napoleon himself had noticed her in the theater and said of her (in French): "That's a superb creature." Her success as a beautiful and elegant woman did not surprise Pierre, for she had become even more attractive than before. What did surprise him was that during these last two years his wife had somehow acquired the reputation (in French) of being as charming and witty as she was beautiful. The distinguished Prince de Ligne wrote her eight-page letters. Bilibin saved up his best witticisms to deliver them in Countess Bezukhova's presence. To be received in the Countess Bezukhova's salon was considered a mark of intellectual distinction. Young men read books before attending Helene's evenings so they would have something to say in her salon, and secretaries of the embassy, and even ambassadors, confided diplomatic secrets to her, so that in a way Helene became a force. Pierre, who knew she was very stupid, sometimes attended her evenings and dinner parties — where politics, poetry, and philosophy were discussed — with a strange feeling of bewilderment and dread. At these parties he felt like a conjurer who always expects his trick to be found out. But whether because stupidity was exactly what was needed to run such a salon, or because the people being deceived found pleasure in the deception, the illusion was never exposed, and Helene Bezukhova's reputation as a lovely and clever woman became so firmly established that she could say the emptiest and most foolish things and everybody would go into raptures over every word, finding deep meaning in it that she herself never intended.
* C'est un superbe animal.
* D'une femme charmante, aussi spirituelle que belle.
* das soll mein Weib werden.

Natasha looked in the mirrors and could not pick out her own reflection from the rest. Everything blurred into one brilliant procession. On entering the ballroom, the steady murmur of voices, footsteps, and greetings overwhelmed her, and the light and glitter dazzled her even more. The host and hostess, who had already been standing at the door for half an hour repeating the same phrase to each arrival — "Delighted to see you" (in French) — greeted the Rostovs and Peronskaya in the same manner.
* Charmé de vous voir.

"Oh, you know him?" said Peronskaya. "I can't stand him. He's the man of the moment right now (in French). And so proud! Takes after his father. He's hand in glove with Speransky, writing some kind of legislation. Just look how he treats the ladies! There's one speaking to him and he's turned away," she said, pointing at him. "I'd give him a piece of my mind if he treated me like that."
* Il fait à présent la pluie et le beau temps.

Berg smiled with a sense of superiority over his weak-natured wife and paused, reflecting that this dear wife of his was after all only a weak woman who could not understand everything that constitutes a man's dignity — what it means to be a man (in German). Vera, at the same time, smiled with a sense of superiority over her good, conscientious husband, who nevertheless understood life incorrectly, as in Vera's view all men did. Berg, judging by his wife, thought all women weak and foolish. Vera, judging by her husband alone and generalizing from that, believed that all men, though they understand nothing and are conceited and selfish, credit only themselves with common sense.
* ein Mann zu sein.
"Yes, you know — between cousins, closeness often leads to love. Le cousinage est un dangereux voisinage — cousinhood is a dangerous neighborhood, don't you think?"

After Prince Andrew's engagement to Natasha, Pierre suddenly felt — without any apparent reason — that it was impossible to go on living as before. Although he had been firmly convinced of the truths revealed to him by his benefactor, and happy in perfecting his inner self, to which he had devoted himself with such passion, all the zest of such a life vanished after Andrew and Natasha's engagement and the death of Joseph Alexeevich, the news of which reached him almost simultaneously. Only the skeleton of life remained: his house, a brilliant wife who now enjoyed the favors of a very important personage, acquaintance with all of Petersburg, and his court service with its dull formalities. And this life suddenly seemed unexpectedly loathsome to Pierre. He stopped keeping a diary, avoided the Brothers, began going to the club again, drank heavily, and fell back in with the bachelor crowd, leading such a life that Countess Helene thought it necessary to speak severely to him about it. Pierre felt she was right, and to avoid compromising her he left for Moscow.

In Moscow he entered his huge house, where the faded and aging princesses still lived with their enormous household. He drove through the city and saw the Iberian shrine with its countless candles burning before the golden icon covers, the Kremlin Square with its snow untouched by traffic, the cabbies and hovels of the Sivtsev Vrazhok — those old Muscovites who wanted nothing, hurried nowhere, and were peacefully living out their days. He saw the old Moscow ladies, the Moscow balls, and the English Club — and felt himself at home in a quiet haven. In Moscow he felt at peace, at home, warm and slovenly as in an old dressing gown.

Moscow society, from the old women down to the children, received Pierre like a long-awaited guest whose place was always ready and waiting. For Moscow society Pierre was the nicest, kindest, most intellectual, jolliest, and most magnanimous of eccentrics — a heedless, good-natured nobleman of the old Russian type. His purse was always empty because it was open to everyone.

Benefit performances, bad paintings, statues, charitable societies, gypsy choirs, schools, subscription dinners, sprees, Freemasons, churches, and books — nothing and no one ever met with a refusal from him, and if it hadn't been for two friends who had borrowed large sums and taken him under their wing, he would have given everything away. There was never a dinner or soiree at the club without him. As soon as he sank into his spot on the sofa after two bottles of Margaux, people gathered around and the talking, arguing, and joking began. When quarrels broke out, his kindly smile and well-timed jokes reconciled the opponents. The Masonic dinners were dreary and dull when he wasn't there.

When, after a bachelor supper, he got up with his amiable, kindly smile and yielded to entreaties to go off somewhere with the revelers, shouts of delight and triumph arose among the young men. At balls he danced whenever a partner was needed. Young ladies, married and unmarried, liked him because he was equally friendly to all without making love to any of them, especially after supper. "He's charming; he has no sex," they said of him (in French).

But instead of all that — here he was, the wealthy husband of an unfaithful wife, a retired gentleman-in-waiting, fond of eating and drinking and of grumbling about the government a bit as he unbuttoned his waistcoat; a member of the Moscow English Club and a universal favorite in Moscow society. For a long time he couldn't reconcile himself to the idea that he was one of those same retired Moscow gentlemen-in-waiting he had so despised seven years ago.

Sometimes he consoled himself with the thought that he was only living this way temporarily; but then he was shocked by the thought of how many others, like him, had entered this life and this club temporarily, with all their teeth and hair still in place, and had only left when not a single tooth or hair remained.

In moments of pride, when he reflected on his position, it seemed to him that he was quite different from and distinct from those other retired gentlemen-in-waiting he had formerly despised: they were empty, stupid, contented fellows, content with their lot: "while I am still dissatisfied and want to do something for humanity," he thought. In moments of humility he told himself: "But perhaps all these comrades of mine struggled just as I did, looking for something new, a path of their own, and like me were brought by force of circumstances, of society, of birth — by that elemental force against which man is powerless — to the state I'm in." And after living in Moscow for a while he no longer despised but began to grow fond of, respect, and pity his fellows in fate, just as he pitied himself.

Pierre no longer suffered moments of despair, hypochondria, and disgust with life. But the same illness that had once expressed itself in such acute attacks was now driven inward and never left him for a moment. "What for? Why? What is going on in the world?" he would ask himself several times a day, perplexed, involuntarily starting to ponder anew the meaning of the phenomena of life. But knowing from experience that there were no answers to these questions, he quickly turned away from them and picked up a book, or hurried off to the club or to Apollon Nikolaevich's to swap the town's gossip.

"Helene, who has never cared about anything except her own body and is one of the stupidest women alive," thought Pierre, "is regarded by people as the pinnacle of intelligence and refinement, and they worship her. Napoleon Bonaparte was despised by everyone as long as he was great, but now that he has become a pathetic comedian, Emperor Francis wants to offer him his daughter in an illegal marriage. The Spaniards, through the Catholic clergy, offer thanks to God for their victory over the French on the fourteenth of June — and the French, also through the Catholic clergy, give thanks for defeating the Spaniards on that same fourteenth of June. My brother Masons swear by the blood that they are ready to sacrifice everything for their neighbor, but they won't give a ruble each to the collections for the poor, and they scheme — the Astraea Lodge against the Manna Seekers, rival Masonic lodges — and fuss over an authentic Scottish carpet and a charter that nobody needs and whose meaning not even the man who wrote it understands. We all profess the Christian law of forgiving injuries and loving our neighbors — the law in whose honor we've built forty times forty churches in Moscow — but yesterday a deserter was knouted to death, and a minister of that same law of love and forgiveness, a priest, gave the soldier a cross to kiss before his execution." So thought Pierre, and this whole universal deception — which everyone accepted, and to which he was himself accustomed — astonished him afresh each time, as if it were something new. "I understand the deception and confusion," he thought, "but how am I to tell them all that I see? I have tried, and I've always found that they too, deep in their souls, understand it as I do — they just try not to look. So it seems this is how things must be! But I — what is to become of me?" he thought. He had the unfortunate capacity — common among men, especially Russians — of seeing and believing in the possibility of goodness and truth, but of seeing the evil and falsehood of life too clearly to be able to take any serious part in it. Every sphere of activity was connected, in his eyes, with evil and deception. Whatever he tried to be, whatever he took up, the evil and falsehood repelled him and blocked every path. Yet he had to live and find something to do. It was too terrible to exist under the burden of these unsolvable problems, so he abandoned himself to every distraction in order to forget them. He frequented every kind of society, drank a great deal, bought paintings, took up construction, and above all — read.

He read, and read everything that came to hand. On coming home, while his valets were still helping him undress, he would pick up a book and start reading. From reading he passed to sleeping, from sleeping to gossip in the drawing rooms of the club, from gossip to carousals and women; from carousals back to gossip, reading, and wine. Drinking became more and more both a physical and a moral necessity. Though the doctors warned him that wine was dangerous for someone of his weight, he drank heavily. He only felt fully at ease when, having mechanically poured several glasses of wine into his large mouth, he felt a pleasant warmth in his body, an amiability toward everyone, and a readiness to respond superficially to any idea without probing it deeply. Only after a bottle or two did he feel dimly that the terribly tangled skein of life that had previously horrified him was not as dreadful as he had thought. He was always conscious of some thread of that skein as, with a buzzing in his head after dinner or supper, he chatted, listened to conversation, or read. But under the influence of wine he would tell himself: "It doesn't matter. I'll untangle it. I have a solution worked out, but I don't have time right now — I'll think it all through later." But the "later" never came.

Sometimes he recalled how he had heard that soldiers in war, when entrenched under the enemy's fire with nothing to do, try hard to find some occupation to make it easier to bear the danger. To Pierre, all people seemed like those soldiers, seeking refuge from life: some in ambition, some in cards, some in lawmaking, some in women, some in toys, some in horses, some in politics, some in sport, some in wine, some in government affairs. "Nothing is trivial and nothing is important — it's all the same — only to save oneself from it as best one can," thought Pierre. "Only not to see it — that dreadful it!"

From the end of 1811, an intensified buildup and concentration of the forces of Western Europe began, and in 1812 these forces — millions of men, counting those transporting and feeding the army — moved from the west eastward to the Russian frontier, toward which since 1811 Russian forces had been similarly drawn. On June twelfth, 1812, the forces of Western Europe crossed the Russian frontier and war began — that is, an event took place contrary to human reason and to human nature. Millions of men committed against one another such innumerable crimes, frauds, betrayals, thefts, forgeries, counterfeiting, burglaries, arson, and murders as in whole centuries are not recorded in the annals of all the law courts of the world, but which those who committed them did not at the time regard as crimes.

What produced this extraordinary event? What were its causes? The historians tell us with naive assurance that its causes were the wrongs inflicted on the Duke of Oldenburg (whose duchy Napoleon had annexed), the failure to observe the Continental System (Napoleon's trade embargo), the ambition of Napoleon, the firmness of Alexander, the mistakes of the diplomats, and so on.

We can understand that the matter appeared that way to contemporaries. It naturally seemed to Napoleon that the war was caused by England's intrigues (as in fact he said on the island of St. Helena). It naturally seemed to members of the English Parliament that the cause of the war was Napoleon's ambition; to the Duke of Oldenburg, that the cause was the violence done to him; to businessmen, that the cause was the Continental System which was ruining Europe. It seemed to the generals and old soldiers that the main reason for the war was the necessity of giving them employment; to the legitimists of that day, that it was the need of restoring les bons principes (good principles). And it seemed to the diplomats that it all resulted from the fact that the alliance between Russia and Austria in 1809 had not been sufficiently well concealed from Napoleon, and from the clumsy wording of Memorandum No. 178, a diplomatic dispatch. It is natural that these and a countless and infinite number of other reasons — the number depending on the endless diversity of viewpoints — presented themselves to the people of that day; but to us, to posterity, who view the event in all its magnitude and perceive its plain and terrible meaning, these causes seem inadequate. To us it is incomprehensible that millions of Christian men killed and tortured each other either because Napoleon was ambitious or Alexander was firm, or because England's policy was astute or the Duke of Oldenburg was wronged. We cannot grasp what connection such circumstances have with the actual fact of slaughter and violence. Why, because the Duke was wronged, thousands of men from the other side of Europe killed and ruined the people of Smolensk and Moscow and were killed by them.

Had Napoleon not taken offense at the demand that he should withdraw beyond the Vistula, and not ordered his troops to advance, there would have been no war; but had all his sergeants objected to serving a second term, there could have been no war either. Nor could there have been a war had there been no English intrigues and no Duke of Oldenburg, had Alexander not felt insulted, and had there not been an autocratic government in Russia. Nor could there have been a war without the Revolution in France and the dictatorship and Empire that followed it, or without all the things that produced the French Revolution, and so on. Without each of these causes nothing could have happened. So all these causes — myriads of causes — combined to bring it about. And so there was no single cause for that event, but it had to occur because it had to. Millions of men, abandoning their human feelings and reason, had to march from west to east to slay their fellows, just as some centuries earlier hordes of men had come from the east to the west, slaying their fellows.

The actions of Napoleon and Alexander, on whose words the event seemed to depend, were as little voluntary as the actions of any soldier drawn into the campaign by lot or by conscription. This could not be otherwise, for in order that the will of Napoleon and Alexander (on whom the event seemed to depend) should be carried out, the concurrence of innumerable circumstances was needed, without any one of which the event could not have taken place. It was necessary that millions of men in whose hands lay the real power — the soldiers who fired, or transported provisions and guns — should consent to carry out the will of these weak individuals, and should have been induced to do so by an infinite number of diverse and complex causes.

Each man lives for himself, using his freedom to achieve his personal aims, and feels with his whole being that he can now do or refrain from doing this or that action. But as soon as he has done it, that action performed at a certain moment in time becomes irrevocable and belongs to history, in which it has not a free but a predestined significance.

There are two sides to the life of every man: his individual life, which grows freer the more abstract its interests are, and his elemental hive life, in which he inevitably obeys laws laid down for him.

Though Napoleon at that time, in 1812, was more convinced than ever that it depended on him whether to shed (or not to shed) the blood of his peoples (in French) — as Alexander expressed it in the last letter he wrote him — he had never been so much in the grip of inevitable laws, which compelled him, while thinking that he was acting on his own free will, to perform for the hive life — that is, for history — whatever had to be performed.

The people of the west moved eastward to slay their fellow men, and by the law of coincidence thousands of minute causes aligned and combined to produce that movement and war. There were complaints about the failure to observe the Continental System, the Duke of Oldenburg's wrongs, and the movement of troops into Prussia — undertaken (as it seemed to Napoleon) solely to secure an armed peace. There was the French Emperor's love and habit of war coinciding with his people's inclinations, the allure of the grand preparations, the expenditure on those preparations and the need to recoup them, and the intoxicating honors he received in Dresden. There were the diplomatic negotiations, too, which contemporaries believed were conducted with a sincere desire for peace but which only wounded the self-love of both sides — and millions of other causes that adapted themselves to the event or coincided with it.

Nothing is the cause. All this is merely the coincidence of conditions in which all vital organic and elemental events occur. And the botanist who finds that the apple falls because the cellular tissue decays and so forth is equally right with the child who stands under the tree and says the apple fell because he wanted to eat it and prayed for it. Equally right or wrong is he who says Napoleon went to Moscow because he wanted to, and perished because Alexander desired his destruction. And equally right or wrong is he who says that an undermined hill weighing a million tons fell because the last laborer struck it for the last time with his pickaxe. In historic events, the so-called great men are labels giving names to events, and like labels they have only the smallest connection with the event itself.
Every act of theirs, which appears to them an act of their own will, is in a historical sense involuntary and is related to the whole course of history and predestined from eternity.

Prince Andrew found Barclay de Tolly, to whom he had been assigned, on the bank of the Drissa. As there was not a single town or large village in the vicinity of the camp, the immense number of generals and courtiers accompanying the army were living in the best houses of villages on both sides of the river, over a radius of six miles. Barclay de Tolly was quartered nearly three miles from the Emperor. He received Bolkonski stiffly and coldly and told him in his foreign accent that he would mention him to the Emperor for a decision on his assignment, but asked him meanwhile to remain on his staff. Anatole Kuragin, whom Prince Andrew had hoped to find with the army, was not there. He had gone to Petersburg, but Prince Andrew was glad to hear this. His mind was occupied with the affairs of the center that was conducting a gigantic war, and he was glad to be free for a while from the distraction caused by thoughts of Kuragin. During the first four days, while no duties were required of him, Prince Andrew rode all around the fortified camp and, using his own knowledge and his conversations with experts, tried to form a definite opinion about it. But the question of whether the camp was advantageous or not remained unresolved in his mind. Already from his military experience and from what he had seen in the Austrian campaign, he had reached the conclusion that in war the most carefully considered plans have no significance and that everything depends on how unexpected movements of the enemy — which cannot be foreseen — are met, and on how and by whom the whole matter is handled. To understand this last point, Prince Andrew, using his position and connections, tried to grasp the character of the army's leadership and of the men and factions involved, and he arrived at the following picture of the situation.

While the Emperor had still been at Vilna, the forces had been divided into three armies. First, the army under Barclay de Tolly; second, the army under Bagration; and third, the one commanded by Tormasov. The Emperor was with the first army, but not as commander in chief. In the orders issued, it was not stated that the Emperor would take command, only that he would be with the army. The Emperor moreover had with him not a commander in chief's staff but the imperial headquarters staff. In attendance on him was the head of the imperial staff, Quartermaster General Prince Volkonsky, as well as generals, imperial aides-de-camp, diplomatic officials, and a large number of foreigners — but not the army staff. Besides these, there were in attendance on the Emperor without any definite assignments: Arakcheev, the former Minister of War; Count Bennigsen, the senior general by rank; the Grand Duke Tsarevich Constantine Pavlovich; and Count Rumyantsev, the Chancellor. There were also Stein, a former Prussian minister; Armfeldt, a Swedish general; Pfuel, the chief author of the plan of campaign; Paulucci, an adjutant general and Sardinian émigré; Wolzogen — and many others. Though these men held no military position in the army, their standing gave them influence, and often a corps commander, or even the commander in chief, did not know in what capacity he was questioned by Bennigsen, the Grand Duke, Arakcheev, or Prince Volkonsky, or was given this or that piece of advice, and did not know whether a certain order received in the form of advice came from the man who gave it or from the Emperor, and whether it had to be carried out or not. But this was only the surface; the essential significance of the Emperor's presence and of all these people, from a courtier's perspective (and in an Emperor's vicinity all became courtiers), was clear to everyone. It was this: the Emperor did not take the title of commander in chief but controlled all the armies; the men around him were his assistants. Arakcheev was a faithful enforcer of order who served as the sovereign's bodyguard. Bennigsen was a landowner in the Vilna province who appeared to be doing the honors of the district but was actually a good general, useful as an adviser and ready to replace Barclay. The Grand Duke was there because it suited him. The former Minister Stein was there because his advice was valuable and Emperor Alexander held him in high personal esteem. Armfeldt bitterly hated Napoleon and was a general full of self-confidence — a quality that always influenced Alexander. Paulucci was there because he was bold and decisive in speech. The adjutants general were there because they always accompanied the Emperor, and lastly and chiefly, Pfuel was there because he had drawn up the plan of campaign against Napoleon and, having persuaded Alexander to believe in its effectiveness, was directing the whole business of the war. With Pfuel was Wolzogen, who expressed Pfuel's thoughts in a more comprehensible way than Pfuel himself — who was a harsh, bookish theorist, self-confident to the point of despising everyone else — could manage.

The second faction was the direct opposite of the first; as always, one extreme was met by representatives of the other. Its members demanded an advance from Vilna into Poland and freedom from all prearranged plans. Besides advocating bold action, this group also represented nationalism, which made them still more one-sided in the dispute. They were Russians: Bagration, Ermolov (who was beginning to come to prominence), and others. At that time a famous joke of Ermolov's was circulating: as a great favor he had petitioned the Emperor to make him a German. The men of this faction, remembering Suvorov, the Russian general, said that what one had to do was not to reason or stick pins in maps, but fight, beat the enemy, keep him out of Russia, and not let the army get demoralized.

Of a fourth opinion the most conspicuous representative was the Tsarevich, who could not forget his disillusionment at Austerlitz, where he had ridden out at the head of the Guards in his helmet and cavalry uniform as to a review, expecting to crush the French gallantly, but had unexpectedly found himself in the front line and had narrowly escaped amid the general confusion. The men of this faction had both the quality and the defect of frankness in their opinions. They feared Napoleon, recognized his strength and their own weakness, and openly said so. They said: "Nothing but sorrow, shame, and ruin will come of all this! We have abandoned Vilna and Vitebsk and shall abandon Drissa. The only sensible thing left is to make peace as soon as possible, before we are thrown out of Petersburg."

The fifth faction consisted of supporters of Barclay de Tolly, not so much of the man as of the minister of war and commander in chief. "Be he what he may" (they always began like that), "he is an honest, practical man and we have nobody better. Give him real power, for war cannot be waged successfully without unity of command, and he will show what he can do, as he did in the war in Finland. If our army is well organized and strong and has retreated to Drissa without suffering any defeats, we owe this entirely to Barclay. If Barclay is now replaced by Bennigsen, all will be lost, for Bennigsen showed his incapacity already in 1807."

The sixth faction, the Bennigsenites, said on the contrary that there was at any rate no one more active and experienced than Bennigsen: "Twist about as you may, you'll have to come to Bennigsen in the end. Let the others make mistakes now!" said they, arguing that our retreat to Drissa was a most shameful reverse and an unbroken chain of blunders. "The more mistakes that are made the better. At least it will be understood sooner that things can't go on like this. What is needed is not some Barclay or other, but a man like Bennigsen, who proved himself in 1807 and to whom Napoleon himself gave credit — a man whose authority would be willingly accepted, and Bennigsen is the only such man."

The seventh faction consisted of the sort of people who are always to be found, especially around young sovereigns, and of whom there were particularly many around Alexander — generals and imperial aides-de-camp passionately devoted to the Emperor not merely as a monarch but as a man, adoring him sincerely and selflessly as Rostov had done in 1805, and who saw in him not only all the virtues but all human capabilities as well. These men, though delighted with the sovereign's refusal to command the army, nevertheless blamed him for such excessive modesty and only desired and insisted that their adored sovereign should abandon his diffidence and openly announce that he would take personal command of the army, gather a commander in chief's staff around him, and — consulting experienced theoreticians and practical men as needed — lead the troops himself, whose spirits would thereby be raised to the highest pitch.

The eighth and largest group, which outnumbered the others as ninety-nine to one, consisted of men who desired neither peace nor war, neither an advance nor a defensive camp at Drissa or anywhere else, neither Barclay nor the Emperor, neither Pfuel nor Bennigsen, but only the one most essential thing — as much advantage and pleasure for themselves as possible. In the troubled waters of conflicting and intersecting intrigues that swirled around the Emperor's headquarters, it was possible to succeed in many ways unthinkable at other times. A man who simply wanted to keep his lucrative post would today agree with Pfuel, tomorrow with his opponent, and the day after — merely to avoid responsibility or to please the Emperor — would declare that he had no opinion at all on the matter. Another who wished to gain some advantage would attract the Emperor's attention by loudly advocating the very thing the Emperor had hinted at the day before, and would argue and shout at the council, beating his chest and challenging those who disagreed to duels, thereby proving his readiness to sacrifice himself for the common good. A third, in the absence of opponents, between two councils, would simply ask for a special bonus for his faithful services, well knowing that at such a moment people would be too busy to refuse. A fourth, while seemingly overwhelmed with work, would often come accidentally under the Emperor's eye. A fifth, to achieve his long-cherished aim of dining with the Emperor, would stubbornly argue for or against some newly emerging opinion and produce arguments more or less convincing and correct to that end.

All the men of this group were fishing for rubles, decorations, and promotions, and in this pursuit they watched only the weathercock of imperial favor; as soon as they noticed it turning in any direction, this whole drone population of the army began blowing hard that way, making it all the harder for the Emperor to turn it elsewhere. Amid the uncertainties of the situation, with the threat of serious danger lending a peculiarly menacing character to everything, amid this vortex of intrigue, egotism, conflicting views and feelings, and the diversity of nationalities among these people, this eighth and largest group — the people preoccupied with personal gain — introduced great confusion and obscurity into the common task. Whatever question arose, a swarm of these drones, without having finished buzzing about the previous topic, flew to the new one and by their noise drowned out and obscured the voices of those who were arguing honestly.

From among all these factions, just at the time Prince Andrew reached the army, another — a ninth — was being formed and beginning to raise its voice. This was the party of older, reasonable men experienced and capable in state affairs, who, without sharing any of those conflicting opinions, were able to take a detached view of what was happening at headquarters and to consider ways out of this muddle, indecision, intricacy, and weakness.

The men of this faction said and thought that the problems stemmed mainly from the Emperor's presence in the army with his military court and the resulting indefinite, conditional, and unstable fluctuation of relations, which was appropriate at court but harmful in an army; that a sovereign should reign but not command the army, and that the only solution was for the Emperor and his court to leave; that the mere presence of the Emperor paralyzed the action of fifty thousand men needed to guarantee his personal safety; and that the worst commander in chief acting independently would be better than the best one hampered by the presence and authority of the monarch.

Just at the time Prince Andrew was living idly at Drissa, Shishkov, the Secretary of State and one of the chief representatives of this faction, wrote a letter to the Emperor which Arakcheev and Balashev agreed to sign. In this letter, taking advantage of the permission given him by the Emperor to discuss the general course of affairs, he respectfully suggested — on the plea that it was necessary for the sovereign to rouse the people of the capital to a warlike spirit — that the Emperor should leave the army.

This stirring of the people by their sovereign, and his call to them to defend their country—the very incitement which was the chief cause of Russia's triumph, insofar as it was produced by the Tsar's personal presence in Moscow—was suggested to the Emperor, and accepted by him, as a pretext for leaving the army.

"Excuse me, your excellency," he began. (He knew the senator well but thought it necessary to address him formally on this occasion.) "Though I don't agree with the gentleman"—he hesitated, wanting to say "my very honorable opponent"—"with the gentleman whom I have not the honor of knowing, I believe the nobility have been summoned not merely to express sympathy and enthusiasm but also to consider the means by which we can help our Fatherland! I believe," he went on, warming to his subject, "that the Emperor himself would not be satisfied to find in us merely owners of serfs whom we are willing to hand over for his service, and cannon fodder (in French) we are ready to make of ourselves—and not to obtain from us any co-co-counsel."

Alexander refused negotiations because he felt himself personally insulted. Barclay de Tolly tried to command the army in the best way because he wanted to fulfill his duty and earn fame as a great commander. Rostov charged the French because he couldn't resist the urge to gallop across a level field. In the same way, the countless people who took part in the war acted according to their personal characteristics, habits, circumstances, and aims. They were moved by fear or vanity, they rejoiced or were outraged, they reasoned, imagining they knew what they were doing and did it of their own free will. But they were all involuntary tools of history, carrying on a work hidden from them but understandable to us. Such is the inevitable fate of men of action, and the higher they stand in the social hierarchy, the less free they are.

Providence compelled all these men, striving to achieve personal aims, to further the accomplishment of an immense result that none of them at all expected—neither Napoleon, nor Alexander, nor still less any of those who did the actual fighting.

The cause of the destruction of the French army in 1812 is clear to us now. No one will deny that it was, on the one hand, their advance into the heart of Russia late in the season without any preparation for a winter campaign, and on the other, the character given to the war by the burning of Russian towns and the hatred of the enemy this aroused among the Russian people. But no one at the time foresaw what now seems so obvious. It was the only way an army of eight hundred thousand men — the best in the world and led by the best general — could be destroyed: in conflict with a raw army of half its numerical strength, led by inexperienced commanders, as the Russian army was. Not only did no one foresee this, but on the Russian side every effort was made to hinder the only thing that could save Russia, while on the French side, despite Napoleon's experience and so-called military genius, every effort was directed toward pushing on to Moscow at the end of summer—that is, toward doing the very thing that was bound to lead to destruction.

In historical works on 1812, French writers are very fond of saying that Napoleon sensed the danger of extending his line, that he sought a battle, and that his marshals advised him to stop at Smolensk, and of making similar claims to show that even then the danger of the campaign was understood. Russian authors are even more fond of telling us that from the very start a Scythian war plan was adopted to lure Napoleon into the depths of Russia, and this plan is attributed by some to Pfuel, by others to a certain Frenchman, by others to Toll, and by others again to Alexander himself—pointing to notes, plans, and letters that contain hints of such a strategy. But all these hints at what happened, from both the French side and the Russian, are advanced only because they happen to fit the event. Had the event not occurred, these hints would have been forgotten, as we have forgotten the thousands and millions of contrary hints and expectations that circulated at the time but have now been forgotten because events proved them wrong. There are always so many conjectures about the outcome of any event that however it may end, there will always be people to say: "I said then that it would be so," quite forgetting that among their innumerable conjectures, many pointed in the opposite direction.

Conjectures as to Napoleon's awareness of the danger of extending his line, and on the Russian side about luring the enemy into the depths of Russia, are clearly of this kind, and only by great stretching can historians attribute such conceptions to Napoleon and his marshals, or such plans to the Russian commanders. All the facts flatly contradict these conjectures. Throughout the entire war, there was no wish on the Russian side to draw the French into the heart of the country; on the contrary, from the moment the French entered Russia, everything was done to stop them. And not only was Napoleon not afraid to extend his line, but he welcomed every step forward as a triumph and did not seek battle as eagerly as in his former campaigns, but very lazily.

At the very start of the war our armies were divided, and our only aim was to unite them—though uniting the armies was no advantage if we intended to retreat and lure the enemy deeper into Russia. Our Emperor joined the army to encourage it to defend every inch of Russian soil and not to retreat. The enormous fortified camp at Drissa was built according to Pfuel's plan, with no intention of retreating further. The Emperor reproached the commanders in chief for every step they fell back. He could not bear the idea of letting the enemy even reach Smolensk, much less could he contemplate the burning of Moscow, and when our armies did unite, he was displeased that Smolensk had been abandoned and burned without a major battle being fought under its walls.

The facts show plainly that Napoleon did not foresee the danger of advancing on Moscow, nor did Alexander and the Russian commanders think of luring Napoleon on—quite the opposite. The luring of Napoleon into the depths of the country was not the result of any plan, for no one believed it possible; it resulted from a most complex web of intrigues, aims, and desires among those who took part in the war and had no understanding whatever of the inevitable outcome, or of the one way to save Russia. Everything came about by chance. The armies were divided at the start of the campaign. We tried to unite them, with the clear intention of giving battle and checking the enemy's advance, and by this effort to unite them while avoiding battle with a much stronger enemy—necessarily retreating at an acute angle—we led the French on to Smolensk. But we withdrew at an acute angle not only because the French advanced between our two armies; the angle became still more acute and we withdrew still farther, because Barclay de Tolly was an unpopular foreigner disliked by Bagration (who would come under his command), and Bagration, commanding the second army, tried to postpone the junction and avoid coming under Barclay's authority as long as he could. Bagration was slow in effecting the junction—though it was the chief aim of all at headquarters—because, as he claimed, he was putting his army at risk on this march, and it was better for him to withdraw more to the left and south, harassing the enemy from flank and rear and recruiting men from Ukraine for his army; and it seems he planned this in order to avoid serving under the detested foreigner Barclay, whose own rank was lower than Bagration's.
The Emperor was with the army to encourage it, but his presence and ignorance of what steps to take, and the enormous number of advisers and plans, destroyed the first army's energy and it retired.

The intention was to make a stand at the Drissa camp, but Paulucci, aiming to become commander in chief, suddenly turned his energy to influencing Alexander, and Pfuel's entire plan was abandoned and the command given to Barclay. But since Barclay didn't inspire confidence, his power was limited. The armies were divided, there was no unity of command, and Barclay was unpopular; but from this confusion, division, and the unpopularity of the foreign commander in chief, there resulted, on the one hand, indecision and the avoidance of battle (which we could not have refrained from had the armies been united and had someone other than Barclay been in command), and on the other, an ever-increasing indignation against the foreigners and a rising patriotic fervor.

Barclay stood for caution. The Tsarevich hinted at treachery and demanded a general engagement. Lubomirsky, Bronnitsky, Wlocki, and the others of that group stirred up so much trouble that Barclay, under the pretext of sending papers to the Emperor, dispatched these Polish adjutant generals to Petersburg and plunged into open conflict with Bennigsen and the Tsarevich.

Despite his higher rank, Bagration — in this contest of magnanimity — took orders from Barclay. But having submitted, he agreed with him less than ever. By the Emperor's orders, Bagration reported directly to Alexander. He wrote to Arakcheev, the Emperor's confidant: "It must be as my sovereign pleases, but I cannot work with the Minister" (meaning Barclay). "For God's sake send me somewhere else, if only to command a regiment. I can't stand it here. Headquarters are so full of Germans that a Russian cannot exist and nothing makes any sense. I thought I was truly serving my sovereign and the Fatherland, but it turns out I am serving Barclay. I confess I have no desire to."

The swarm of Bronnitskys and Wintzingerodes and their kind further embittered the relations between the commanders in chief, and even less unity resulted. Preparations were made to fight the French in front of Smolensk. A general was sent to survey the position. This general, who hated Barclay, rode off to visit a friend of his, a corps commander, and having spent the day with him, returned to Barclay and condemned, as unsuitable from every point of view, the battleground he hadn't seen.

Among the countless categories that can be applied to the phenomena of human life, one may distinguish between those where substance matters most and those where form does. To the latter—as distinct from village, country, provincial, or even Moscow life—we may assign Petersburg life, and especially the life of its salons. That salon life is unchanging. Since 1805 we had made peace and quarreled again with Bonaparte and had made constitutions and unmade them again, but the salons of Anna Pavlovna and Helene remained just as they had been—the one seven and the other five years before. At Anna Pavlovna's they spoke with puzzlement of Bonaparte's successes, just as before, and saw in them and in the subservience shown to him by the European sovereigns a malicious conspiracy whose sole purpose was to cause unpleasantness and anxiety to the court circle that Anna Pavlovna represented. And in Helene's salon, which Rumyantsev himself honored with his visits, regarding Helene as a remarkably intelligent woman, they spoke with the same ecstasy in 1812 as in 1808 of the "great nation" and the "great man" and regretted our rift with France, a rift which, according to them, ought to be promptly ended by peace.

Lately, since the Emperor's return from the army, there had been some excitement in these rival salon circles and some demonstrations of hostility between them, but each camp kept to its own line. In Anna Pavlovna's circle, only those Frenchmen who were deep-rooted legitimists were admitted, and patriotic views were expressed: that one shouldn't attend the French theater and that maintaining the French troupe was costing the government as much as a whole army corps. The war's progress was eagerly followed, and only the most flattering reports about our army were circulated. In the French circle of Helene and Rumyantsev, reports of the enemy's cruelty and of the war were challenged, and all Napoleon's attempts at conciliation were discussed. In that circle they frowned on those who advised hurried preparations for moving the court and the girls' educational institutions under the Dowager Empress's patronage to Kazan. In Helene's circle, the war was regarded as a series of formal demonstrations that would very soon end in peace. The view that prevailed there was Bilibin's—he was now quite at home in Helene's house, which every clever man was obliged to visit—that matters would be settled not by gunpowder, but by those who had invented it. In that circle, the Moscow enthusiasm (news of which had reached Petersburg along with the Emperor's return) was ridiculed sarcastically and very cleverly, though with great caution.

Soon after the Emperor's return, Prince Vasili, in a conversation about the war at Anna Pavlovna's, severely criticized Barclay de Tolly but was undecided as to who ought to be appointed commander in chief. One of the visitors, usually referred to as "a man of great merit," having described how he had that day seen Kutuzov—the newly chosen chief of the Petersburg militia—presiding over the enrollment of recruits at the Treasury, cautiously ventured to suggest that Kutuzov would be the man to satisfy all requirements.

"I've talked and talked at the Assembly of the Nobility," Prince Vasili interrupted, "but they did not listen to me. I told them his election as chief of the militia would not please the Emperor. They did not listen to me."

This was perfectly correct on the twenty-fourth of July. But on the twenty-ninth of July, Kutuzov was given the title of Prince. This might indicate a wish to get rid of him, and so Prince Vasili's opinion remained valid, though he was not now in any hurry to express it. But on the eighth of August, a committee consisting of Field Marshal Saltykov, Arakcheev, Vyazmitinov, Lopukhin, and Kochubey met to consider the progress of the war. This committee concluded that our failures were due to a lack of unified command, and though its members were aware of the Emperor's dislike of Kutuzov, after brief deliberation they agreed to recommend his appointment as commander in chief. That same day Kutuzov was appointed commander in chief with full powers over the armies and over the entire region they occupied.

"Well, have you heard the great news? Prince Kutuzov is field marshal! All disagreements are over! I am so glad, so delighted! At last we have a man!" he said, glancing sternly and significantly around at everyone in the drawing room.
"But, Prince, they say he's blind!" he said, reminding Prince Vasili of his own words.
"Eh? Nonsense! He sees well enough," said Prince Vasili quickly, in a deep voice with a slight cough—the voice and cough he always used to dismiss difficulties.

"He sees well enough," he added. "And what I'm so pleased about is that our sovereign has given him full powers over all the armies and the whole region—powers no commander in chief has ever had before. He's a second autocrat," he concluded with a triumphant smile.

"They say the Emperor was reluctant to give Kutuzov those powers. They say he blushed like a girl to whom La Fontaine's Joconde is read, when he said to Kutuzov: 'Your Emperor and the Fatherland award you this honor.'"

"Oh, no, no!" warmly rejoined Prince Vasili, now unwilling to yield Kutuzov to anyone; in his opinion Kutuzov was not only admirable but was adored by everybody. "No, that's impossible," he said, "for our sovereign valued him so highly before."

Moscow, the Asiatic capital of this great empire, the sacred city of Alexander's people, Moscow with its countless churches shaped like Chinese pagodas (in French)—this Moscow gave Napoleon's imagination no rest. On the march from Vyazma to Tsarevo-Zaimishche, he rode his light bay bobtailed horse accompanied by his Guards, his bodyguard, his pages, and his aides-de-camp. Berthier, his chief of staff, dropped behind to question a Russian prisoner captured by the cavalry. Followed by the interpreter Lelorgne d'Ideville, he overtook Napoleon at a gallop and reined in his horse with an amused expression.
* Moscou, la capitale asiatique de ce grand empire, la ville sacrée des peuples d'Alexandre, Moscou avec ses innombrables églises en forme de pagodes chinoises.

The interpreter translated these words without the final phrase, and Bonaparte smiled. "The young Cossack made his mighty interlocutor smile," says Thiers. After riding a few paces in silence, Napoleon turned to Berthier and said he wanted to see how the news that he was talking to the Emperor himself—to that very Emperor who had inscribed his immortally victorious name on the Pyramids—would affect this child of the Don. "Go your way and God be with you. I know your path is the path of honor!" He paused. "I missed you at Bucharest, but I needed someone to send." And changing the subject, Kutuzov began to speak of the Turkish war and the peace that had been concluded. "Yes, I was much criticized," he said, "both for that war and the peace... but everything came at the right time. Everything comes to him who knows how to wait. (in French) And there were just as many advisers there as here..." he went on, returning to the topic of "advisers" that clearly preoccupied him. "Ah, those advisers!" he said. "If we had listened to them all, we'd never have made peace with Turkey and would never have finished that war. Everything in haste, but the more haste, the less speed. Kamensky would have been ruined if he hadn't died. He stormed fortresses with thirty thousand men. It's not hard to capture a fortress, but it's hard to win a campaign. For that, you don't need storming and attacking—you need patience and time. Kamensky sent soldiers against Rushchuk, but I used only those two things—patience and time—and I took more fortresses than Kamensky, and made the Turks eat horseflesh!" He swayed his head. "And the French will too, believe me," he went on, growing more animated and striking his chest, "I'll make them eat horseflesh!" And tears again dimmed his eyes.
