Why and how were the battles of Shevardino and Borodino given and accepted? Why was the battle of Borodino fought? There was not the slightest sense in it for either the French or the Russians. Its immediate result for the Russians was, and was bound to be, that we were brought closer to the destruction of Moscow—which we feared more than anything in the world; and for the French, its immediate result was that they were brought closer to the destruction of their whole army—which they feared more than anything in the world. The outcome was completely obvious, and yet Napoleon offered and Kutuzov accepted the battle.

If the commanders had been guided by reason, it would seem obvious to Napoleon that by advancing thirteen hundred miles and fighting with a probability of losing a quarter of his army, he was marching toward certain destruction; and it would have been equally clear to Kutuzov that by accepting battle and risking the loss of a quarter of his army, he would certainly lose Moscow. For Kutuzov this was as mathematically clear as a simple rule in checkers: if I have one piece fewer than my opponent and keep trading pieces evenly, I will certainly lose, and so I should stop trading. Say my opponent has sixteen pieces and I have fourteen—I am only one-eighth weaker than he is. But if we go on trading and I lose thirteen more pieces to his thirteen, he ends up three times as strong as I am.

Before the battle of Borodino our strength relative to the French was about five to six, but after the battle it was little more than one to two: before the battle we had a hundred thousand against a hundred and twenty thousand; afterward, barely fifty thousand against a hundred thousand. Yet the shrewd and experienced Kutuzov accepted the battle, while Napoleon, supposedly a commander of genius, offered it—losing a quarter of his army and lengthening his lines of communication even further. If we are told he expected to end the campaign by capturing Moscow, as he had ended a previous campaign by capturing Vienna, there is much evidence to the contrary. Napoleon's own historians tell us that from Smolensk onward he wanted to stop, that he knew the danger of his extended position, and that he knew the occupation of Moscow would not end the campaign, for at Smolensk he had seen what condition the Russians were leaving their own towns in—left to him—and he had received not a single reply to his repeated announcements of his wish to negotiate.

In giving and accepting battle at Borodino, Kutuzov acted involuntarily and irrationally. But later, to fit what had occurred, historians provided cleverly crafted evidence of the foresight and genius of the generals who, of history's blind tools, were the most enslaved and involuntary.

The ancients left us model heroic poems in which the heroes supply the entire interest of the story, and we still cannot accustom ourselves to the fact that, in our era, history written in that same heroic mode is meaningless.

On the other question—how the battle of Borodino and the preceding battle of Shevardino were fought—there also exists a definite, well-known, but quite false account. All the historians describe the affair as follows:

The Russians did not seek the best position; on the contrary, during the retreat they passed many positions better than Borodino. They did not stop at any of them because Kutuzov did not wish to occupy a position he had not chosen himself, because the popular demand for battle had not yet been expressed strongly enough, because Miloradovich had not yet arrived with the militia, and for many other reasons. The fact is that other positions they had passed were stronger, and the position at Borodino (where the battle was fought), far from being strong, was no more of a position than any other spot one might find in the Russian Empire by sticking a pin into the map at hazard.

Not only did the Russians not fortify the position on the field of Borodino to the left of and at right angles to the highway (the position where the battle took place), but never until the twenty-fifth of August, 1812, did they even consider that a battle might be fought there. This is shown, first, by the fact that there were no entrenchments there by the twenty-fifth, and those begun on the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth were never completed; and second, by the position of the Shevardino Redoubt. That redoubt was quite senseless in front of the position where the battle was accepted. Why was it more heavily fortified than any other point? And why were all efforts exhausted and six thousand men sacrificed defending it until late at night on the twenty-fourth? A Cossack patrol would have sufficed to observe the enemy. Third, as proof that the position where the battle was fought had not been planned, and that the Shevardino Redoubt was not an advanced post of that position, there is this: until the twenty-fifth, both Barclay de Tolly and Bagration were convinced the Shevardino Redoubt was the left flank of the position. Kutuzov himself, in his report written hastily after the battle, calls the Shevardino Redoubt the left flank of the position. Only much later, when reports on the battle of Borodino were written at leisure, was the incorrect and extraordinary claim invented—probably to justify the mistakes of a commander in chief who had to be portrayed as infallible—that the Shevardino Redoubt had been an advanced post (whereas in reality it was simply a fortified point on the left flank), and that the battle of Borodino was fought by us on a pre-selected, entrenched position (whereas it was fought on a quite unexpected and almost unfortified spot).

Napoleon, riding to Valuevo on the twenty-fourth, did not see (as the history books claim) the Russian position from Utitsa to Borodino (he could not have seen that position because it did not exist), nor did he see an advanced post of the Russian army. Instead, while pursuing the Russian rearguard, he came upon the left flank of the Russian position—at the Shevardino Redoubt—and unexpectedly for the Russians moved his army across the Kolocha. The Russians, not having time to begin a general battle, pulled back their left wing from the position they had intended to hold and took up a new position that had not been planned and was not fortified. By crossing the Kolocha to the left of the highway, Napoleon shifted the entire coming battle from right to left, as seen from the Russian side, and moved it onto the plain between Utitsa, Semenovsk, and Borodino—a plain no more advantageous as a position than any other in Russia. It was there that the entire battle of the twenty-sixth of August took place.

Had Napoleon not ridden out on the evening of the twenty-fourth to the Kolocha, and had he not then ordered an immediate attack on the redoubt, but instead begun the attack the next morning, then no one would have doubted that the Shevardino Redoubt was the left flank of our position. The battle would have taken place where we expected it. In that case, we would probably have defended the Shevardino Redoubt—our left flank—even more stubbornly. We would have attacked Napoleon in the center or on the right, and the battle would have been fought on the twenty-fifth, in the position we had intended and fortified. But the attack on our left flank came instead in the evening, after the retreat of our rearguard—that is, immediately after the fight at Gridneva. Because of this, and because the Russian commanders did not wish, or were not in time, to begin a general engagement that same evening, the first and chief action of the battle of Borodino was already lost on the twenty-fourth. This loss obviously led to the loss of the battle fought on the twenty-sixth.

Not only was the Russian army on the twenty-sixth defended by weak, unfinished entrenchments, but the disadvantage of that position was increased by the fact that the Russian commanders—not having fully grasped what had happened, namely the loss of our position on the left flank and the shifting of the entire forthcoming battlefield from right to left—maintained their extended position from the village of Novoe to Utitsa, and consequently had to shift their forces from right to left during the battle. So throughout the entire battle, the Russians opposed the entire French army launched against our left flank with only half as many men. (Poniatowski's action against Utitsa and Uvarov's on the right flank against the French were separate actions from the main battle.) So the battle of Borodino was not fought at all as it has been described (in an effort to conceal our commanders' mistakes, even at the cost of diminishing the glory due to the Russian army and people). The battle of Borodino was not fought on a pre-chosen, entrenched position with forces only slightly weaker than the enemy's. Rather, as a result of the loss of the Shevardino Redoubt, the Russians fought the battle of Borodino on an open and almost unfortified position, with forces only half as numerous as the French. Under those conditions, it was not merely unthinkable to fight for ten hours and achieve an indecisive result—it was unthinkable to keep the army even from complete collapse and rout.

The officers were about to leave, but Prince Andrew, apparently reluctant to be left alone with his friend, asked them to stay and have tea. Seats were brought and tea was served. The officers gazed with surprise at Pierre's huge, stout figure and listened to his talk about Moscow and the position of our army, around which he had ridden. Prince Andrew remained silent, and his expression was so forbidding that Pierre directed his remarks mainly to the good-natured battalion commander.
"Yes—that is, how do you mean?" said Pierre. "Not being a military man, I can't say I've fully understood it, but I get the general position."
"And tell me your opinion of Barclay de Tolly. In Moscow they're saying heaven knows what about him... What do you think of him?"

"Well, to mention only firewood and fodder, let me inform you. Why, when we were retreating from Sventsyani, we didn't dare touch a stick or a wisp of hay or anything. You see, we were leaving, so the enemy would get it all; isn't that right, your excellency?" and Timokhin again looked at the prince. "But we didn't dare. In our regiment two officers were court-martialed for that kind of thing. But once his Serenity took command, everything became straightforward. Now we can see the light..."
Timokhin looked about in confusion, not knowing what or how to answer such a question. Pierre put the same question to Prince Andrew.

"So as not to lay waste the country we were leaving to the enemy," said Prince Andrew with venomous irony. "It's very sound: you can't allow the land to be pillaged or accustom the troops to looting. At Smolensk too he calculated correctly that the French might outflank us since they had larger forces. But he couldn't understand this," cried Prince Andrew in a shrill voice that seemed to escape him involuntarily: "he couldn't understand that there, for the first time, we were fighting for Russian soil, and that there was a spirit in the men such as I had never seen before, and that we had held the French for two days, and that that success had increased our strength tenfold. He ordered us to retreat, and all our efforts and losses went for nothing. He didn't intend to betray us; he tried to do his best; he thought out everything carefully—and that is exactly why he's unfit. He's unfit now precisely because he plans everything very thoroughly and precisely, as every German must. How can I explain it?... Well, say your father has a German valet, and the valet is splendid and satisfies your father's needs better than you could—then it's fine to let him serve. But if your father is mortally ill, you'll send the valet away and attend to your father with your own clumsy, unpracticed hands, and will comfort him better than a skilled stranger could. That's how it's been with Barclay. While Russia was healthy, a foreigner could serve her and be a splendid minister; but the moment she's in danger, she needs one of her own kin. But in your Club they've been calling him a traitor! They've slandered him as a traitor, and the only result will be that later, ashamed of their false accusations, they'll make him out to be a hero or genius instead of a traitor—and that will be even more unjust. He is an honest and very meticulous German."
"A skillful commander?" said Pierre. "Well, one who foresees all possibilities... and foresees the enemy's intentions."

"Yes," replied Prince Andrew, "but with this little difference: in chess you can think over each move as long as you like and aren't limited by time, and with this further difference too: in chess, a knight is always stronger than a pawn, and two pawns are always stronger than one. In war, though, a battalion is sometimes stronger than a division and sometimes weaker than a company. The relative strength of bodies of troops can never be known to anyone. Believe me," he continued, "if things depended on plans made by the staff, I would be there making plans. But instead I have the honor of serving here in the regiment with these gentlemen, and I believe that on us—not on those others—tomorrow's battle will depend... Success never depends, and never will depend, on position, equipment, or even numbers—and least of all on position."

Prince Andrew glanced at Timokhin, who looked at his commander in alarm and confusion. In contrast to his former reserved taciturnity, Prince Andrew now seemed stirred up. He apparently couldn't stop himself from expressing the thoughts that had suddenly occurred to him.

"A battle is won by those who firmly resolve to win it! Why did we lose the battle of Austerlitz? Our losses were nearly equal to the French, but very early we told ourselves we were losing the battle—and we lost it. And we said so because we had nothing to fight for there, we wanted to get away from the battlefield as fast as possible. 'We've lost, so let's run,' and we ran. If we hadn't said that till evening, God knows what might have happened. But tomorrow we won't say it! You talk about our position—the left flank weak, the right flank overextended," he went on. "That's all nonsense, there's nothing of the kind. But what awaits us tomorrow? A hundred million most diverse chances that will be decided in an instant by whether our men or theirs run or don't run, and whether this man or that man is killed. Everything being done now is just play. The fact is that those men you've been riding around the position with don't just fail to help—they actually hinder. They're only concerned with their own petty interests."

"At such a moment!" Prince Andrew repeated. "To them it's only a moment affording opportunities to undermine a rival and earn an extra cross or ribbon. For me, tomorrow means this: a Russian army of a hundred thousand and a French army of a hundred thousand have met to fight, and the point is that these two hundred thousand men will fight, and whichever side fights more fiercely and spares itself less will win. And if you want to know: whatever happens, whatever blunders those at the top may make, we will win tomorrow's battle. Tomorrow, happen what may, we will win!"
"The war must be extended widely. I cannot sufficiently commend that view," said one of them (in German).

"Oh, yes," said the other (in German), "the only aim is to weaken the enemy, so of course one cannot take into account the loss of private individuals."

"Oh, no," agreed the other (in German).

"Yes, yes," answered Prince Andrew absently. "One thing I would do if I had the power," he began again, "I would not take prisoners. Why take prisoners? It's chivalry! The French have destroyed my home and are on their way to destroy Moscow; they have outraged and continue to outrage me every moment. They are my enemies. In my view they are all criminals. And Timokhin thinks so too, and the whole army. They should be executed! Since they are my enemies, they cannot be my friends, whatever may have been said at Tilsit."

"If there were none of this magnanimity in war, we would go to war only when it was worth going to certain death, as now. Then there would be no war because some Paul Ivanovich had offended some Michael Ivanovich. And when there was a war like this one, it would be real war! And then the determination of the troops would be completely different. Then all these Westphalians and Hessians whom Napoleon is dragging along would not follow him into Russia, and we would not go fight in Austria and Prussia without knowing why. War is not a polite game but the most horrible thing in life; and we ought to understand that and not play at it. We ought to accept this terrible necessity sternly and seriously. It all comes down to this: get rid of the falsehood and let war be war and not a game. As it is now, war is the favorite pastime of the idle and frivolous. The military profession is the most highly honored."

"But what is war? What is needed for success in warfare? What are the habits of the military? The aim of war is murder; the methods of war are spying, treachery, and their encouragement, the ruin of a country's inhabitants, robbing them or stealing to feed the army, and fraud and falsehood called military craft. The habits of the military class are the absence of freedom—that is, discipline—plus idleness, ignorance, cruelty, debauchery, and drunkenness. And in spite of all this, it is the highest class, respected by everyone. All the kings except the Chinese wear military uniforms, and the man who kills the most people gets the highest rewards."

For some time he stood in silence, wondering whether he should follow him or go away. "No, he doesn't want it!" Pierre decided. "And I know that this is our last meeting!" He sighed deeply and rode back to Gorki.

He closed his eyes. One image succeeded another in his imagination. On one of them he dwelt long and joyfully. He vividly recalled an evening in Petersburg. Natasha, with an animated, excited face, was telling him how she had gone looking for mushrooms the previous summer and had gotten lost in the big forest. She described the depths of the forest, her feelings, and a conversation with a beekeeper she met, incoherently and constantly interrupting her story to say: "No, I can't! I'm not telling it right; no, you don't understand," though he encouraged her by saying that he did understand, and he really had understood all she wanted to say. But Natasha was not satisfied with her own words: she felt they didn't convey the passionately poetic feeling she had experienced that day and wished to convey. "He was such a delightful old man, and it was so dark in the forest... and he had such kind... No, I can't describe it," she had said, flushed and excited. Prince Andrew smiled now the same happy smile as he had then when he looked into her eyes. "I understood her," he thought. "I not only understood her, but it was that inner, spiritual force—that sincerity, that openness of soul—that very soul of hers, which seemed bound by her body—it was that soul I loved in her... loved so deeply and happily..." and suddenly he remembered how his love had ended. "He didn't need anything like that. He neither saw nor understood anything of the kind. He only saw in her a pretty, fresh young girl with whom he didn't deign to join his fate. And I?... and he is still alive and happy!"

The original Russian line along the river Kolocha had been disrupted by the capture of the Shevardino Redoubt on the twenty-fourth, and part of the line—the left flank—had been pulled back. That part was not entrenched, and in front of it the ground was more open and level than elsewhere. It was obvious to anyone, military or civilian, that this was where the French should attack. It would seem that no great deliberation was needed to reach this conclusion, nor any particular care or trouble on the part of the Emperor and his marshals, nor was there any need of that special and supreme quality called genius which people are so ready to attribute to Napoleon; yet the historians who described the event later, and the men who surrounded Napoleon at the time, and Napoleon himself, all thought otherwise.

Napoleon rode across the plain, surveyed the terrain with a profound air and in silence, nodded approvingly or shook his head dubiously, and without explaining to the generals around him the deep course of reasoning behind his decisions, merely gave them his final conclusions as commands. Having heard a suggestion from Davout (now called the Prince of Eckmühl) to turn the Russian left wing, Napoleon said it should not be done, without explaining why. General Compans (who was to attack the flèches) proposed leading his division through the woods, and Napoleon agreed. The so-called Duke of Elchingen (Ney), though, ventured to remark that a move through the woods was dangerous and might throw the division into disorder.

After inspecting the terrain opposite the Shevardino Redoubt, Napoleon pondered briefly in silence and then indicated where two batteries should be set up by the morrow to act against the Russian entrenchments, and where the field artillery should be positioned in line with them.
After giving these and other orders, he returned to his tent, and the dispositions for the battle were written down from his dictation.
At dawn the two new batteries established during the night on the plain occupied by the Prince of Eckmühl will open fire on the opposing batteries of the enemy.

At the same time the commander of the artillery of the 1st Corps, General Pernetti, with thirty cannon of Compans's division and all the howitzers of Dessaix's and Friant's divisions, will move forward, open fire, and overwhelm with shellfire the enemy's battery, against which will operate:

The commander of the artillery of the 3rd Corps, General Fouché, will place the howitzers of the 3rd and 8th Corps, sixteen in all, on the flanks of the battery that is to bombard the entrenchment on the left, which will have forty guns in all directed against it.

The Viceroy will occupy the village and cross by its three bridges, advancing to the same heights as Morand's and Gérard's divisions, which under his command will be directed against the redoubt and fall into line with the rest of the forces.
All this must be done in good order (le tout se fera avec ordre et méthode), retaining troops in reserve as far as possible.
September 6, 1812 (New Style).

These dispositions, which are very obscure and confused if one allows oneself to regard the arrangements without religious awe of Napoleon's genius, related to Napoleon's orders to deal with four points—four different orders. Not one of them was, or could be, carried out.

The dispositions say first that the batteries placed at the spot Napoleon chose, together with Pernetti's and Fouché's guns, which were to come in line with them, 102 guns in all, were to open fire and shower shells on the Russian flèches and redoubts. This could not be done, because from the spots Napoleon selected, the projectiles did not carry to the Russian works, and those 102 guns fired into the air until the nearest commander, contrary to Napoleon's instructions, moved them forward.

The second order was that Poniatowski, advancing on the village through the wood, should turn the Russian left flank. This could not be done and was not done, because Poniatowski, advancing on the village through the wood, met Tuchkov there blocking his way, and could not and did not turn the Russian position.

The third order was: General Compans will move through the wood to seize the first fortification. Compans's division did not seize the first fortification but was driven back, because on emerging from the wood it had to re-form under grapeshot, of which Napoleon was unaware.

The fourth order was: The Viceroy will occupy the village (Borodino) and cross by its three bridges, advancing to the same heights as Morand's and Gérard's divisions (for whose movements no directions are given), which under his command will be directed against the redoubt and fall into line with the rest of the forces.

As far as one can make out—not so much from this unintelligible sentence as from the attempts of the Viceroy to execute the orders given him—he was to advance from the left through Borodino to the redoubt while Morand's and Gérard's divisions advanced simultaneously from the front.

All of this, like the other parts of the disposition, was not and could not be executed. After passing through Borodino, the Viceroy was driven back to the Kolocha and could get no farther; while Morand's and Gérard's divisions did not take the redoubt but were beaten back, and the redoubt was only captured at the end of the battle by cavalry (something probably unforeseen and unheard of by Napoleon). So not one of the orders in the disposition was, or could be, carried out. But the dispositions state that after the fight begins in this manner, orders will be given according to the enemy's movements—and so it might be supposed that Napoleon would make all necessary adjustments during the battle. But this was not and could not be done, because throughout the entire battle Napoleon was so far away that (as later became clear) he could not know the course of the battle, and not one of his orders during the fight could be carried out.

The more the Russian army retreated, the more fiercely a spirit of hatred for the enemy flared up, and as it fell back, the army grew and consolidated. At Borodino, a collision occurred. Neither army was shattered, but the Russian army retreated immediately after the clash — as inevitably as a ball recoils after striking another that carries greater momentum. And with equal inevitability, the ball of the invasion, which had advanced with such momentum, rolled on for some distance, even though the collision had stripped it of all its power.

The Russians retreated eighty miles — beyond Moscow — and the French reached Moscow, where they came to a standstill. For five weeks there was not a single battle. The French didn't move. Like a bleeding, mortally wounded animal licking its wounds, they remained inert in Moscow for five weeks. Then suddenly, for no fresh reason, they fled back — dashing for the Kaluga road, and after a victory (at Malo-Yaroslavets, where the field of battle again remained theirs) without fighting a single serious engagement, they fled even faster toward Smolensk, beyond Smolensk, beyond the Berezina, beyond Vilna, and farther still.

On the evening of August 26, Kutuzov and the entire Russian army were convinced that the Battle of Borodino was a victory. Kutuzov reported this to the Emperor. He gave orders to prepare for a fresh battle to finish off the enemy, and did so not to deceive anyone but because he knew the enemy had been beaten — as everyone who had taken part in the battle knew.

It was impossible to fight before information was gathered, the wounded collected, ammunition supplies replenished, the dead counted, new officers appointed to replace those killed, and the men had eaten and slept. And meanwhile, the very next morning, the French army advanced on its own, carried forward by its own momentum, which seemed now to be growing in inverse proportion to the square of the distance from its goal. Kutuzov wanted to attack the next day, and the whole army wanted the same. But wanting to attack is not enough — there must also be the possibility of doing so, and that possibility did not exist. It was impossible not to retreat one day's march, and then in the same way it was impossible not to retreat another day's march, and a third, and at last, on September 1, when the army drew near Moscow — despite the powerful feelings that had risen in every rank — circumstances forced it to retreat beyond Moscow. And the troops made one final day's march and abandoned Moscow to the enemy.

For people accustomed to thinking that campaign plans and battles are made by generals — as any of us, sitting over a map in a study, can imagine how we'd have arranged things in this or that battle — certain questions arise: Why didn't Kutuzov do this or that during the retreat? Why didn't he take up a position before reaching Fili? Why didn't he retreat at once by the Kaluga road, abandoning Moscow? And so on. People who think this way forget, or don't know, the inevitable constraints that always limit any commander in chief. The activity of a commander in chief bears no resemblance to what we imagine when sitting comfortably at our desks studying a campaign on a map, with known numbers of troops on each side in a known location, starting from a given moment. A commander in chief never deals with the beginning of any event — the starting point from which we always view it. He is always in the midst of a series of shifting events, and at no moment can he grasp the full significance of what is happening. From moment to moment the event takes shape imperceptibly, and at every moment of this continuous, uninterrupted shaping of events the commander in chief finds himself in the midst of a most complex web of intrigues, worries, contingencies, authorities, projects, counsels, threats, and deceptions, constantly forced to respond to countless questions that conflict with one another.

A commander in chief's job might seem to be simply choosing one of these proposals. But he cannot even do that. Events and time do not wait. For instance, on the twenty-eighth it is suggested to him that he cross to the Kaluga road, but just then an adjutant gallops up from Miloradovich asking whether to engage the French or retreat. An order must be given him at once, that instant. And the order to retreat carries us past the turn to the Kaluga road. After the adjutant comes the commissary general asking where the stores are to be taken, then the head of hospitals asking where to send the wounded, then a courier from Petersburg with a letter from the sovereign refusing to contemplate abandoning Moscow. The commander in chief's rival — the man undermining him (and there are always several such men, not just one) — presents a new plan diametrically opposed to the Kaluga road idea. The commander in chief himself needs sleep and refreshment to maintain his energy. A respected general overlooked in the distribution of awards comes to complain. Local residents beg for protection. An officer sent to inspect the area comes in and gives a report quite contrary to what was said by the officer previously sent; and a spy, a prisoner, and a general back from reconnaissance all describe the enemy's position differently. People accustomed to misunderstanding or forgetting these inevitable constraints describe, for instance, the army's position at Fili and assume the commander in chief could freely decide on September 1 whether to abandon or defend Moscow — whereas with the Russian army less than four miles away, no such question existed. When had it been decided? At the Drissa camp, at Smolensk, and most clearly of all on August 24 at the Shevardino Redoubt and the twenty-sixth at Borodino, and every day, hour, and minute of the retreat from Borodino to Fili.

A few days later, at one of those enchanting parties Helene gave at her country house on the Stone Island, the charming Monsieur de Jobert — a man no longer young, with snow-white hair and brilliant black eyes, a Jesuit in lay clothing — was introduced to her. In the garden, by the light of the illuminations and to the sound of music, he spoke to her at length about the love of God, of Christ, of the Sacred Heart, and of the consolations offered by the one true Catholic faith in this world and the next. Helene was moved, and more than once tears rose to her eyes and to Monsieur de Jobert's, and their voices trembled. A dance, for which her partner came to claim her, ended her discourse with her future spiritual director, but Monsieur de Jobert came to see Helene again the next evening when she was alone, and after that he visited often.

Helene understood that the question was very simple and easy from the Church's point of view, and that her spiritual directors were creating difficulties only because they feared how the secular authorities would react.

So she decided to prepare public opinion. She provoked the jealousy of the elderly magnate and told him what she had told the other suitor — that the only way for him to have a claim on her was to marry her. The elderly magnate was at first just as startled by the suggestion of marrying a woman whose husband was still alive as the younger man had been, but Helene's unshakable conviction that it was as simple and natural as marrying a maiden had its effect on him too. Had Helene herself shown the slightest sign of hesitation, shame, or secrecy, her cause would certainly have been lost; but not only did she show no such signs — on the contrary, with good-natured naïveté she told her close friends (which meant all of Petersburg) that both the prince and the magnate had proposed, and that she loved both and was afraid of hurting either.

A rumor immediately spread through Petersburg — not that Helene wanted to divorce her husband (had such a report spread, many would have opposed so illegal an intention), but simply that the unfortunate and interesting Helene was in doubt which of the two men she should marry. The question was no longer whether this was possible, but only which was the better match and how the court would view it. There were, admittedly, some rigid individuals unable to rise to the height of such a question, who saw the scheme as a desecration of the sacrament of marriage, but there weren't many, and they kept quiet. The majority were interested in Helene's good fortune and in the question of which match would be more advantageous. Whether it was right or wrong to remarry while one's husband was living, they did not discuss — that question had obviously been settled by people "wiser than you or me," as they said, and to doubt that decision was to risk exposing one's own stupidity and incapacity to live in society.

Only Marya Dmitrievna Akhrosimova, who had come to Petersburg that summer to visit one of her sons, allowed herself plainly to express an opinion contrary to the general one. Meeting Helene at a ball, she stopped her in the middle of the room and, amid general silence, said in her gruff voice: "So wives of living men have started marrying again! Maybe you think you've invented something new? You've been beaten to it, my dear! It was thought of long ago. It's done in all the brothels." And with those words, Marya Dmitrievna rolled up her wide sleeves with her usual threatening gesture, glanced sternly around, and moved across the room.
Prince Vasili, who lately often forgot what he'd said and repeated the same thing a hundred times, remarked to his daughter whenever he happened to see her:

"You're not catching me off guard, you know," he said. "As a true friend, I've thought and thought about your situation. You see, if you marry the prince" — he meant the younger man, and he crooked one finger — "you lose forever the chance of marrying the other, and you'll displease the court besides. (You know there's some sort of connection.) But if you marry the old count, you'll make his last days happy, and as widow of the Grand... the prince would no longer be making a mésalliance by marrying you." And Bilibin smoothed out his forehead.

"That's a true friend!" said Helene, beaming, and she touched Bilibin's sleeve again. "But I love them both, you know, and I don't want to hurt either. I would give my life for the happiness of both."
"A masterly woman!" (in French) "That's what is called putting things squarely. She would like to be married to all three at the same time," thought he.
* Une maîtresse-femme!
"But tell me, how will your husband view the matter?" Bilibin asked — his reputation was so well established that he didn't fear asking so naïve a question. "Will he agree?"
Bilibin puckered his skin in preparation for something witty.

"Oh, Mama, don't talk nonsense. You don't understand anything. In my position I have obligations," Helene said (in French), switching from Russian — in which language she always felt her case didn't sound quite clear — to French, which suited it better.
* Ah, Maman, ne dites pas de bêtises. Vous ne comprenez rien. Dans ma position j'ai des devoirs.
Just then the lady companion who lived with Helene came in to announce that His Highness was in the ballroom and wished to see her.
"No, tell him I don't wish to see him. I am furious with him for not keeping his word to me." (in French)
* Non, dites-lui que je ne veux pas le voir, que je suis furieuse contre lui, parce qu'il m'a manqué parole.
"Countess, there is mercy for every sin," said (in French) a fair-haired young man with a long face and nose as he entered the room.
* Comtesse, à tout péché miséricorde.

By the beginning of August, Helene's affairs were clearly defined, and she wrote a letter to her husband — who, she imagined, loved her very much — informing him of her intention to marry N.N. and of her conversion to the one true faith, and asking him to complete all the formalities necessary for a divorce, which would be explained to him by the letter's bearer.

Berg, the Rostovs' son-in-law, was already a colonel wearing the decorations of the Order of Vladimir and the Order of Anna, and still held his quiet, agreeable post as assistant to the head of staff of the assistant commander of the First Division of the Second Army.

He had nothing to do in Moscow, but he'd noticed that everyone in the army was requesting leave to go there, each with something to attend to. So he felt it necessary to request leave too, for family and domestic reasons.
From the anteroom Berg ran with smooth though impatient steps into the drawing room, embraced the count, kissed the hands of Natasha and Sonya, and rushed to ask about "Mamma's" health.

"Only God Almighty can decide the fate of our fatherland, Papa," said Berg. "The army is burning with heroic spirit and the leaders have, so to speak, now assembled in council. No one knows what's coming. But in general I can tell you, Papa, that such a heroic spirit, the truly ancient valor of the Russian army, which they — which it" — he corrected himself — "has shown or displayed in the battle of the twenty-sixth — there are no words worthy of it! I tell you, Papa" — he smote his breast as a general he'd heard speaking had done, though Berg did it slightly late, since the gesture should have accompanied the words "Russian army" — "I tell you frankly that we, the commanders, far from having to urge the men on or anything of that kind, could hardly restrain those... those... yes, those exploits of antique valor," he went on rapidly. "General Barclay de Tolly risked his life everywhere at the head of the troops, I assure you. Our corps was positioned on a hillside. You can imagine!"

And Berg recounted everything he remembered from the various stories he'd heard in recent days. Natasha watched him with an intent gaze that confused him, as if she were trying to find in his face the answer to some question.

Just then the countess came in from the sitting room with a weary, discontented expression. Berg hurriedly jumped up, kissed her hand, asked about her health, and, tilting his head from side to side to express sympathy, remained standing beside her.
"Yes, Mamma, I tell you honestly, these are difficult and sad times for every Russian. But why are you so worried? You still have time to get away..."

"I can't imagine what the servants are doing," said the countess, turning to her husband. "I've just been told nothing is ready. Someone has to take charge. One misses Mitenka, the steward, at times like these. There'll be no end to it."

"I was driving past Yusupov's house just now," Berg said with a laugh, "when the steward — a man I know — ran out and asked if I wanted to buy something. I went in out of curiosity, and there's a small chiffonier — a chest of drawers — and a dressing table. You know how dear Vera wanted a chiffonier like that, and how we argued about it." (At the mention of the chiffonier and dressing table, Berg's tone involuntarily shifted to one of pleasure at his admirable domestic arrangements.) "And it's such a beauty! It pulls out and has a secret English drawer, you know! Vera has wanted one for ages. I'd love to surprise her. I noticed all those peasant carts in your yard. Could you let me have one? I'll pay the man well, and..."
"Yes, Mamma! Yes, these are very hard times!" said Berg.
"I think," Natasha nearly shouted, turning her furious face toward Petya, "I think it's so horrid, so vile, so... I don't know what! Are we despicable Germans?"

Berg was sitting beside the countess, consoling her with the respectful attentiveness of a relative. The count, pipe in hand, was pacing up and down the room, when Natasha burst in like a storm, her face distorted with rage, and rushed up to her mother.
"Mamma, it's impossible — look what's going on in the yard!" she cried. "They'll be left behind!"

"The wounded! It's impossible, Mamma — it's monstrous! No, Mamma darling, it's not right. Please forgive me, darling. Mamma, what does it matter what we take? Just look at what's going on out there... Mamma! It's impossible!"
The count stood by the window, listening, without turning around. Suddenly he sniffed and put his face closer to the window.
"Mamma, darling — forgive me!"
"The eggs... the eggs are teaching the hen," the count muttered through tears of joy, and he embraced his wife, who was glad to hide her look of shame on his breast.
"Papa! Mamma! May I take charge? May I?" asked Natasha. "We'll still take all the most essential things."

The servants gathered around Natasha but couldn't believe the strange order she brought until the count himself, in his wife's name, confirmed it: give up all the carts to the wounded and put the trunks in the storerooms. When they understood, the servants set about this new task with pleasure and enthusiasm. It no longer seemed strange to them but on the contrary it seemed the only thing that could be done, just as a quarter of an hour before it had not seemed strange to anyone that the wounded should be left behind and the goods carted away, but that had seemed the only thing to do.

The whole household, as if to make up for not having done it sooner, threw themselves eagerly into the new work of getting the wounded into the carts. The wounded dragged themselves out of their rooms and stood with pale but happy faces around the carts. The news that carts were to be had spread to the neighboring houses, from which wounded men began to come into the Rostovs' yard. Many asked not to have the carts unloaded but only to be allowed to sit on top of the luggage. But the unloading, once started, couldn't be stopped. It seemed not to matter whether half or all the belongings were left behind. Cases of china, bronzes, pictures, and mirrors that had been so carefully packed the night before now lay about the yard, and still they went on searching for and finding possibilities of unloading this or that and letting the wounded have another and yet another cart.

They unloaded the wardrobe cart and sent it to pick up wounded from a house two doors down. The whole household, servants included, was bright and animated. Natasha was in a state of rapturous excitement she hadn't known for a long time.
The phaeton was packed with people, and there was some question about where Count Peter would sit.

"That Asian city of countless churches — holy Moscow! Here it is at last, that famous city. It was high time," he said (in French), and dismounting, he ordered a map of Moscow spread before him and summoned his interpreter, Lelorgne d'Ideville.
* Cette ville asiatique aux innombrables églises, Moscou la sainte. La voilà donc enfin, cette fameuse ville! Il était temps.
"Bring the boyars to me," he said (in French) to his entourage.
* Qu'on m'amène les boyars.

He was carried away by the tone of magnanimity he planned to adopt toward Moscow. In his mind he set dates for assemblies at the Tsar's palace where Russian dignitaries and his own people would mingle. He mentally appointed a governor, one who would win the people's hearts. Knowing there were many charitable institutions in Moscow, he decided he would shower them all with favors. He thought that just as in Africa he had worn a burnoose and sat in a mosque, so in Moscow he must be beneficent like the Tsars. And to touch the hearts of the Russians — and being, like all Frenchmen, unable to imagine anything sentimental without a reference to his dear, tender, poor mother (in French) — he decided to place an inscription on every institution: "Dedicated to my dear mother." Or no, simply: "House of My Mother," he concluded. "But am I really in Moscow? Yes, here it lies before me — but why is the city delegation taking so long?" he wondered.
* Ma chère, ma tendre, ma pauvre mère.
* (2) Maison de ma Mère.

From an unfinished building on Varvarka Street — its ground floor a tavern — came drunken shouts and singing. On benches around the tables in a dirty little room sat about ten factory workers. Tipsy and sweating, with glazed eyes and wide-open mouths, they were all laboring to sing some song or other — singing discordantly, straining, with great effort, clearly not because they wanted to sing but to prove they were drunk and having a good time. One of them — a tall, fair-haired young man in a clean blue coat — stood over the others. His face, with its fine straight nose, would have been handsome if not for his thin, compressed, twitching lips and dull, gloomy, fixed eyes. Clearly possessed by some idea, he stood over the singers, solemnly and jerkily waving his white arm — its sleeve rolled up to the elbow — above their heads, trying to spread his dirty fingers in an unnatural way. The sleeve kept slipping down, and he always carefully rolled it up again with his left hand, as if it were most important that this sinewy white arm be bare. In the midst of the song cries were heard, and fighting and blows in the passage and porch. The tall young man waved his arm.

The factory workers followed him. These men, who under the tall fellow's leadership were drinking in the tavern that morning, had brought the publican some skins from the factory and in return had been served drinks. Blacksmiths from a neighboring smithy, hearing the sounds of revelry and assuming the tavern had been broken into, tried to force their way in too, and a fight at the door had resulted.
The lad with the turned-up sleeve gave the smith a blow in the face and shouted wildly: "They're fighting us, boys!"
"Oh, gracious me, a man beaten to death — killed!..." screamed a woman coming out of a gate nearby.
"Murderer!" he suddenly shouted at the publican. "Bind him, boys!"
"I daresay you would like to bind me!" the publican shouted, pushing away the men advancing on him, and snatching his cap from his head, he flung it to the ground.
"I know the law perfectly well, friends! I'll take this to the police captain. You think I can't reach him? Robbery is not permitted to anybody nowadays!" the publican shouted, picking up his cap.

At the corner of Moroseyka Street, opposite a large house with closed shutters that bore a bootmaker's sign, stood a score of thin, worn-out, gloomy-faced bootmakers in overalls and long, tattered coats.
"He should pay his workers properly," a thin workingman with a furrowed brow and scraggly beard was saying.
Seeing the crowd and the bloodied man, the workman ceased speaking, and with eager curiosity all the bootmakers joined the moving crowd.
"I say, is it true that we have been beaten?" "And what did you think? Look what folks are saying."
Questions and answers were heard. The publican, taking advantage of the growing crowd, dropped back and returned to his tavern.

"Why talk nonsense?" voices in the crowd replied. "Will they just hand over Moscow like that? They told you that as a joke and you believed it! Aren't there plenty of troops on the march? Let him in, indeed! That's what the government is for. You'd better listen to what people are saying," said some in the mob, pointing at the tall young man.
By the wall of China-Town, a district of Moscow, a smaller group had gathered around a man in a frieze coat who held a paper in his hand.
"A decree, they are reading a decree! Reading a decree!" voices cried, and the crowd rushed toward the reader.

The man in the frieze coat was reading the broadsheet of August 31. When the crowd gathered around him he seemed flustered, but at the demand of the tall young man, who had pushed his way to the front, he began in a rather trembling voice to read the sheet from the beginning.

"Early tomorrow I shall go to his Serene Highness," he read. ("Sirin Highness," said the tall fellow with a triumphant smile on his lips and a frown on his brow.) "— to consult with him, to act, and to aid the army to exterminate these scoundrels. We too shall take part..." the reader continued, then paused. ("See?" the young man shouted victoriously. "He's going to sort the whole thing out for you!") "...in destroying them, and will send these visitors to the devil. I shall come back for dinner, and we'll get to work. We will deal with them, completely deal with and undo these scoundrels."

The superintendent of police — who had gone that morning, on Rostopchin's orders, to burn the barges and had in connection with that errand acquired a large sum of money now sitting in his pocket — on seeing the crowd bearing down on him, told his coachman to stop.
"The count has not left — he is here — and an order will be issued concerning you," said the superintendent. "Go on!" he ordered his coachman.
The superintendent of police turned around at that moment with a frightened look, said something to his coachman, and his horses picked up speed.

"It's a fraud, boys! Take us to the man himself!" shouted the tall young man. "Don't let him go, boys! Let him answer us! Hold him!" shouted various voices, and the crowd dashed in pursuit of the carriage.

The French attributed the Fire of Moscow to the ferocious patriotism of Rostopchin (in French); the Russians blamed the barbarity of the French. In reality, however, the burning of Moscow could not be attributed to any individual or any group of people. Moscow burned because it found itself in a position where any town built of wood was bound to burn, quite apart from whether it had a hundred and thirty inferior fire engines or not. Deserted Moscow had to burn as inevitably as a heap of shavings must burn when sparks continuously fall on it for several days. A town built of wood, where fires break out almost daily even when homeowners are present and a police force is maintained, cannot help burning when its inhabitants have left and it is occupied by soldiers who smoke pipes, make campfires of Senate chairs in the Senate Square, and cook themselves meals twice a day. In peacetime, merely billeting troops in the villages of any district immediately increases the number of fires. How much more must the probability of fire increase in an abandoned, wooden town occupied by foreign troops? "The ferocious patriotism of Rostopchin" and the barbarity of the French were not to blame. Moscow was set on fire by soldiers' pipes, kitchens, and campfires, and by the carelessness of enemy soldiers occupying houses they did not own. Even if there was any arson (which is very doubtful, since no one had any reason to burn the houses—in any case a troublesome and dangerous thing to do), arson cannot be regarded as the cause, for the same thing would have happened without it.
* Au patriotisme féroce de Rostopchíne.

He had left home only to escape the complicated tangle of life's demands that enmeshed him, and which in his present condition he was unable to sort out. He had gone to Joseph Alexeevich's house on the pretext of organizing the deceased's books and papers, but really in search of rest from life's turmoil, for in his mind the memory of Joseph Alexeevich was connected with a world of eternal, solemn, and calm thoughts, quite opposite to the restless confusion into which he felt himself being drawn. He sought a quiet refuge, and in Joseph Alexeevich's study he really found it. When he sat with his elbows on the dusty writing table in the deathlike stillness of the study, calm and significant memories of the last few days rose one after another in his imagination, particularly the battle of Borodino and that vague sense of his own insignificance and insincerity compared with the truth, simplicity, and strength of the class of men he mentally classed as "they." When Gerasim roused him from his reverie, the idea occurred to him of taking part in the popular defense of Moscow, which he knew was being planned. With that aim he had asked Gerasim to get him a peasant's coat and a pistol, and had confided his intentions of remaining in Joseph Alexeevich's house and keeping his name secret. Then during the first day spent in inaction and solitude (he tried several times to concentrate on the Masonic manuscripts but couldn't), the idea that had previously occurred to him of the hidden meaning he had found in his own name set against Bonaparte's more than once vaguely presented itself. But the idea that he, L'russe Besuhof, was destined to set a limit to the power of the Beast was as yet only one of those fancies that often passed through his mind and left no trace.

The next day, focused solely on not sparing himself and not lagging behind them, Pierre went to the Three Hills gate. But when he returned to the house, convinced that Moscow would not be defended, he suddenly felt that what had previously seemed merely a possibility had now become absolutely necessary and inevitable. He must remain in Moscow, conceal his name, meet Napoleon, and kill him—either perishing himself or putting an end to the misery of all Europe, which seemed to him entirely due to Napoleon.

"Yes, alone, for the sake of all, I must do it or die!" he thought. "Yes, I will approach... and then suddenly... with pistol or dagger? But that doesn't matter! 'It is not I but the hand of Providence that punishes thee,' I shall say," thought he, imagining what he would say when killing Napoleon. "Well then, take me and execute me!" he went on, speaking to himself and bowing his head with a sad but determined expression.
"Good day, everybody!" he said (in French) gaily, smiling and looking about him.
* Bonjour, la compagnie!
"Are you the master here?" the officer asked Gerasim (in French).
* Vous êtes le bourgeois?
* Quartier, quartier, logement! Les français sont de bons enfants. Que diable! Voyons! Ne nous fâchons pas, mon vieux!

"Bah, really? So much the better! You are certainly brave enemies. The great redoubt held out well, by my pipe!" continued the Frenchman. "And you made us pay dearly for it. I was at it three times—I swear it. Three times we reached the guns and three times we were thrown back like cardboard figures. Oh, it was magnificent, Monsieur Pierre! Your grenadiers were superb, by heaven! I saw them close up their ranks six times in a row and march as if on parade. Wonderful men! Our King of Naples, who knows what's what, cried 'Bravo!' Ha, ha! So you are one of us soldiers!" he added, smiling, after a momentary pause. "So much the better, so much the better, Monsieur Pierre! Terrible in battle... gallant with the ladies" (he winked and smiled), "that's what the French are, Monsieur Pierre, isn't it?"

The captain was so naïvely and good-humoredly cheerful, so genuine, and so pleased with himself that Pierre almost winked back as he looked merrily at him. Probably the word "gallant" turned the captain's thoughts to the state of Moscow.
"Is he in Moscow?" Pierre stammered with a guilty look.

Thus the captain touchingly recounted the story of his love for a fascinating marquise of thirty-five and at the same time for a charming, innocent child of seventeen—the bewitching marquise's daughter. The conflict of magnanimity between mother and daughter, ending in the mother sacrificing herself and offering her daughter in marriage to her lover, still moved the captain, though it was a distant memory. Then he recounted an episode in which the husband played the part of the lover and he—the lover—played the part of the husband, as well as several amusing incidents from his time in Germany, where "shelter" is called Unterkunft and where the husbands eat sauerkraut and the young girls are "too blonde."

Finally, the most recent episode—in Poland, still fresh in the captain's memory—which he narrated with rapid gestures and a glowing face, was of how he had saved the life of a Pole (in general, the saving of lives continually occurred in the captain's stories) and the Pole had entrusted to him his enchanting wife (a Parisian at heart) while himself entering the French service. The captain was happy, the enchanting Polish lady wished to elope with him, but, prompted by magnanimity, the captain restored the wife to the husband, saying as he did so: "I have saved your life, and I save your honor!" Having repeated these words, the captain wiped his eyes and gave himself a shake, as if driving away the weakness that overcame him at this touching recollection.
"You can't pass!" cried a voice (in French).
* On ne passe pas!
"Look here, no nonsense!" he cried (in French).
* Voyons, pas de bêtises!

In Petersburg at that time, a complicated struggle was being carried on with greater heat than ever in the highest circles—between the parties of Rumyantsev, the French, Marya Fedorovna, the Tsarevich (heir to the throne), and others—drowned as usual by the buzzing of the court drones. But the calm, luxurious life of Petersburg, concerned only with phantoms and reflections of real life, went on as before, and it took great effort to realize the danger and the difficult position of the Russian people. There were the same receptions and balls, the same French theater, the same court interests and service interests and intrigues as usual. Only in the very highest circles were attempts made to keep the true difficulty of the situation in mind. Stories were whispered about how differently the two empresses were behaving in these difficult circumstances. Empress Marya, concerned for the welfare of the charitable and educational institutions under her patronage, had ordered them all moved to Kazan, and the things belonging to these institutions had already been packed up. Empress Elisabeth, however, when asked what instructions she would be pleased to give—with her characteristic Russian patriotism—had replied that she could give no directions about state institutions, as that was the sovereign's affair, but as far as she personally was concerned, she would be the last to leave Petersburg.

At Anna Pavlovna's on the twenty-sixth of August—the very day of the battle of Borodino—there was an evening party, the chief feature of which was to be the reading of a letter from His Lordship the Bishop sending the Emperor an icon of the Venerable Sergius. It was considered a model of ecclesiastical, patriotic eloquence. Prince Vasili himself, famous for his delivery, was to read it. (He used to read at the Empress's.) The art of his reading was supposed to lie in rolling out the words, quite independently of their meaning, in a loud and singsong voice alternating between a despairing wail and a tender murmur, so that the wail fell randomly on one word and the murmur on another. This reading, as was always the case at Anna Pavlovna's parties, had a political significance. That evening she expected several important personages who had to be made ashamed of their visits to the French theater and aroused to a patriotic spirit. A good many people had already arrived, but Anna Pavlovna, not yet seeing everyone she wanted in her drawing room, did not let the reading begin but wound up the springs of general conversation.

The news of the day in Petersburg was the illness of Countess Bezukhova. She had fallen ill unexpectedly a few days before, had missed several gatherings where she was usually the ornament, and was said to be receiving no one. Instead of the famous Petersburg doctors who usually attended her, she had entrusted herself to some Italian doctor who was treating her with some new and unusual method.

Everyone knew perfectly well that the enchanting countess's illness arose from an inconvenience resulting from having married two husbands at the same time, and that the Italian's cure consisted of removing that inconvenience; but in Anna Pavlovna's presence no one dared to think of this, or even appear to know it.

"You are speaking of the poor countess?" said Anna Pavlovna, coming up just then. "I sent to ask for news, and hear that she is a little better. Oh, she is certainly the most charming woman in the world," she went on, with a smile at her own enthusiasm. "We belong to different camps, but that does not prevent my esteeming her as she deserves. She is very unfortunate!" added Anna Pavlovna.

And having thus demolished the young man, Anna Pavlovna turned to another group where Bilibin was talking about the Austrians. Having wrinkled up his face, he was evidently preparing to smooth it out again and utter one of his mots.

"I think it is delightful," he said, referring to a diplomatic note sent to Vienna with some Austrian banners captured from the French by the Russian general Wittgenstein, "the hero of Petropol" as he was then called in Petersburg.
"What? What's that?" asked Anna Pavlovna, securing silence for the mot, which she had heard before.

"The path to Warsaw, perhaps," Prince Hippolyte remarked loudly and unexpectedly. Everybody looked at him, understanding what he meant. Prince Hippolyte himself glanced around with amused surprise. He knew no more than the others what his words meant. During his diplomatic career he had more than once noticed that such remarks were received as very witty, and at every opportunity he uttered in that way the first words that entered his head. "It may turn out very well," he thought, "but if not, they'll know how to handle it." And indeed, during the awkward silence that followed, the insufficiently patriotic person whom Anna Pavlovna had been waiting for and wished to convert entered, and she, smiling and shaking a finger at Hippolyte, invited Prince Vasili to the table, brought him two candles and the manuscript, and begged him to begin. Everyone fell silent.

Bilibin attentively examined his nails, and many of those present appeared intimidated, as if asking in what they were to blame. Anna Pavlovna whispered the next words in advance, like an old woman murmuring the prayer at Communion: "Let the bold and insolent Goliath..." she whispered.

"Let the bold and insolent Goliath from the borders of France encompass the realms of Russia with death-bearing terrors; humble Faith, the sling of the Russian David, shall suddenly smite his head in his bloodthirsty pride. This icon of the Venerable Sergius, the servant of God and zealous champion of old of our country's weal, is offered to Your Imperial Majesty. I grieve that my waning strength prevents me from rejoicing in the sight of your most gracious presence. I raise fervent prayers to Heaven that the Almighty may exalt the race of the just, and mercifully fulfill the desires of Your Majesty."
"You will see," said Anna Pavlovna, "that tomorrow, on the Emperor's birthday, we shall receive news. I have a favorable presentiment!"

Anna Pavlovna's premonition was in fact fulfilled. Next day during the service at the palace church in honor of the Emperor's birthday, Prince Volkonsky was called out of the church and received a dispatch from Prince Kutuzov. It was Kutuzov's report, written from Tatarinova on the day of the battle. Kutuzov wrote that the Russians had not retreated a step, that the French losses were much heavier than ours, and that he was writing in haste from the field of battle before collecting full information. It followed that there must have been a victory. And at once, without leaving the church, thanks were given to the Creator for His help and for the victory.

It is very difficult for events to be reflected in their real strength and completeness amid the conditions of court life and far from the scene of action. General events involuntarily group themselves around some particular incident. So now the courtiers' pleasure was based as much on the fact that the news arrived on the Emperor's birthday as on the fact of the victory itself. It was like a successfully arranged surprise. Mention was made in Kutuzov's report of the Russian losses, among which figured the names of Tuchkov, Bagration, and Kutaysov. In the Petersburg world, this sad aspect of the affair again involuntarily centered around a single incident: the death of Kutaysov. Everybody knew him, the Emperor liked him, and he was young and interesting. That day everyone met with the words:
But the next day no news arrived from the army, and the public mood grew anxious. The courtiers suffered because of the suffering that the suspense was causing the Emperor.

"Imagine the Emperor's position!" they said, and instead of praising Kutuzov as they had the day before, they condemned him as the cause of the Emperor's anxiety. That day Prince Vasili no longer boasted of his protege Kutuzov but remained silent when the commander in chief was mentioned. Moreover, toward evening, as if everything conspired to make Petersburg society anxious and uneasy, a terrible piece of news was added. Countess Helene Bezukhova had suddenly died of that terrible malady it had been so agreeable to mention. Officially, at large gatherings, everyone said that Countess Bezukhova had died of a terrible attack of angina pectoris, but in intimate circles details were mentioned of how the Queen of Spain's private physician had prescribed small doses of a certain drug to produce a certain effect; but Helene, tormented by the fact that the old count suspected her and that her husband—to whom she had written (that wretched, dissolute Pierre)—had not replied, had suddenly taken a very large dose of the drug and had died in agony before help could be given. It was said that Prince Vasili and the old count had turned on the Italian, but the latter had produced such letters from the unfortunate deceased that they had immediately let the matter drop.

On the third day after Kutuzov's report, a country gentleman arrived from Moscow, and news of the surrender of Moscow to the French spread through the whole town. This was terrible! What a position for the Emperor to be in! Kutuzov was a traitor, and Prince Vasili, during the condolence visits paid to him on the occasion of his daughter Helene's death, said of Kutuzov—whom he had formerly praised (it was excusable for him in his grief to forget what he had said)—that nothing else could be expected from a blind and depraved old man.
On receiving this dispatch the Emperor sent Prince Volkonsky to Kutuzov with the following rescript:

Nine days after the abandonment of Moscow, a messenger from Kutuzov reached Petersburg with the official announcement of that event. This messenger was Michaud, a Frenchman who did not know Russian, but who was, as he said of himself (in French), "though a foreigner, Russian in heart and soul."
* Quoique étranger, russe de cœur et d'âme.

The Emperor at once received this messenger in his study at the palace on Stone Island. Michaud, who had never seen Moscow before the campaign and who did not know Russian, was nevertheless deeply moved (as he wrote) when he appeared before "our most gracious sovereign" (in French) with the news of the burning of Moscow, "whose flames illumined his route."
* Notre très gracieux souverain.
* (2) Dont les flammes éclairaient sa route.

Half of Russia had been conquered, the inhabitants were fleeing to distant provinces, and one levy after another was being raised for the defense of the fatherland. It is natural for those of us who did not live in those days to imagine that in such a time, all Russians, from greatest to least, were solely engaged in sacrificing themselves, saving their fatherland, or weeping over its downfall. The tales and descriptions of that time without exception speak only of the self-sacrifice, patriotic devotion, despair, grief, and heroism of the Russians. But it was not really so. It appears so to us because we see only the general historical interest of that time and do not see all the personal human interests that people had. Yet in reality those personal interests of the moment so much transcend the general interests that they always prevent the public interest from being felt or even noticed. Most of the people at that time paid no attention to the general course of events but were guided only by their private interests, and they were precisely the people whose activities in that period were most useful.

Those who tried to understand the general course of events and take part in it through self-sacrifice and heroism were the most useless members of society; they saw everything backward, and all they did for the common good turned out to be useless and foolish—like Pierre's and Mamonov's regiments which looted Russian villages, and the lint the young ladies prepared and that never reached the wounded, and so on. Even those who were fond of intellectual talk and of expressing their feelings, who discussed Russia's position at the time, involuntarily introduced into their conversations either a shade of pretense and falsehood or useless condemnation and anger directed against people accused of actions no one could possibly be guilty of. In historic events, the rule forbidding us to eat of the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge is especially applicable. Only unconscious action bears fruit, and the person who plays a part in a historic event never understands its significance. If he tries to understand it, his efforts are fruitless.

The more closely a person was involved in the events taking place in Russia, the less did he understand their significance. In Petersburg and in the provinces far from Moscow, ladies and gentlemen in militia uniforms wept for Russia and its ancient capital and talked of self-sacrifice and so on; but in the army, which had retreated beyond Moscow, there was little talk or thought of Moscow, and when they caught sight of its burned ruins no one swore to be avenged on the French. Instead they thought about their next pay, their next quarters, about Matreshka the vivandière, and similar matters.

Since the war had caught him in the service, Nicholas Rostov took a close and prolonged part in the defense of his country, but did so casually, without any aim at self-sacrifice, and he therefore looked at what was going on in Russia without despair and without dismally racking his brains over it. Had he been asked what he thought of the state of Russia, he would have said it was not his business to think about it, that Kutuzov and others were there for that, but that he had heard the regiments were to be made up to their full strength, that fighting would probably go on for a long time yet, and that given how things were, he might quite possibly be commanding a regiment in a couple of years.

Viewing the situation this way, he learned that he was being sent to Voronezh to buy remounts for his division—not only without regret at missing the coming battle, but with the greatest pleasure, which he made no attempt to hide and which his comrades fully understood.

The commander of the militia was a civilian general, an old man who was obviously pleased with his military title and rank. He received Nicholas brusquely (imagining this to be characteristically military) and questioned him with an important air, as if considering the general progress of affairs and approving and disapproving with full right to do so. Nicholas was in such good spirits that this merely amused him.
When he had changed, poured water over his head, and scented himself, Nicholas arrived at the governor's rather late, but with the phrase "better late than never" on his lips.

It was not a ball, nor had dancing been announced, but everyone knew that Catherine Petrovna would play waltzes and the ecossaise (a Scottish dance) on the clavichord (an early keyboard instrument), and that there would be dancing, and so everyone had come as to a ball.

There were a great many ladies and some of Nicholas's Moscow acquaintances, but there were no men who could at all compete with the cavalier of St. George, the hussar remount officer, the good-natured and well-bred Count Rostov. Among the men was an Italian prisoner, an officer of the French army; and Nicholas felt that the presence of this prisoner enhanced his own importance as a Russian hero. The Italian was, as it were, a war trophy. Nicholas felt this; it seemed to him that everyone regarded the Italian the same way, and he treated him cordially though with dignity and restraint.

As soon as Nicholas entered in his hussar uniform, spreading around him a fragrance of perfume and wine, and had uttered the words "better late than never" and heard them repeated several times by others, people clustered around him; all eyes turned on him, and he felt at once that he had entered his proper position in the province—that of a universal favorite: a very pleasant position, and intoxicatingly so after his long privations. At posting stations, at inns, and in the landowner's cozy den, maidservants had been flattered by his notice, and here too at the governor's party there were (as it seemed to Nicholas) an inexhaustible number of pretty young women, married and unmarried, impatiently awaiting his notice. The women and girls flirted with him, and from the very first day, the people concerned themselves to get this fine young daredevil of a hussar married and settled down. Among these was the governor's wife herself, who welcomed Rostov as a close relative and called him "Nicholas."

Catherine Petrovna did actually play waltzes and the ecossaise, and dancing began in which Nicholas further captivated provincial society with his agility. His particularly free manner of dancing even surprised them all. Nicholas was himself rather surprised at how he danced that evening. He had never danced like that in Moscow and would even have considered such a very free and easy manner improper and in bad form there, but here he felt it was his duty to astonish them all with something unusual, something they would have to accept as the standard in the capital, though new to them in the provinces.

All evening Nicholas paid attention to a blue-eyed, plump and pleasing little blonde, the wife of one of the provincial officials. With the naive conviction of young men in a merry mood that other men's wives were created for them, Rostov did not leave the lady's side and treated her husband in a friendly and conspiratorial manner, as if, without saying so, they both knew how perfectly Nicholas and the lady would get along. The husband, however, did not seem to share that conviction and tried to behave morosely with Rostov. But Nicholas's good-natured naïveté was so boundless that sometimes even the husband involuntarily yielded to his good humor. Toward the end of the evening, however, as the wife's face grew more flushed and animated, the husband's became more and more gloomy and solemn, as though there were but a given amount of animation between them—and as the wife's share increased, the husband's diminished.

The first two were convicts with shaven heads. One was tall and thin, the other dark, shaggy, and sinewy, with a flat nose. The third was a domestic serf, about forty-five years old, with graying hair and a plump, well-nourished body. The fourth was a peasant, a very handsome man with a broad, light-brown beard and black eyes. The fifth was a factory worker, a thin, sallow-faced boy of eighteen in a loose coat.

Pierre heard the French consulting whether to shoot them one at a time or in pairs. "In pairs," replied the officer in command in a calm voice. There was a stir in the ranks of the soldiers, and it was obvious they were all hurrying—not as men hurry to do something they understand, but as people hurry to finish a necessary but unpleasant and incomprehensible task.

Then two pairs of Frenchmen approached the criminals and, at the officer's command, took the two convicts who stood first in the row. The convicts stopped when they reached the post, and while sacks were being brought, looked dumbly around as a wounded beast looks at an approaching hunter. One crossed himself continuously, the other scratched his back and made a movement of the lips resembling a smile. With hurried hands the soldiers blindfolded them, drawing the sacks over their heads, and tied them to the post.

Again Pierre did not wish to look and again turned away; but again the sound of a frightful explosion struck his ear, and at the same moment he saw smoke, blood, and the pale, scared faces of the Frenchmen who were again doing something by the post, their trembling hands getting in one another's way. Pierre, breathing heavily, looked around as if asking what it meant. The same question was expressed in all the looks that met his.

He read the same dismay, horror, and inner conflict in the faces of all the Russians and of the French soldiers and officers, without exception—the same feelings that filled his own heart. "But who, after all, is doing this? They are all suffering as I am. Who then is it? Who?" flashed for an instant through his mind.

"Sharpshooters of the 86th, forward!" shouted someone. The fifth prisoner, the one next to Pierre, was led away—alone. Pierre did not understand that he himself was saved, that he and the rest had been brought there only to witness the execution. With ever-growing horror, and no sense of joy or relief, he gazed at what was happening. The fifth man was the factory boy in the loose cloak. The moment they laid hands on him he sprang aside in terror and clutched at Pierre. (Pierre shuddered and shook himself free.) The boy could not walk. They dragged him along, holding him up under the arms, and he screamed. When they got him to the post he grew quiet, as if he suddenly understood something. Whether he understood that screaming was useless, or thought it unbelievable that men would kill him, in any case he took his stand at the post, waiting to be blindfolded like the others, and looked around him with glittering eyes like a wounded animal.

Pierre was no longer able to turn away and close his eyes. His curiosity and agitation, like that of the whole crowd, reached the highest pitch at this fifth murder. Like the others, this fifth man seemed calm; he wrapped his loose cloak closer and rubbed one bare foot with the other.

Probably a word of command was given, followed by the reports of eight muskets; but try as he would, Pierre could not afterwards remember hearing the slightest sound of the shots. He only saw how the worker suddenly sank down on the cords that held him, how blood appeared in two places, how the ropes slackened under the weight of the hanging body, and how the worker sat down, his head hanging unnaturally and one leg bent under him. Pierre ran up to the post. No one stopped him. Pale, frightened people were doing something around the worker. The lower jaw of an old Frenchman with a thick mustache trembled as he untied the ropes.
