The body collapsed. The soldiers dragged it awkwardly from the post and began pushing it into the pit.

Pierre gazed now with dazed eyes at these sharpshooters who ran in pairs out of the circle. All but one rejoined their companies. This one, a young soldier, his face deathly pale, his shako pushed back, and his musket resting on the ground, still stood near the pit at the spot from which he had fired. He swayed like a drunken man, taking some steps forward and back to keep himself from falling. An old noncommissioned officer ran out of the ranks and, taking him by the elbow, dragged him to his company. The crowd of Russians and Frenchmen began to disperse. They all went away silently and with drooping heads.

Pierre glanced at the speaker and saw that it was a soldier who was trying to find some relief after what had been done, but could not. Without finishing what he had begun to say, he made a hopeless gesture with his arm and went away.
"My child!" she murmured (in French), "I love you and have known you a long time."
* Mon enfant! Je vous aime et vous connais depuis longtemps.
"Thank you for coming, my dear." (in French)
* Merci, chère amie, d'être venue.

The human mind cannot grasp the causes of events in their totality, but the desire to find those causes is planted deep in the human soul. Without considering the countless complexity of conditions—any one of which, taken alone, might seem to be the cause—a person seizes on the first approximation that seems intelligible and says: "This is the cause!" In historical events (where the actions of men are the subject of observation), the first and most primitive approximation was the will of the gods, and after that, the will of those who stood in the most prominent positions—the heroes of history. But we need only penetrate to the essence of any historical event—which lies in the activity of the masses who take part in it—to see that the will of the historical hero doesn't control the actions of the masses, but is itself constantly controlled. It may seem unimportant whether we understand historical events one way or another. Yet there is the same difference between someone who says "the peoples of the West moved eastward because Napoleon wished it" and someone who says "this happened because it had to happen," as between those who believed the earth was stationary and the planets revolved around it, and those who admitted they didn't know what held the earth in place but knew there were laws directing its movement and that of the other planets. There is, and can be, no cause of a historical event except the one cause of all causes. But there are laws directing events, and some of these laws are known to us while we are conscious of others we cannot comprehend. Discovering these laws becomes possible only when we completely abandon the attempt to find the cause in the will of any single individual, just as the laws of planetary motion were discovered only when people abandoned the idea that the earth was fixed.

Historians consider that, next to the Battle of Borodino and the occupation of Moscow by the enemy and its destruction by fire, the most important episode of the 1812 war was the movement of the Russian army from the Ryazan to the Kaluga road and to the Tarutino camp—the so-called flank march across the Krasnaya Pakhra River. They attribute this stroke of genius to various individuals and debate who deserves the credit. Even foreign historians, including the French, acknowledge the genius of the Russian commanders when they discuss this flank march. But it's hard to understand why military writers, and others following them, consider this maneuver to be some brilliant conception by a single man who saved Russia and destroyed Napoleon. First, it's hard to see where the profundity and genius lay, because it didn't take much brainpower to see that the best position for an army not under attack is where supplies are most plentiful—even a dull thirteen-year-old could have guessed that the best position after the retreat from Moscow was on the Kaluga road. So it's impossible to understand how historians conclude this was a profound maneuver. And it's even harder to understand why they think it saved Russia and destroyed the French, since this flank march—had it been preceded, accompanied, or followed by other circumstances—might have proved ruinous for the Russians and salutary for the French. If the Russian army's position did begin to improve after this march, it doesn't follow at all that the march was the cause.

That flank march might not only have failed to benefit the Russian army but, under other circumstances, could have led to its destruction. What would have happened if Moscow hadn't burned down? If Murat hadn't lost sight of the Russians? If Napoleon hadn't remained inactive? If the Russian army at Krasnaya Pakhra had given battle, as the Russian generals Bennigsen and Barclay advised? What if the French had attacked the Russians while they were marching beyond the Pakhra? What if, on approaching Tarutino, Napoleon had attacked the Russians with even a tenth of the energy he showed at Smolensk? What if the French had marched on Petersburg? In any of these scenarios, the flank march that brought salvation might have proved disastrous.

The third and most baffling thing is that people studying history deliberately avoid seeing that this flank march cannot be attributed to any single person, that no one foresaw it, and that in reality—like the retreat from Fili—it never occurred to anyone as a complete plan. It emerged moment by moment, step by step, event by event, from an endless number of diverse circumstances, and was only seen as a whole after it was accomplished and belonged to the past.

At the council at Fili, the prevailing idea among the Russian commanders was the one naturally suggesting itself, namely, a direct retreat along the Nizhni road. Proof of this lies in the fact that the majority voted for such a retreat, and especially in the well-known conversation after the council between the commander in chief and Lanskoy, who was in charge of supplies. Lanskoy informed the commander in chief that army provisions were mostly stored along the Oka River in the Tula and Ryazan provinces, and that retreating toward Nizhni would separate the army from its supplies by the broad Oka, which can't be crossed early in winter. This was the first indication that they needed to deviate from what had previously seemed the most natural course—a direct retreat toward Nizhni-Novgorod. The army turned more to the south, along the Ryazan road and closer to its supplies. Later, the French inactivity (they even lost sight of the Russian army), concern for the safety of the arsenal at Tula, and especially the advantage of moving closer to provisions caused the army to turn still further south onto the Tula road. After crossing to the Tula road beyond the Pakhra by a forced march, the Russian commanders planned to stay at Podolsk and had no thought of the Tarutino position. But countless circumstances forced our army to turn even further south: the reappearance of French troops who had for a time lost touch with the Russians, plans for giving battle, and above all the abundance of food in Kaluga province. The army crossed from the Tula to the Kaluga road and proceeded to Tarutino, which lay between the supply routes. Just as it's impossible to say when the decision was made to abandon Moscow, it's impossible to say precisely when, or by whom, the decision was made to move to Tarutino. Only when the army had arrived there, as the result of innumerable and varying forces, did people begin assuring themselves that they had desired this movement and long ago foreseen its result.

The Russian army was being commanded by Kutuzov and his staff, and also by the Emperor from Petersburg. Before news of the abandonment of Moscow had reached Petersburg, a detailed plan for the entire campaign had been drawn up and sent to Kutuzov for guidance. Though this plan was based on the supposition that Moscow was still in our hands, it was approved by the staff and accepted as the basis for action. Kutuzov replied only that movements arranged from a distance were always difficult to execute. So fresh instructions were sent for handling difficulties that might arise, along with new people to watch Kutuzov's actions and report on them.

Beyond this, the entire Russian army staff was being reorganized. The positions left vacant by Bagration, who had been killed, and by Barclay, who had departed in a huff, had to be filled. Very serious thought was given to whether it would be better to put officer A in B's place and B in D's, or on the contrary to put D in A's place, and so on—as if anything beyond A's or B's personal satisfaction depended on these decisions.

As a result of the hostility between Kutuzov and Bennigsen (his chief of staff), the presence of the Emperor's confidential representatives, and all these personnel changes, a more than usually complicated play of parties was going on among the staff. Among the officers, A was undermining B, D was undermining C, and so on in all possible combinations and permutations. In all these intrigues, the subject of intrigue was generally the conduct of the war, which everyone believed they were directing; but this affair of the war went on independently of them, as it had to go—never the way people planned it, but flowing always from the essential attitude of the masses. Only in the highest circles did all these schemes, crossings, and interminglings appear to reflect what actually had to happen.

"Prince Michael Ilarionovich!" wrote the Emperor on the second of October, in a letter that reached Kutuzov after the battle of Tarutino. "Since September 2, Moscow has been in enemy hands. Your last reports were dated the twentieth, and since then no action has been taken against the enemy or to relieve the ancient capital. According to your latest dispatch, you have even retreated further. Serpukhov is already occupied by an enemy detachment, and Tula with its famous arsenal, so vital to the army, is in danger. From General Wintzingerode's reports, I see that an enemy corps of ten thousand is moving on the Petersburg road. Another of several thousand moves on Dmitrov. A third has advanced along the Vladimir road, and a fourth, quite sizable detachment, is stationed between Ruza and Mozhaysk. Napoleon himself was in Moscow as late as the twenty-fifth. Given all this, when the enemy has scattered his forces into large detachments and Napoleon sits in Moscow with his Guards, is it really possible that the forces facing you are too strong for you to take the offensive? On the contrary, he is probably only chasing you with detachments, or at most with a corps far weaker than your army. It would seem that, availing yourself of these circumstances, you might advantageously attack a weaker force and destroy it, or at least force it to retreat, retaining in our hands an important part of the provinces now under enemy control and averting the danger to Tula and other interior towns. You will be held responsible if the enemy manages to direct a force of any size against Petersburg to threaten this capital, in which it has not been possible to retain many troops. With the army entrusted to you, acting with resolution and energy, you have ample means to prevent this fresh disaster. Remember that you still must answer to our offended country for the loss of Moscow. You have seen my readiness to reward you. That readiness will not weaken, but I and Russia have a right to expect from you all the zeal, firmness, and success that your intellect, military talent, and the courage of your troops justify us in expecting."

But by the time this letter—which proved that the real balance of forces had already made itself felt in Petersburg—was sent, Kutuzov had found himself unable to hold back his army any longer, and a battle had already taken place.

On October second, a Cossack named Shapovalov, who was out scouting, killed one hare and wounded another. Following the wounded hare, he wandered deep into the forest and stumbled upon the left flank of Murat's army, camped there without any precautions. The Cossack laughingly told his comrades how he'd nearly fallen into French hands. A cornet, hearing the story, informed his commander.

The Cossack was brought in and questioned. The Cossack officers wanted to seize the chance to capture some horses, but one of the senior officers, who was acquainted with the higher authorities, reported the incident to a general on the staff. Things at staff headquarters had been extremely tense lately. Ermolov had been to see Bennigsen a few days previously and begged him to use his influence to persuade the commander in chief to take the offensive.

The Cossack's report, confirmed by cavalry patrols sent out afterward, was the final proof that events had ripened. The tightly coiled spring was released, the clock began to whir and the chimes to play. Despite all his supposed power, his intellect, his experience, and his knowledge of men, Kutuzov—taking into account the Cossack's report, a note from Bennigsen, who sent personal reports to the Emperor, the wishes he assumed the Emperor held, and the fact that all the generals expressed the same wish—could no longer check the inevitable movement. He gave the order to do what he considered useless and harmful—he approved, that is, the accomplished fact.

With regard to military matters, Napoleon immediately upon entering Moscow gave General Sebastiani strict orders to monitor the Russian army's movements, sent army corps along the various roads, and instructed Murat to find Kutuzov. Then he gave careful directions about the fortification of the Kremlin and drew up a brilliant plan for a future campaign covering the entire map of Russia.

With regard to diplomatic questions, Napoleon summoned Captain Yakovlev—who had been robbed, was dressed in rags, and had no idea how to get out of Moscow—and explained his entire policy and his magnanimity in great detail. Having written a letter to Emperor Alexander in which he felt duty-bound to inform his Friend and Brother that Rostopchin, the governor of Moscow, had badly mismanaged things in Moscow, he dispatched Yakovlev to Petersburg.
With regard to legal matters, immediately after the fires, he ordered that the arsonists be found and executed. And the scoundrel Rostopchin was punished by an order to burn down his houses.
With regard to administrative matters, Moscow was granted a constitution. A municipal government was established and the following announcement issued:
INHABITANTS OF MOSCOW!

Your misfortunes are terrible, but His Majesty the Emperor and King wishes to end them. Harsh examples have shown you how he punishes disobedience and crime. Strict measures have been taken to restore order and public safety. A fatherly administration, chosen from among yourselves, will form your municipality or city government. It will care for you, your needs, and your welfare. Its members will be marked by a red ribbon worn across the shoulder, and the mayor will also wear a white belt. But when not on duty, they will wear only a red ribbon on the left arm.

The city police has been restored on its former basis, and its activity has already improved public order. The government has appointed two commissaries general, or police chiefs, and twenty commissaries or captains of wards have been appointed to the different wards of the city. You will know them by the white ribbon on their left arm. Several churches of various denominations are open, and services continue without interference. Your fellow citizens are returning daily to their homes, and orders have been given that they shall find in them the help and protection due to their misfortunes. These are the government's measures to restore order and ease your condition. But to achieve this, you must add your own efforts: forget, if possible, the misfortunes you've suffered; hope for a less cruel fate; be certain that inevitable, shameful death awaits anyone who threatens your persons or your remaining property; and you should not doubt that these will be safeguarded, since such is the will of the greatest and most just of monarchs. Soldiers and citizens, whatever your nation—restore public trust, the foundation of a state's welfare. Live as brothers, give each other aid and protection, unite to defeat the intentions of the evil-minded, obey the military and civil authorities, and your tears will soon dry!

With regard to supplies for the army, Napoleon decreed that all troops should take turns entering Moscow à la maraude (as looters) to obtain provisions for themselves, so that the army might have its future provided for.
With regard to religion, Napoleon ordered the priests brought back and services resumed in the churches.
With regard to commerce and to provisioning the army, the following was posted everywhere:

You, peaceful citizens of Moscow, artisans and workers driven from the city by misfortune, and you scattered farmers still kept out in the fields by groundless fear—listen! Peace is returning to this capital and order is being restored. Your countrymen are emerging boldly from hiding, finding they are treated with respect. Any violence to them or their property is promptly punished. His Majesty the Emperor and King protects them and considers none of you his enemy except those who disobey his orders. He wishes to end your suffering and return you to your homes and families. Respond, therefore, to his benevolent intentions and come to us without fear. Citizens, return confidently to your dwellings! You will soon find ways to meet your needs. Craftsmen and industrious artisans, return to your trades, your homes, your shops, where guards await to protect you! You will receive proper pay for your work. And lastly you too, peasants, come from the forests where you are hiding in terror, return to your huts without fear, knowing you will find protection! Markets have been set up in the city where peasants can bring their surplus supplies and the products of the soil. The government has taken the following steps to ensure freedom of sale for them: (1) From today, peasants, husbandmen, and those living in the neighborhood of Moscow may safely bring supplies of all kinds to two designated markets—one on Mokhovaya Street and the other at the Provision Market. (2) Goods will be purchased at prices agreed between buyer and seller, and if a seller cannot get a fair price, he may freely take his goods back to his village, and no one may hinder him under any pretense. (3) Sundays and Wednesdays are the main market days, with sufficient troops stationed along the highways on Tuesdays and Saturdays at such distances from the town as to protect the carts. (4) Similar measures will be taken that peasants with their carts and horses may meet with no hindrance on their return journey. (5) Steps will be taken immediately to restore normal trade.

Citizens and villagers, workers and artisans of all nations—you are called to carry out the fatherly intentions of His Majesty the Emperor and King and to work with him for the common good! Place your respect and confidence at his feet and join us without delay!

In regard to philanthropy, the greatest virtue of crowned heads, Napoleon did everything in his power. He had the words Maison de ma Mère (House of My Mother) inscribed on charitable institutions, blending tender filial devotion with a monarch's majestic generosity. He visited the Foundling Hospital and, allowing the orphans he had saved to kiss his white hands, conversed graciously with Tutolmin. Then, as Thiers eloquently recounts, he ordered his soldiers to be paid in forged Russian currency he had prepared: "Raising the use of these means by an act worthy of himself and of the French army, he let relief be distributed to those who had been burned out. But as food was too precious to give to foreigners—most of whom were enemies—Napoleon preferred to supply them with money to buy food from outside, and had paper rubles distributed to them."
With reference to army discipline, orders were continually issued imposing severe punishment for the nonperformance of military duties and to suppress looting.

Early in the morning of October sixth, Pierre went out of the shed and, on his way back, stopped by the door to play with a little blue-gray dog with a long body and short, bowed legs that was jumping around him. This little dog lived in their shed, sleeping beside Karataev at night. It sometimes wandered into town but always came back. It had probably never had an owner—it belonged to nobody and had no name. The French called it Azor; the soldier who told stories called it Femgalka; Karataev and the others called it Gray, or sometimes Flabby. Having no master, no name, and not even a breed or definite color didn't seem to bother the blue-gray dog in the least. Its furry tail stood up firm and round like a plume, its crooked little legs served it so well that it would often gracefully lift a hind leg and trot along very easily and quickly on three legs, as if disdaining to use all four. Everything pleased it. One moment it would roll on its back yelping with delight, the next it would bask in the sun with an air of self-important thoughtfulness, then frolic around playing with a chip of wood or a straw.

Pierre first looked across the field where vehicles and riders were passing that morning, then into the distance across the river, then at the dog pretending to seriously bite him, and then down at his own bare feet, which he placed in various positions with pleasure, wiggling his dirty, thick big toes. Every time he looked at his bare feet, a smile of animated self-satisfaction crossed his face. The sight of them reminded him of everything he had experienced and learned during these weeks, and the memory was pleasant.
For several days the weather had been calm and clear, with slight frosts in the morning—what people call an ‘old wives’ summer,’ a spell of warm weather in autumn.

On everything near and far lay that magical crystal glitter seen only at that time of autumn. The Sparrow Hills were visible in the distance—the village, the church, the large white house. The bare trees, the sand, the bricks and rooftops, the green church spire, and the corners of the white house in the distance, all stood out in the transparent air in delicate outline and with unnatural clarity. Nearby were the familiar ruins of a half-burned mansion occupied by the French, with lilac bushes still showing dark green beside the fence. Even that ruined, defiled house—repulsively ugly in dull weather—looked quietly beautiful now in the clear, motionless brilliance.
'What sunshine, Monsieur Kiril!' (That was their name for Pierre.) 'Eh? Just like spring!'
And the corporal leaned against the door and offered Pierre his pipe, though whenever he offered it Pierre always declined it.

Pierre asked what was being said about leaving, and the corporal told him that nearly all the troops were departing and there should be orders about the prisoners that day. Sokolov, one of the soldiers sharing Pierre's shed, was dying, and Pierre told the corporal that something should be done about him. The corporal replied that Pierre needn't worry—they had an ambulance and a permanent hospital, and arrangements would be made for the sick. In general, everything that could happen had been anticipated by the authorities.

'"You see, St. Thomas," he said to me the other day, "Monsieur Kiril is an educated man who speaks French. He's a Russian gentleman who's had bad luck, but he's a man. He knows what's what. If he needs anything and asks me, he won't be refused. When a man has had an education, you see, he appreciates learning and well-bred people." I mention this for your sake, Monsieur Kiril. The other day, if it hadn't been for you, that business would have ended badly.'
A week earlier, the French had been issued boot leather and linen, which they'd given to the prisoners to make into boots and shirts for them.
‘A promise is own brother to performance! I said Friday, and here it is—ready,’ said Platon—Karataev’s first name—smiling as he unfolded the shirt he had sewn.

The Frenchman glanced around nervously, then, as if overcoming his hesitation, quickly pulled off his uniform and put on the shirt. He wore a long, greasy, flowered silk waistcoat next to his sallow, thin bare body—but no shirt. He was clearly afraid the watching prisoners would laugh at him, and thrust his head into the shirt quickly. None of the prisoners said a word.
The Frenchman pushed his head and hands through without looking up, looked down at the shirt and examined the seams.

'You know, my friend, this isn't a tailor's shop, and I didn't have the right tools. As they say, you need a tool even to crack a louse,' said Platon with one of his round smiles, clearly pleased with his work.
'It's good, quite good, thank you,' said the Frenchman in French, 'but there must be some linen left over.'
'Thanks, thanks, old fellow... But the leftover pieces?' the Frenchman said again, smiling. He took out an assignation ruble note and gave it to Karataev. 'But give me the scraps that are left.'

Pierre saw that Platon didn't want to understand what the Frenchman was saying, and he watched without interfering. Karataev thanked the Frenchman for the money and went on admiring his own work. The Frenchman insisted on getting back the leftover linen and asked Pierre to translate.

And Karataev, his face suddenly changed and saddened, took a small bundle of scraps from inside his shirt and handed it to the Frenchman without looking at him. 'Oh dear!' muttered Karataev, and walked away. The Frenchman looked at the linen, thought for a moment, then glanced inquiringly at Pierre and—as if Pierre's expression told him something—suddenly blushed and shouted in a squeaky voice:

'There, look at that,' said Karataev, swaying his head. 'People said they weren't Christians, but they have souls too. It's what the old folks used to say: "A sweating hand is an open hand, a dry hand is a tight one." He's naked, but he's given it back.'
Karataev smiled thoughtfully and was silent for a while, looking at the pieces of cloth.

In the early days of October, another envoy came to Kutuzov with a letter from Napoleon proposing peace, falsely dated from Moscow, though Napoleon was already not far from Kutuzov on the old Kaluga road. Kutuzov replied just as he had to the earlier peace letter brought by Lauriston, an earlier French envoy, saying there could be no question of peace.

Soon after, a report came in from Dorokhov's guerrilla detachment, operating to the left of Tarutino, that troops from Broussier's division had been spotted at Forminsk and, being separated from the main French army, could easily be destroyed. The soldiers and officers again demanded action. Generals on the staff, excited by the memory of the easy victory at Tarutino, urged Kutuzov to follow Dorokhov's suggestion. Kutuzov didn't think any offensive was necessary. The result was an inevitable compromise: a small detachment was sent to Forminsk to attack Broussier.

By a strange coincidence, this task—a most difficult and important one—was given to Dokhturov, that same modest little Dokhturov whom no one had described to us as drawing up plans of battles, dashing about in front of regiments, showering crosses on batteries, and so on, and who was considered and spoken of as indecisive and undiscerning. Yet we find him commanding wherever the position was most difficult all through the Russo-French wars, from the Battle of Austerlitz to 1813. At Austerlitz he was the last to hold the Augezd dam, rallying regiments and saving what he could when everyone was fleeing and perishing and not a single general remained in the rear guard. Ill with fever, he went to Smolensk with twenty thousand men to defend it against Napoleon's entire army. At the Malakhov Gate in Smolensk, he had barely dozed off in a bout of fever before being woken by the bombardment—and Smolensk held out all day. At Borodino, when Bagration was killed and nine-tenths of the men on our left flank had fallen and the full force of French artillery was directed there, the man sent to that spot was this same irresolute and undiscerning Dokhturov—Kutuzov rushing to correct a mistake he'd made by first sending someone else. And the quiet little Dokhturov rode there, and Borodino became the greatest glory of the Russian army. Many heroes have been described to us in verse and prose, but about Dokhturov, scarcely a word has been said.

It was Dokhturov again who was sent to Forminsk and from there to Malo-Yaroslavets—the site of the last battle with the French, where the obvious disintegration of the French army began. We hear about many geniuses and heroes of that period of the campaign, but about Dokhturov, nothing or almost nothing, and even that is said doubtfully. This silence about Dokhturov is the clearest testimony to his merit.

It's natural for someone who doesn't understand how a machine works to assume that a shaving that has accidentally fallen into it and is bouncing around, interfering with its operation, must be its most important part. Someone who doesn't understand the machine's construction can't grasp that the small connecting cog, turning quietly, is one of the most essential parts—not the shaving that merely damages and hinders it.

On October tenth, when Dokhturov had gone halfway to Forminsk and stopped at the village of Aristovo, faithfully preparing to carry out his orders, the entire French army—having, in its convulsive movement, reached Murat's position as if to give battle—suddenly, for no reason, veered left onto the new Kaluga road and began to enter Forminsk, where previously only Broussier had been. At that point, Dokhturov had under his command, besides Dorokhov's detachment, the two small guerrilla bands of Figner and Seslavin.

On the evening of October eleventh, Seslavin arrived at Aristovo headquarters with a captured French guardsman. The prisoner said the troops entering Forminsk that day were the vanguard of the entire army—Napoleon was there, and the whole army had left Moscow four days earlier. That same evening, a house serf from Borovsk said he'd seen an enormous army entering the town. Some Cossacks from Dokhturov's detachment reported sighting the French Guards marching along the road to Borovsk. From all these reports, it was clear that where they had expected to find a single division, they now faced the entire French army, marching from Moscow in an unexpected direction along the Kaluga road. Dokhturov was unwilling to act, as it was no longer clear to him what he should do. He'd been ordered to attack Forminsk, but at that time only Broussier had been there—now the whole French army was there. Ermolov wanted to act on his own judgment, but Dokhturov insisted on getting instructions from Kutuzov. So it was decided to send a dispatch to the staff.

For this mission, a capable officer, Bolkhovitinov, was chosen to explain the situation verbally as well as deliver a written report. Toward midnight, Bolkhovitinov received the dispatch and verbal instructions and galloped off to the General Staff, accompanied by a Cossack with spare horses.

From the moment he received this news until the end of the campaign, all of Kutuzov's activity was directed toward restraining his troops—by authority, by cunning, and by pleading—from useless attacks, maneuvers, or encounters with the dying enemy. Dokhturov went to Malo-Yaroslavets, but Kutuzov lingered with the main army and gave orders for the evacuation of Kaluga—a retreat beyond that town seemed entirely possible to him.

Napoleon's historians describe to us his skillful maneuvers at Tarutino and Malo-Yaroslavets and speculate about what would have happened if Napoleon had managed to penetrate into the rich southern provinces in time.

But setting aside the fact that nothing prevented him from advancing into those southern provinces (the Russian army wasn't blocking his way), the historians forget that nothing could have saved his army, because it already carried within itself the seeds of inevitable destruction. How could that army—which had found abundant supplies in Moscow and had trampled them underfoot instead of preserving them, and on reaching Smolensk had looted provisions instead of storing them—how could that army recover in Kaluga province, inhabited by the same kind of Russians who had lived in Moscow, where fire had the same property of consuming whatever was set ablaze?
That army could not recover anywhere. Since the Battle of Borodino and the pillaging of Moscow, it had carried within itself, as it were, the chemical elements of dissolution.

The members of what had once been an army—Napoleon himself and all his soldiers—fled without knowing where, each concerned only with escaping as quickly as possible from this position, of the hopelessness of which they were all more or less vaguely conscious.

So at the council at Malo-Yaroslavets, when the generals pretended to deliberate and offered various opinions, all mouths were shut by the opinion of the simple-minded soldier Mouton, who spoke last and said what they all felt: the one thing needful was to get away as fast as possible. And no one—not even Napoleon—could argue against that truth they all recognized.

But though everyone realized they had to retreat, there remained a feeling of shame at admitting they had to flee. An outside jolt was needed to overcome that shame, and it came in due time. It was what the French called 'the Emperor's hurrah'—le hourra de l'Empereur.

The day after the council at Malo-Yaroslavets, Napoleon rode out early among the lines of his army with his suite of marshals and an escort, ostensibly to inspect the troops and the scene of the recent and upcoming battle. Some Cossacks out looking for plunder ran into the Emperor and very nearly captured him. If the Cossacks did not capture Napoleon then, what saved him was the very thing that was destroying the French army—the booty on which the Cossacks fell. The Cossacks went after the plunder, just as they had at Tarutino, leaving the men behind. Ignoring Napoleon, they chased the booty, and Napoleon managed to escape.

When les enfants du Don—the children of the Don, the Cossacks—could so easily have captured the Emperor himself in the midst of his army, it was clear there was nothing to do but flee as fast as possible along the nearest, familiar road. Napoleon, with his forty-year-old stomach, understood the hint. No longer feeling his former agility and boldness, and shaken by the fright the Cossacks had given him, he immediately agreed with Mouton and issued orders—as the historians tell us—to retreat along the Smolensk road.

That Napoleon agreed with Mouton, and that the army retreated, doesn't prove that Napoleon caused it to retreat, but that the forces influencing the entire army and directing it along the Mozhaysk (that is, the Smolensk) road were simultaneously acting on him as well.

A person in motion always invents a purpose for that motion. To be able to go a thousand miles, you must imagine that something good awaits you at the end of those thousand miles. You need the prospect of a promised land to have the strength to keep moving.

For the French during their advance, the promised land had been Moscow. During their retreat, it was their homeland. But their homeland was too far away, and for someone traveling a thousand miles, it's absolutely necessary to set aside the final goal and say to himself: 'Today I'll reach a place twenty-five miles ahead, where I'll rest and spend the night.' And during that first day's journey, the resting place eclipses the ultimate destination and draws all his hopes and desires. The impulses felt by a single person are always magnified in a crowd.

For the French retreating along the old Smolensk road, the final goal—their homeland—was too remote. Their immediate goal was Smolensk, toward which all their desires and hopes, enormously intensified in the mass, propelled them onward. It wasn't that they knew plenty of food and fresh troops awaited them in Smolensk, nor were they told so (on the contrary, their superior officers, and Napoleon himself, knew that provisions there were scarce). But this was the only thing that could give them the strength to keep moving and endure their present privations. So those who knew and those who didn't both deceived themselves and pushed on toward Smolensk as toward a promised land.

Reaching the highway, the French fled with astonishing energy and unheard-of speed toward their chosen goal. Besides the shared impulse that bound the whole crowd of French into one mass and gave it a kind of energy, there was another cause binding them together: their sheer numbers. As with the physical law of gravity, their enormous mass drew individual human atoms to itself. In their hundreds of thousands, they moved like an entire nation.

Each man wanted nothing more than to give himself up as a prisoner and escape the horror and misery. But on one hand, the force of this common attraction to Smolensk, their goal, drew every one of them in the same direction; on the other, an army corps can't surrender to a company. Though the French availed themselves of every convenient opportunity to break away and surrender on the slightest decent pretext, such pretexts did not always occur. Their very numbers and their crowded and swift movement deprived them of that possibility and made it not just difficult but impossible for the Russians to stop this movement, to which the French were directing all their energies. Beyond a certain limit, no mechanical disruption of the body could hasten the process of decomposition.

A lump of snow can't be melted all at once. There is a minimum time required, and no amount of heat can melt it faster. On the contrary, the more heat you apply, the harder the remaining snow becomes.

Of the Russian commanders, Kutuzov alone understood this. When the flight of the French army along the Smolensk road became well defined, what Konovnitsyn had foreseen on the night of the eleventh of October began to happen. Every senior officer wanted to distinguish himself—to cut off, seize, capture, and overthrow the French—and all clamored for action.

He couldn't tell them what we say now: 'Why fight? Why block the road, losing our own men and inhumanely slaughtering miserable wretches? What's the point, when a third of their army has melted away on the road from Moscow to Vyazma without any battle?' But drawing on his years of wisdom, he told them what they could understand—about the golden bridge, the old idea of leaving a beaten enemy an open road rather than cornering it—and they laughed at him and slandered him, flinging themselves on, tearing at, and gloating over the dying beast.

And try as Kutuzov might to hold the troops back, our men attacked, trying to block the road. Infantry regiments, we are told, advanced to the attack with music playing and drums beating, and killed and lost thousands of men.
But they didn't cut off or overthrow anyone. The French army, closing ranks more tightly in the face of danger, continued, while steadily melting away, to pursue its fatal path toward Smolensk.
The Battle of Borodino, followed by the occupation of Moscow and the flight of the French without further conflicts, is one of the most instructive phenomena in history.

All historians agree that the external activity of states and nations in their conflicts with one another is expressed through wars, and that military success or failure directly causes the political strength of states and nations to rise or fall.

It seems strange: some king or emperor quarrels with another, raises an army, fights the enemy's forces, wins by killing three, five, or ten thousand men, and thereby subjugates a kingdom and an entire nation of several million people. Yet as far as we know, every fact of history confirms the rule that the greater or lesser success of one army against another is the cause, or at least an essential indication, of a nation's strength rising or falling. This holds even though it is unintelligible that the defeat of an army—a hundredth part of a nation—should force the whole nation to submit. A victorious army wins, and at once the rights of the conquering nation grow at the expense of the defeated. A defeated army loses, and at once its people lose rights in proportion to the severity of the loss; if its army suffers a complete defeat, the nation is fully subjugated.

According to history, this has been true since the most ancient times, right up to the present day. All of Napoleon's wars confirm this rule. As Austria's army is defeated, Austria loses its rights, and France's rights and power grow. The French victories at Jena and Auerstadt destroy the independent existence of Prussia.

But then, in 1812, the French win a victory near Moscow. Moscow is taken, and after that—with no further battles—it isn't Russia that ceases to exist, but the French army of six hundred thousand, and then Napoleonic France itself. To bend the facts to fit the rules of history and say that the battlefield at Borodino remained in Russian hands, or that subsequent battles destroyed Napoleon's army, is impossible.

After the French victory at Borodino, there was no major engagement—nor any truly serious fighting—yet the French army ceased to exist. What does this mean? Suppose this had happened in the history of China: we might wave it off as 'not a historical phenomenon' (the historians' usual expedient when something doesn't fit their standards). Or suppose it had been only a brief skirmish with a handful of troops: we could call it an exception. But this happened before our fathers' eyes. For them it was a question of the life or death of their fatherland. And it took place in the greatest of all known wars.

The 1812 campaign, from the Battle of Borodino to the expulsion of the French, proved that winning a battle does not produce a conquest, and isn't even an invariable indicator of one. It proved that the force deciding the fate of nations lies not in conquerors, nor even in armies and battles, but in something else.

French historians, describing the state of the French army before it left Moscow, assert that everything was in order in the Grand Army except the cavalry, the artillery, and the transport—there was no forage for the horses or cattle. That was a misfortune no one could fix, since the peasants of the district burned their hay rather than let the French have it.

The victory that was won brought none of the usual results, because two peasants, Karp and Vlas—who after the French evacuated Moscow drove their carts in to loot the city, and who in general personally displayed no heroic feelings—along with the innumerable multitude of similar peasants, did not bring their hay to Moscow for the high prices offered them. They burned it instead.

After the burning of Smolensk, a war began that followed no previous traditions. The burning of towns and villages, the retreats after battles, the blow struck at Borodino and the renewed retreat, the burning of Moscow, the capture of marauders, the seizure of supply trains, and guerrilla warfare—all were departures from the rules.

Napoleon felt this. From the time he assumed the correct fencing stance in Moscow and, instead of his opponent's rapier, saw a cudgel raised above his head, he never stopped complaining to Kutuzov and to Emperor Alexander that the war was being fought contrary to all the rules—as if there were any rules for killing people. The French complained that it wasn't fair play. Some highly placed Russians felt it was rather disgraceful to fight with a cudgel; they wanted to assume the fencing positions—en quarte or en tierce, according to all the rules—and deliver an adroit thrust en prime. But despite all of that, the cudgel of the people's war was raised with all its threatening, majestic strength and, without consulting anyone's preferences or rules and regardless of anything else, it rose and fell with stupid simplicity, but consistently, hammering the French until the entire invasion had perished.

And it is well for a people who do not—as the French did in 1813—salute according to all the rules of art, gracefully present the hilt of their rapier, and politely hand it to their magnanimous conqueror. It is well for a people who, at the moment of trial, without asking what rules others have followed in similar cases, simply and easily pick up the first cudgel at hand and strike with it until the feelings of resentment and revenge in their souls give way to contempt and compassion.

This contradiction arises because military science equates an army's strength with its numbers. Military science says: more troops means more strength. Les gros bataillons ont toujours raison — big battalions are always right.

After October twenty-eighth, when the frosts set in, the French flight took on an even more tragic character. Men froze to death or roasted themselves to death at campfires, while carriages carrying people dressed in furs continued to roll past, hauling away the property that had been stolen by the Emperor, kings, and dukes. But the essential nature of the flight and disintegration of the French army continued as before.

From Moscow to Vyazma, the French army of seventy-three thousand men—not counting the Guards, who did nothing during the entire war but loot—was reduced to thirty-six thousand, though no more than five thousand had fallen in battle. From this starting point, the succeeding terms of the progression could be calculated mathematically. The French army melted away and perished at the same rate whether marching from Moscow to Vyazma, from Vyazma to Smolensk, from Smolensk to the Berezina, or from the Berezina to Vilna—regardless of the greater or lesser intensity of the cold, the pursuit, the blocking of their path, or any other particular conditions. Beyond Vyazma, the French army stopped moving in three columns and huddled together into one mass, continuing that way to the end. Berthier wrote to his Emperor (and we know how far commanding officers allow themselves to stray from the truth when describing their army's condition), and this is what he said:

I consider it my duty to report to Your Majesty on the condition of the various corps I have had the opportunity to observe during different stages of the last two or three days' march. They are nearly disbanded. Scarcely a quarter of the soldiers remain with the standards of their regiments; the others wander off by themselves in different directions hoping to find food and escape discipline. In general, they look to Smolensk as the place where they hope to recover. During the last few days many soldiers have been seen throwing away their cartridges and their weapons. In such circumstances, whatever your ultimate plans may be, the interest of Your Majesty's service demands that the army be reassembled at Smolensk and, first of all, freed from ineffectives, such as dismounted cavalry, unnecessary baggage, and artillery equipment no longer proportionate to our present forces. The soldiers, worn out by hunger and fatigue, need these supplies as well as a few days' rest. Many have died these last days on the road or at the bivouacs. This state of affairs is continually growing worse and raises the fear that, unless prompt measures are taken, the troops will be beyond control in the event of a battle.

They all went without knowing where or why they were going. Still less did that genius, Napoleon, know it, for no one was issuing any orders to him. But still he and those about him retained their old habits: writing commands, letters, reports, and orders of the day; calling one another "Sire," "Mon Cousin," "Prince of Eckmuhl," "King of Naples," and so on. But these orders and reports existed only on paper. Nothing in them was carried out, because nothing could be carried out. And though they addressed one another as Majesties, Highnesses, or Cousins, they all felt they were miserable wretches who had done much evil for which they now had to pay. And though they pretended to be concerned about the army, each was thinking only of himself and how to get away as quickly as possible and save himself.

The movements of the Russian and French armies during the campaign from Moscow back to the Niemen were like a game of Russian blindman's buff, in which two players are blindfolded and one of them occasionally rings a little bell to let the catcher know where he is. At first, the one with the bell rings it fearlessly, but when he gets cornered, he runs away as quietly as he can—and often, thinking he's escaping, runs straight into his opponent's arms.

Because of the speed of the French flight and the Russian pursuit, and the resulting exhaustion of the horses, the main means of approximately determining the enemy's position—cavalry scouting—was unavailable. Besides, the frequent and rapid changes of position by both armies meant that even information received couldn't be delivered in time. If news came one day that the enemy had been at a certain position the day before, by the third day when anything could have been done, that army was already two days' march farther on and in quite another position.

One army fled and the other pursued. Beyond Smolensk there were several different roads available to the French, and one would have thought that during their four-day halt there they might have learned where the enemy was, devised a better plan, and tried something new. But after a four-day halt, the mob—with no maneuvers or plans—started running again along the beaten track, neither turning right nor left but taking the old, worst road through Krasnoe and Orsha.

Expecting the enemy from behind rather than ahead, the French separated in their flight and spread out over a distance of twenty-four hours' march. At the very front fled the Emperor, then the kings, then the dukes. The Russian army, expecting Napoleon to take the road to the right beyond the Dnieper—which was the only sensible thing for him to do—turned right themselves and came out on the highway at Krasnoe. And here, as in a game of blindman's buff, the French ran into our vanguard. Spotting their enemy unexpectedly, the French fell into confusion and froze with sudden fright, then resumed their flight, abandoning comrades who were farther behind. For three days, separate portions of the French army—first Murat's (the Viceroy's), then Davout's, then Ney's—ran, as it were, the gauntlet of the Russian army. They abandoned one another, abandoned all their heavy baggage, artillery, and half their men, fleeing past the Russians at night by making semicircles to the right.

Ney, who came last, had been busy blowing up the walls of Smolensk, which were in nobody's way—because despite their unfortunate plight, or because of it, the French wanted to punish the floor that had hurt them. Ney, who had started with a corps of ten thousand men, reached Napoleon at Orsha with only a thousand left, having abandoned all the rest and all his cannon, and having crossed the Dnieper by stealth at night at a wooded spot.

From Orsha they fled farther along the road to Vilna, still playing blindman's buff with the pursuing army. At the Berezina they fell into disarray again—many drowned, many surrendered—but those who got across the river fled on. Their supreme chief put on a fur coat and, climbing into a sleigh, galloped off alone, abandoning his companions. The others who could manage it drove away too, leaving those who could not to surrender or die.
"I have played the Emperor long enough; it is time to play the general" (in French)—but then immediately ran away again, abandoning the scattered remnants of the army he left behind.
* J'ai assez fait l'empereur; il est temps de faire le général.

"It is grand!" say the historians (in French), and there is no longer any good or evil, only "grand" and "not grand." Grand is good, not grand is bad. Grand is the defining trait, in their view, of certain special creatures called "heroes." And Napoleon, escaping home in a warm fur coat while leaving his comrades—men he himself had brought there—to perish, feels that this is grand, and his conscience is at peace.
* C'est grand!
* (2) que c'est grand

"Du sublime (he saw something sublime in himself) au ridicule il n'y a qu'un pas — from the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step," he said. And the whole world has been repeating for fifty years: "Sublime! Grand! Napoleon the Great!" Du sublime au ridicule il n'y a qu'un pas — from the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step.
* From the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step.

Princess Mary postponed her departure. Sonya and the count tried to take Natasha's place but couldn't. They saw that she alone was able to restrain her mother from unreasoning despair. For three weeks Natasha stayed constantly at her mother's side, sleeping on a lounge chair in her room, making her eat and drink, and talking to her endlessly, because the mere sound of her tender, caressing tones soothed her mother.

A spiritual wound, caused by a tearing of the spiritual body, is like a physical wound. Strange as it may seem, just as a deep wound may heal until its edges join, physical and spiritual wounds alike can only heal completely through a vital force from within.

Natasha's wound healed in that way. She had believed her life was over, but her love for her mother unexpectedly showed her that the essence of life—love—was still active within her. Love awoke, and so did life.

Prince Andrew's last days had drawn Princess Mary and Natasha together; this new sorrow brought them closer still. Princess Mary postponed her departure and for three weeks looked after Natasha as though she were a sick child. The last weeks spent in her mother's bedroom had strained Natasha's physical strength.

"Is she like him?" thought Natasha. "Yes, like and yet not like. But she is quite original, strange, new, and unknown. And she loves me. What is in her heart? Everything good. But how? What is her mind like? What does she think about me? Yes, she is wonderful!"
"Mary," she said timidly, drawing Princess Mary's hand toward her, "Mary, you mustn't think I'm wicked. You don't, do you? Mary darling, how I love you! Let's be quite, quite friends."
And Natasha, embracing her, began kissing her face and hands, making Princess Mary feel shy but happy by this demonstration of her feelings.

From that day a tender and passionate friendship—the kind that exists only between women—was established between Princess Mary and Natasha. They were constantly kissing and saying tender things to each other and spent most of their time together. When one left the room, the other grew restless and hurried to rejoin her. Together they felt more in harmony with each other than either felt with herself when alone. A feeling stronger than friendship arose between them—an exclusive feeling of life being possible only in each other's presence.

Sometimes they were silent for hours; other times, after they were already in bed, they would begin talking and continue until morning. They spoke mostly of the distant past. Princess Mary told of her childhood, her mother, her father, and her dreams; and Natasha, who had previously turned away from that life of devotion, submission, and the poetry of Christian self-sacrifice with passive incomprehension, now—feeling bound to Princess Mary by affection—learned to love her past too and to understand a side of life that had been entirely foreign to her. She did not think of applying submission and self-denial to her own life, for she was used to seeking other kinds of joy; but she understood and loved those previously incomprehensible virtues in someone else. For Princess Mary, listening to Natasha's stories of childhood and youth, an equally new and previously unknown side of life opened up: a belief in life and its pleasures.

Just as before, they never mentioned him, so as not to lower (as they felt) their exalted feelings by putting them into words. But this silence gradually—without their realizing it—caused them to begin forgetting him.

One day she went quickly upstairs and found herself out of breath. Without thinking, she immediately invented a reason to go back down, and then, testing her strength, ran upstairs again, carefully noting the result.

She did not know, and would not have believed, that beneath the layer of slime that seemed to her impenetrable, covering her soul, delicate young shoots of grass were already sprouting. They would take root and so cover with their living green the grief that weighed her down that it would soon no longer be seen or noticed. The wound had begun to heal from within.

After the encounter at Vyazma—where Kutuzov had been unable to hold back his troops in their eagerness to overwhelm and cut off the enemy, and so on—the farther movement of the fleeing French and the Russians pursuing them continued as far as Krasnoe without a battle. The flight was so rapid that the Russian army pursuing the French could not keep up; cavalry and artillery horses broke down, and the information about French movements was never reliable.

To understand the degree of exhaustion of the Russian army, you only need to grasp clearly the meaning of one fact: while losing no more than five thousand killed and wounded after Tarutino, and fewer than a hundred prisoners, the Russian army that had left Tarutino a hundred thousand strong reached Krasnoe with only fifty thousand.

The rapid Russian pursuit was just as destructive to our army as the French flight was to theirs. The only difference was that the Russian army moved voluntarily, with no such threat of destruction as hung over the French, and that sick Frenchmen were left behind in enemy hands while sick Russians were left among their own people. The main cause of Napoleon's army wasting away was the speed of its movement, and convincing proof of this is the corresponding decline of the Russian army.

As far as it was in his power, Kutuzov did not try to check the French movement, though that was what Petersburg and the Russian generals wanted. Instead, as he had at Tarutino and Vyazma, he directed all his efforts toward speeding the retreat along while easing the movement of our army.

But besides this, since the army's exhaustion and enormous reduction from the speed of the advance had become obvious, another reason for slackening the pace and delaying presented itself: the aim of the Russian army was to pursue the French. The French route was unknown, so the closer our troops trod on their heels, the greater the distance they had to cover. Only by keeping some distance back could they cut across the French zigzag path. All the artful maneuvers suggested by our generals meant fresh movements of the army and a lengthening of its marches, whereas the only sensible objective was to shorten those marches. To this end, Kutuzov directed his efforts throughout the entire campaign from Moscow to Vilna—not casually or intermittently, but so consistently that he never once deviated from it.

Kutuzov felt and knew—not through reasoning or military science, but with the whole of his Russian being—what every Russian soldier felt: that the French were beaten, that the enemy was fleeing and must be driven out; but at the same time he, like his soldiers, understood all the hardship of this march, the rapidity of which was unparalleled for such a time of the year.

But the generals—especially the foreign ones in the Russian army—wanted to distinguish themselves, astonish someone, and for some reason capture a king or a duke. Any battle now would be horrible and senseless, yet to them this seemed the perfect time to fight and conquer somebody. Kutuzov merely shrugged his shoulders when one after another they presented him with maneuver plans for soldiers who were ill-shod, insufficiently clad, and half-starved—soldiers who within a month, without fighting a single battle, had dwindled to half their original number and who, at the best, if the flight continued, would have to go a greater distance than they had already traversed before they reached the frontier.

Toll wrote out a battle plan: "The first column will march to such and such a place," and so on. And as usual, nothing happened according to plan. Prince Eugene of Wurttemberg fired from a hilltop over the French crowds running past and demanded reinforcements that never arrived. The French, avoiding the Russians, scattered and hid in the forest by night, making their way around as best they could, and continued their flight.

Miloradovich, who said he did not want to know anything about the commissary affairs of his detachment and could never be found when needed—this man who styled himself chevalier sans peur et sans reproche, "the knight without fear and without reproach," and who loved to parley with the French—sent envoys demanding their surrender, wasted time, and didn't do what he was ordered to do.
* Knight without fear and without reproach.

And the cavalry, with spurs and sabers urging on horses that could barely move, trotted with great effort to the column presented to them—that is, to a crowd of Frenchmen frozen stiff, frostbitten, and starving—and the column that had been presented to them threw down its arms and surrendered, as it had long been anxious to do.

These men, carried away by their passions, were nothing more than blind tools of the most melancholy law of necessity, yet they considered themselves heroes and imagined they were accomplishing a most noble and honorable deed. They blamed Kutuzov, saying that from the very start of the campaign he had prevented them from defeating Napoleon, that he thought of nothing but satisfying his passions and would not advance from the Linen Factories because he was comfortable there, that he had stopped the advance at Krasnoe because he quite lost his head on learning Napoleon was there, and that he probably had an understanding with Napoleon and had been bribed, and so on and so on.

Not only his contemporaries, carried away by their passions, but posterity and history itself have acclaimed Napoleon as grand, while Kutuzov is described by foreigners as a crafty, dissolute, weak old courtier, and by Russians as something indefinite—a sort of puppet useful only because he had a Russian name.

In 1812 and 1813, Kutuzov was openly accused of blundering. The Emperor was dissatisfied with him. And in a history recently written by order of the Highest Authorities, it is stated that Kutuzov was a cunning court liar, frightened of the name of Napoleon, and that by his blunders at Krasnoe and the Berezina he deprived the Russian army of the glory of a complete victory over the French.
* History of the Year 1812. The character of Kutuzov and reflections on the unsatisfactory results of the battles at Krasnoe, by the historian Bogdanovich.

Such is the fate—not of great men ("grands hommes") whom the Russian mind does not acknowledge—but of those rare and always solitary individuals who, perceiving the will of Providence, submit their personal will to it. The hatred and contempt of the crowd is the punishment for those who discern the higher laws.

For Russian historians, strange and terrible to say, Napoleon—that most insignificant tool of history, who never anywhere, even in exile, showed human dignity—Napoleon is the object of adulation and enthusiasm; he is grand. But Kutuzov—the man who, from the beginning to the end of his activity in 1812, never once wavered by word or deed from Borodino to Vilna, gave an example of self-sacrifice unmatched in history, along with a living awareness of the future significance of what was happening—Kutuzov seems to them something indefinite and pitiful, and when they speak of him and of the year 1812, they always seem a little ashamed.

Kutuzov never spoke of "forty centuries looking down from the Pyramids," of the sacrifices he was making for the fatherland, or of what he intended or had accomplished. In general he said nothing about himself, struck no poses, always appeared to be the simplest and most ordinary of men, and said the simplest and most ordinary things. He wrote letters to his daughters and to the writer Madame de Stael, read novels, enjoyed the company of pretty women, joked with generals, officers, and soldiers, and never contradicted anyone who tried to prove anything to him. When Count Rostopchin galloped up to Kutuzov at the Yauza bridge and personally accused him of causing Moscow's destruction, saying: "How was it you promised not to abandon Moscow without a battle?" Kutuzov replied: "And I shall not abandon Moscow without a battle"—though Moscow was already abandoned. When Arakcheev, coming from the Emperor, told him that Ermolov ought to be appointed chief of artillery, Kutuzov replied: "Yes, I was just saying so myself"—though a moment before he had said the exact opposite. What did it matter to him—who then alone amid a senseless crowd understood the whole tremendous significance of what was happening—what did it matter to him whether Rostopchin attributed the calamities of Moscow to him or to himself? Still less could it matter who was named chief of artillery.

But that man, so careless with his words, never once during his entire period of activity uttered a single word inconsistent with the one aim toward which he worked throughout the whole war. Obviously, despite himself, in the most diverse circumstances, he repeatedly expressed his real thoughts with the bitter conviction that he would not be understood. Beginning with the battle of Borodino, from which point his disagreement with those around him began, he alone said that Borodino was a victory, and he repeated this both verbally and in his dispatches and reports until his death. He alone said that the loss of Moscow is not the loss of Russia. In reply to Lauriston's proposal of peace, he said: There can be no peace, for such is the people's will. He alone, during the French retreat, said that all our maneuvers are useless, that everything is being accomplished of itself better than we could desire, that the enemy must be offered a "golden bridge", that the battles at Tarutino, Vyazma, and Krasnoe were unnecessary, that they needed to keep enough strength to reach the border, and that he would not sacrifice a single Russian for ten Frenchmen.

Nor do his words alone prove that only he understood the meaning of the events. His actions—without the slightest deviation—were all directed toward one and the same threefold end: (1) to brace all his strength for the conflict with the French, (2) to defeat them, and (3) to drive them out of Russia, while minimizing as far as possible the suffering of our people and our army.

This procrastinator Kutuzov, whose motto was "Patience and Time," this enemy of decisive action, gave battle at Borodino and invested the preparations for it with unparalleled solemnity. This same Kutuzov, who before the battle of Austerlitz had predicted it would be lost, alone and against everyone else declared to his dying day that Borodino was a victory—despite generals' assurances that the battle was lost, and despite the unprecedented fact that an army had had to retreat after winning it. He alone, throughout the entire retreat, insisted that battles, which were useless then, should not be fought, and that a new war should not be begun, and that the Russian frontier should not be crossed.

It is easy now to understand the significance of these events, now that they and their results lie before us, provided we refrain from attributing to the actions of the masses aims that existed only in the heads of a dozen people.
The source of that extraordinary power of penetrating the meaning of the events then occurring lay in the national feeling that he possessed in full purity and strength.

Only the recognition that he possessed this feeling caused the people, in such a strange manner and contrary to the Tsar's wish, to choose him—an old man in disfavor—as their representative in the national war. And only that feeling placed him on the highest human pedestal from which he, the commander in chief, devoted all his powers not to slaying and destroying men but to saving them and showing them pity.
That simple, modest, and therefore truly great figure could not be cast in the false mold of a European hero—the supposed ruler of men—that history has invented.
To a lackey no man can be great, for a lackey has his own conception of greatness.
"Vive Henri Quatre! Vive ce roi valiant! — Long live Henry the Fourth! Long live that brave king!" sang Morel, winking. "Ce diable à quatre... — That rowdy devil..."
* Long live Henry the Fourth, that valiant king! That rowdy devil.
"Qui eut le triple talent, De boire, de battre, Et d'être un vert galant — who had a triple talent—for drinking, for fighting, and for being a charming fellow..."
* Who had a triple talent For drinking, for fighting, And for being a gallant old boy...

The French army melted away at the steady rate of a mathematical progression, and the crossing of the Berezina—about which so much has been written—was only one intermediate stage in its destruction, not at all the decisive episode of the campaign. If so much has been and still is written about the Berezina, on the French side this is only because at the broken bridge across that river, the calamities their army had been previously enduring were suddenly concentrated at one moment into a tragic spectacle that remained in every memory. On the Russian side, it's simply because in Petersburg—far from the actual fighting—a plan (again one of Pfuel's) had been devised to catch Napoleon in a strategic trap at the Berezina River. Everyone assured himself that everything would go according to plan, and therefore insisted that it was the Berezina crossing that destroyed the French army. In reality, the results of the crossing were far less disastrous to the French—in guns and men lost—than Krasnoe had been, as the numbers show.

The sole importance of the Berezina crossing lies in the fact that it plainly and undeniably proved the fallacy of all the plans to cut off the enemy's retreat and the soundness of the only possible course of action—the one Kutuzov and the general mass of the army had demanded—simply to follow the enemy. The French mob fled at ever-increasing speed, all its energy directed toward reaching its goal. It fled like a wounded animal, and it was impossible to block its path. This was shown not so much by its arrangements for crossing as by what happened at the bridges. When the bridges collapsed, unarmed soldiers, civilians from Moscow, and women with children who were traveling with the French—all carried forward by vis inertiæ—pressed forward into boats and into the ice-covered water and did not surrender.

That impulse was reasonable. The condition of both fugitives and pursuers was equally miserable. As long as they stayed with their own people, each could hope for help from comrades and hold a defined place among them. But those who surrendered—while remaining in that same wretched condition—dropped to a lower level in any claim on the necessities of life. The French didn't need to be told that half the prisoners—whom the Russians didn't know what to do with—perished of cold and hunger despite their captors' desire to save them. They sensed it could not be otherwise. The most compassionate Russian commanders, those favorably disposed toward the French—even the Frenchmen in the Russian service—could do nothing for the prisoners. The French perished from the very conditions to which the Russian army itself was exposed. It was impossible to take bread and clothing from our hungry and indispensable soldiers to give to Frenchmen who, though not harmful, or hated, or guilty, were simply unnecessary. Some Russians even did that, but they were exceptions.

The farther they fled, the more wretched became the plight of the remnant—especially after the Berezina, on which (in consequence of the Petersburg plan) the Russians had placed such high hopes—and the more heated grew the passions of the Russian commanders, who blamed one another and above all Kutuzov. Anticipation that the failure of the Petersburg Berezina plan would be attributed to Kutuzov led to growing dissatisfaction, contempt, and ridicule. The ridicule and contempt were expressed, of course, in respectful form, making it impossible for him to ask wherein he was to blame. They didn't talk seriously to him; when reporting or asking for his approval, they appeared to be fulfilling a regrettable formality while winking behind his back and trying to mislead him at every turn.

Because they couldn't understand him, all these people assumed it was useless to talk to the old man. He would never grasp the profundity of their plans, they thought; he would answer with his phrases (which they thought were mere phrases) about a "golden bridge" and the impossibility of crossing the frontier with a mob of ragged men, and so forth. They had heard all that before. And everything he said—that they needed to wait for supplies, that the men had no boots—was so simple, while what they proposed was so complex and clever, that it was evident that he was old and stupid, and that they, though not in command, were military geniuses.
"On account of your bouts of ill health, would Your Excellency be so good as to proceed to Kaluga upon receipt of this, there to await further commands and appointments from His Imperial Majesty."

But after Bennigsen's departure, the Grand Duke Tsarevich Constantine Pavlovich joined the army. He had participated at the beginning of the campaign but had subsequently been removed from the army by Kutuzov. Now, returning to the army, he informed Kutuzov of the Emperor's displeasure at the poor success of our forces and the slowness of their advance. The Emperor intended to join the army personally in a few days.

The old man was experienced in both court and military affairs. This was the same Kutuzov who in August had been chosen commander in chief against the sovereign's wishes, who had removed the Grand Duke and heir apparent from the army, and who on his own authority and contrary to the Emperor's will had decided to abandon Moscow. Now he instantly understood that his day was over, his role played out, and the power he supposedly held was no longer his. And he understood this not merely from the court's attitude. He saw, on the one hand, that the military business in which he had played his part was finished, and he felt his mission was accomplished. At the same time, he began to feel the physical weariness of his aged body and the need for physical rest.

On November twenty-ninth, Kutuzov entered Vilna—his "dear Vilna," as he called it. Twice during his career he had been governor of Vilna. In that wealthy city, which had not been damaged, he found old friends and associations as well as the comforts of life he had so long been deprived of. And he suddenly turned from the cares of army and state, and as far as the passions seething around him allowed, immersed himself in the quiet life he had once known, as if all that was taking place and all that had still to be done in the realm of history did not concern him at all.

Chichagov was one of the most zealous "cutters-off" and "breakers-up." He had first wanted to effect a diversion in Greece, then in Warsaw, but never wished to go where he was actually sent. He was noted, too, for his bold manner of speaking to the Emperor, and he considered Kutuzov indebted to him—because when he was sent to conclude peace with Turkey in 1811, independently of Kutuzov, he had found the peace already made, and he acknowledged to the Emperor that the credit belonged to Kutuzov. This Chichagov was the first to meet Kutuzov at the castle where the latter was to stay. In undress naval uniform, with a dirk, and holding his cap under his arm, he handed Kutuzov a garrison report and the keys to the city. The contemptuously respectful attitude of the younger men toward the old man in his dotage was expressed to the highest degree by the behavior of Chichagov, who knew of the accusations being leveled at Kutuzov.
In conversation with Chichagov, Kutuzov happened to mention that the vehicles packed with china captured from him at Borisov had been recovered and would be restored to him.

"You mean to imply that I have nothing to eat from.... On the contrary, I can supply you with everything, even if you want to throw dinner parties," Chichagov replied warmly, trying with every word to prove his own integrity and therefore imagining Kutuzov was driven by the same concern.
Kutuzov, shrugging his shoulders, replied with his subtle, penetrating smile: "I meant merely to say what I said."

A courier who galloped to the castle in advance, in a troika with three foam-flecked horses, shouted "Coming!" and Konovnitsyn rushed into the vestibule to inform Kutuzov, who was waiting in the hall porter's little lodge.

A minute later, the old man's large, heavy figure in full-dress uniform—his chest covered with orders and a sash wrapped around his stomach—waddled out onto the porch. He put on his hat with its peaks to the sides, and holding his gloves in his hand, walked with effort sideways down the steps to street level, taking in his hand the report he had prepared for the Emperor.

From the force of fifty years' habit, all this had a physically agitating effect on the old general. He carefully and hastily felt himself all over, readjusted his hat, and pulling himself together, drew himself upright. At the very moment the Emperor stepped down from the sleigh and looked up at him, Kutuzov handed over the report and began speaking in his smooth, ingratiating voice.

The Emperor swept a rapid glance over Kutuzov from head to foot, frowned for an instant, but immediately composed himself, stepped forward, extended his arms, and embraced the old man. This embrace too, because of a long-standing impression related to his innermost feelings, had its usual effect on Kutuzov, and he gave a sob.

When alone with the field marshal, the Emperor expressed his dissatisfaction at the slowness of the pursuit and the mistakes made at Krasnoe and the Berezina, and informed him of his intentions for a future campaign abroad. Kutuzov made no rejoinder or remark. The same submissive, expressionless look with which he had listened to the Emperor's orders on the field of Austerlitz seven years before settled on his face now.

Suddenly he appeared to remember. A barely perceptible smile flashed across his puffy face, and bowing low and respectfully, he took the object from the tray. It was the Order of St. George, First Class.
"What good is freedom to me, your excellency? We lived under the late count—God rest his soul!—and we've lived under you too, and never once been wronged."
"So what are your orders? Are you leaving tomorrow?" asked Savelich.
"I've seen Princess Mary," she replied. "I heard they were arranging a match for her with young Rostov. It would be a very good thing for the Rostovs—they say the family's utterly ruined."
