Though the surface of the sea of history looked motionless, the movement of humanity went on as unceasingly as the flow of time. Various groups of people formed and dissolved; the coming formation and dissolution of kingdoms, and the displacement of peoples, was being prepared.

The sea of history was no longer being driven spasmodically from shore to shore the way it had been before. It was seething in its depths. Historical figures were no longer being carried by the waves from one shore to another, as they had been. Now they seemed to spin in place. The historical figures who stood at the head of armies, and who had once reflected the movement of the masses by ordering wars, campaigns, and battles, now reflected that restless movement through political and diplomatic combinations, laws, and treaties.

In dealing with this period they severely condemn the historical figures who, in their view, caused what they call the reaction. All the well-known people of that era—from Alexander and Napoleon to the writer Madame de Staël, the churchman Photius, the philosophers Schelling and Fichte, and the writer Chateaubriand, and the rest—pass before their severe tribunal and are either acquitted or condemned, depending on whether they are judged to have served progress or reaction.

According to these accounts, a reaction took place in Russia too at that time, and the chief culprit was Alexander I—the same man who, by their own account, had been the chief cause of the liberal movement at the start of his reign, and the savior of Russia.
There is no one in Russian letters today, from schoolboy essayist to learned historian, who doesn't throw his little stone at Alexander for what he did wrong during this stretch of his reign.

"He should have acted this way here, and that way there. In this instance he did well, in that instance badly. He behaved admirably at the start of his reign and during 1812, but he behaved badly by granting Poland a constitution, by forming the Holy Alliance, by handing power over to his minister Arakcheev, by favoring Golitsyn and mysticism, and later the statesman Shishkov and Photius. He also behaved badly by meddling in the affairs of the active army, and by disbanding the Semenov regiment, a guards regiment."
It would take a dozen pages to list every reproach the historians level at him, all of it drawn from their knowledge of what is good for humanity.
What do these reproaches mean?

Don't the very actions the historians praise Alexander I for—his liberal moves at the start of his reign, his struggle against Napoleon, the firmness he showed in 1812 and in the campaign of 1813—flow from the same sources? Those sources are the circumstances of his birth, his education, his life, the things that made him the man he was. And isn't it from those same sources that the actions they blame him for also flowed—the Holy Alliance, the restoration of Poland, the reaction of 1820 and after?
What does the substance of these reproaches come down to?

It comes down to this. A historical figure like Alexander I stands on the very highest peak of human power, with the blinding light of history trained on him. He is a man exposed to the strongest influences there are—the intrigue, the flattery, the self-deception that power inevitably brings with it. He is a man who at every moment of his life felt himself responsible for everything happening across Europe. And he is a living man, not an invented character, a man who like every other man had his personal habits, passions, impulses toward goodness, beauty, and truth. Though not lacking in virtue—even the historians don't deny him that—this man did not hold the same idea of what was good for humanity fifty years ago that a present-day professor holds, a professor who has spent his whole life since youth doing nothing but study, which is to say, reading books and lectures and taking notes on them.

But even granting that Alexander I was mistaken, fifty years ago, in his view of what was good for the people, we're forced to assume something else as well. The historian sitting in judgment on Alexander will, after enough time has passed, turn out to have been mistaken in his view of what's good for humanity. This assumption isn't just natural, it's unavoidable, because if you watch the movement of history, you see that opinion about what's good for mankind shifts every year, with every new writer, so that what looked good ten years ago looks bad now, and the reverse. What's more, we find flatly contradictory views held at one and the same time about what counts as good and bad in history: some people count granting Poland a constitution and forming the Holy Alliance as praiseworthy acts of Alexander's, while others count the very same acts as blameworthy.

The activity of Alexander, or of Napoleon, can't be called either useful or harmful, because there's no way to say what it was useful or harmful for. If that activity displeases someone, it's only because it doesn't line up with that person's limited idea of what's good. I might judge the preservation of my father's house in Moscow, the glory of Russian arms, the prosperity of the universities of Petersburg and elsewhere, the freedom of Poland, the greatness of Russia, the balance of power in Europe, or some particular kind of European culture called "progress" to be good or bad. But whichever way I judge it, I have to admit that beyond all these things, the actions of every historical figure have other, more general purposes that I cannot see.

But let's grant, for argument's sake, that what we call science can reconcile all these contradictions and does possess an unchanging standard of good and bad by which to judge historical figures and events. Let's say Alexander could have done everything differently. Let's say that, guided by the very people who blame him now—people who claim to know the ultimate goal humanity is moving toward—he could have arranged everything according to the program his present-day accusers would hand him: nationality, freedom, equality, progress. Let's say that, I think, covers it. Let's assume this program was achievable, that it had already been worked out at the time, and that Alexander had acted on it. What, then, would have become of the activity of everyone who opposed the government's prevailing tendency at that time—activity that the historians themselves judge to have been good and beneficial? That activity would not have existed. There would have been no life. There would have been nothing.
If we accept that human life can be governed by reason, then the possibility of life is destroyed.

Historians assume that great men lead humanity toward certain goals: the greatness of Russia or of France, the balance of power in Europe, the spread of the ideas of the Revolution, general progress, or anything else. If we make that same assumption, there's no way to explain the facts of history without bringing in the ideas of chance and genius.

If the goal of the European wars at the start of the nineteenth century had been the aggrandizement of Russia, that goal could have been reached without all the wars that came before it, and without the invasion. If the goal was the aggrandizement of France, that could have been reached without the Revolution and without the Empire. If the goal was spreading ideas, the printing press could have done that job far better than warfare. If the goal was the progress of civilization, it's easy enough to see that there are other, more expedient ways of spreading civilization than by destroying wealth and human lives.
Why did it happen this way, and not some other way?

The words "chance" and "genius" don't point to any real, existing thing, and so they can't be defined. They only mark a certain stage in our understanding of phenomena. I don't know why some particular event happens; I think I can't know it; so I do not try to know it, and I call it chance. I see a force producing effects that go beyond the reach of ordinary human power; I don't understand why this is happening, and I call it genius.

To a flock of rams, the one ram that the shepherd drives every evening into a separate pen to be fed, and that grows twice as fat as the rest, must look like a genius. And it must seem an astonishing coincidence of genius with a whole run of extraordinary chances that this particular ram—the one that, instead of going into the general fold every evening, goes into a special pen full of oats—that this very ram, now bursting with fat, ends up slaughtered for meat.

But all the rams would have to do is stop assuming that everything that happens to them happens purely for the sake of their sheepish goals; they'd only have to admit that whatever happens to them might also have purposes beyond their understanding, and right away they'd see a unity, a coherence, in everything that happened to that fattened ram. Even without knowing what purpose they were being fattened for, they would at least know that nothing that happened to the ram happened by accident, and they would no longer need the ideas of chance or genius.

We have to give up our claim to make out some purpose we can immediately grasp, and admit that the ultimate purpose lies beyond our understanding. Only then can we see the sequence running through the experiences of historical figures, and grasp the cause behind the effects they produce—effects out of all proportion to ordinary human capacities. And once we do that, the words "chance" and "genius" become unnecessary.

We need only admit that we don't know the purpose behind the European convulsions. All we know are the facts: the murders, first in France, then in Italy, in Africa, in Prussia, in Austria, in Spain, and in Russia. And we need only admit that the movements from west to east and from east to west form the essence and the point of these events. Once we admit that, we won't just have no need to see extraordinary ability and genius in Napoleon and Alexander—we'll be unable to see them as anything but men like other men. And we won't need to reach for chance to explain the small events that made these men what they were, but it will be plain that every one of those small events was inevitable.

By giving up any claim to know the ultimate purpose, we'll see clearly that no one could imagine a blossom or a seed better suited to any given plant than the ones it produces. In just the same way, it's impossible to imagine any two people more perfectly fitted, down to the smallest detail, for the purpose they had to fulfill, than Napoleon and Alexander, with all their antecedents.

The fundamental, essential meaning of the European events of the early nineteenth century lies in the movement of the mass of European peoples from west to east, and afterward from east to west. The movement from west to east came first. For the peoples of the west to be able to make their warlike march to Moscow, three things had to happen: (1) they had to form themselves into a military group of a size large enough to withstand a collision with the warlike military group of the east; (2) they had to throw off all established traditions and customs; and (3) during their military march they had to have at their head a man who could justify to himself, and to them, the deceptions, the robberies, and the murders that this march would require.

And starting with the French Revolution, the old, inadequately sized group was broken apart, along with the old habits and traditions, and step by step a new group was formed, larger in scale, with new customs and new traditions, and a man was produced who would stand at the head of the coming movement and carry the responsibility for everything it would take.

A man emerges—by what look like the strangest chances—from all the seething French factions. He has no convictions, no habits, no traditions, not even a name; he is not even a Frenchman. Without attaching himself to any one of the factions, he is carried forward into a position of prominence.

The ignorance of his colleagues, the weakness and insignificance of his opponents, the bluntness of his lies, and this man's dazzling, self-assured limitations raise him to the head of the army. The brilliant qualities of the soldiers sent to Italy, his opponents' reluctance to fight, and his childish daring and self-confidence win him military fame. Countless so-called chances follow him wherever he goes. Falling out of favor with the rulers of France turns to his advantage. His attempts to escape his predestined path fail: he is refused a place in the Russian service, and the post he seeks in Turkey comes to nothing. During the war in Italy he comes to the brink of destruction several times, and each time is saved in some unexpected way. And thanks to various diplomatic considerations, the Russian armies—the very ones that might have destroyed his prestige—never turn up on the scene until he is already gone.

When he comes back from Italy he finds the government in Paris in the middle of falling apart—a process in which everyone attached to it is inevitably swept away and destroyed. And by chance, a way out of this dangerous position presents itself, in the form of a pointless, senseless expedition to Africa. Once again so-called chance goes with him. Impregnable Malta surrenders without a shot. His most reckless schemes are crowned with success. The enemy fleet, which afterward would not let a single boat slip past, lets his entire army through. In Africa a whole series of outrages are committed against a nearly unarmed population. And the men who commit these crimes, above all their leader, convince themselves that this is admirable, that this is glory—it resembles Caesar, it resembles Alexander the Great, and so it must be good.

This ideal of glory and grandeur consists not merely in seeing nothing wrong in whatever one does, but in taking pride in every crime one commits, treating it as if it carried some incomprehensible supernatural meaning. It was this ideal, destined to guide this man and everyone around him, that found room to develop in Africa. Whatever he attempts succeeds. The plague does not touch him. The cruelty of murdering prisoners is never held against him as a fault. His childish, reckless, needless, and shameful departure from Africa, abandoning his comrades in the middle of their troubles, is chalked up to his credit, and once again the enemy fleet twice lets him slip past. And when, drunk on the crimes he has carried off so successfully, he reaches Paris, the collapse of the republican government—which a year earlier might have finished him—has now gone as far as it can go, and his arrival there, a newcomer with no ties to any faction, can only lift him higher. And though he himself has no plan, he is quite ready to step into his new role.

He alone—with his ideal of glory and grandeur, worked out in Italy and Egypt, his insane self-worship, his boldness in crime, his bluntness in lying—he alone was capable of justifying what had to be done.

He is needed to fill the place waiting for him, and so, almost apart from his will, despite his indecision, his lack of any plan, and all his blunders, he is drawn into a conspiracy aimed at seizing power, and the conspiracy is crowned with success.

He is pushed into a meeting of the legislature. In a panic he wants to flee, believing himself finished. He pretends to fall into a swoon and says senseless things that should have destroyed him. But the once proud, once shrewd rulers of France, sensing that their part is played out, are even more confused than he is, and fail to say the words that would have destroyed him and kept their power.

Chance—millions of chances—hand him power, and everyone acts as though by agreement to help secure that power for him. Chance shapes the characters of France's rulers, who submit to him. Chance shapes the character of Paul I of Russia, who recognizes his government. Chance arranges a plot against him that not only fails to hurt him but ends up confirming his power. Chance puts the royalist Duc d'Enghien in his hands and unexpectedly causes him to kill him, thereby convincing the mob, more forcefully than anything else could, that he had the right, because he had the might. Chance sees to it that although he throws all his energy into preparing an expedition against England, one that would certainly have ruined him, he never carries it out, but instead unexpectedly falls upon the Austrian general Mack and the Austrians, who surrender without a fight. Chance and genius hand him victory at Austerlitz; and by chance, everyone—not just the French but all of Europe, except England, which takes no part in the events about to unfold—despite their former horror and loathing of his crimes, now recognizes his authority, the title he has given himself, and his ideal of grandeur and glory, which strikes them all as excellent and reasonable.

As if sizing themselves up, as if preparing for the movement to come, the western forces push eastward again and again, in 1805, 1806, 1807, and 1809, gathering strength and growing. In 1811 the group that had formed in France merges into a single body with the peoples of Central Europe. The force of the justification behind the man at the head of this movement grows along with the increased size of the group. Across this ten-year period of preparation, this man has formed ties with every crowned head in Europe. The discredited rulers of the world have no reasonable ideal to set against Napoleon's mad ideal of glory and grandeur. One after another they rush to parade their insignificance before him. The King of Prussia sends his wife to beg the great man for mercy. The Emperor of Austria counts it a favor that this man receives a daughter of the Caesars into his bed. The Pope, guardian of everything the nations hold sacred, puts religion to work glorifying the great man. It isn't so much Napoleon preparing himself to carry out his role, as it is everyone around him preparing him to shoulder the entire responsibility for everything that is happening and has to happen. There is no step he takes, no crime, no petty fraud, that the people around him don't instantly dress up as a great deed. The most suitable celebration the Germans can think up in his honor is a commemoration of the battles of Jena and Auerstädt. Not only is he great, but so are his ancestors, his brothers, his stepsons, his brothers-in-law. Everything is done to strip him of whatever reason he has left and to ready him for his terrible part. And by the time he is ready, so too are the forces.

The invasion pushes eastward and reaches its final goal, Moscow. The city is taken. The Russian army suffers heavier losses than the opposing armies suffered in the earlier fighting, from Austerlitz to Wagram. But suddenly, in place of the chances and the genius that up to now had carried him, without a single break, from success to success toward his predestined goal, an innumerable sequence of chances now runs the other way, from the head cold that strikes him at the battle of Borodino, to the sparks that set Moscow ablaze, to the frosts; and in place of genius, stupidity and boundless baseness come to the surface.

Then a countermovement takes place from east to west, one that bears a remarkable resemblance to the movement from west to east that came before it. Attempted pushes from east to west, much like the earlier counter-movements of 1805, 1807, and 1809, come before the great westward movement; there is the same coming together into a group of enormous size; the same joining of the peoples of Central Europe to the movement; the same hesitation partway through; and the same gathering speed as the goal draws near.

Paris, the final goal, is reached. The Napoleonic government and army are destroyed. Napoleon himself no longer matters; every one of his actions is now plainly pitiful and petty. And yet once again an inexplicable chance occurs. The allies detest Napoleon, whom they blame for their suffering. Stripped of power and authority, his crimes and his scheming laid bare, he should have looked to them as he had looked ten years earlier and would look again a year later: an outlawed brigand. But by some strange chance, no one sees him that way. His part is not finished yet. The man who was considered an outlawed brigand ten years before, and would be considered one again a year later, is sent to an island two days' sail from France, an island that, for some reason, is handed over to him as his dominion, complete with guards and millions of money paid to him.

"I'll bring him to you directly, Monsieur Dessalles. Good night!" said Pierre, offering his hand to the Swiss tutor, and then he turned to young Nicholas with a smile. "You and I haven't seen anything of one another yet.... How like he is growing, Mary!" he added, turning to Countess Mary.

"One used to have to be German—now one has to dance with Tatáwinova and Madame Kwüdener, and wead Ecka'tshausen and the bwethwen. Oh, they should let that fine fellow Bonaparte loose—he'd knock all this nonsense out of them! Fancy giving command of the Semenov wegiment to a fellow like that Schwa'tz!" he cried.

Nicholas, though he lacked Denisov's readiness to find fault with everything, also thought that discussing the government was a very serious, weighty matter, and it seemed to him a matter of real importance that A had been appointed Minister of This, and B Governor General of That, and that the Emperor had said such and such, and this minister had said such and such. And so he thought it necessary to take an interest in these things, and questioned Pierre. The questions the two of them put kept the conversation from straying beyond its ordinary character—gossip about the upper reaches of government.

"Why this," Pierre began, not sitting down but pacing the room, sometimes stopping short, gesturing, and lisping: "the situation in Petersburg is this. The Emperor pays no attention to anything anymore. He's given himself over entirely to this mysticism"—Pierre could no longer stand mysticism in anyone—"he only wants peace, and only these people, sans foi ni loi—without faith or law—can give it to him—people who go around recklessly hacking and strangling everything: Magnitsky, Arakcheev, and tutti quanti—and all the rest.... You'll agree that if you didn't oversee your own estates yourself, and only wanted a quiet life, the harsher your steward was, the more easily your object would be achieved," he said to Nicholas.

"Well, everything is going to ruin! Robbery in the law courts, nothing in the army but flogging, drilling, and Military Settlements; the people are being tormented, enlightenment is being crushed. Everything young and honest is being ground down! Everyone can see this can't go on. Everything is stretched so tight that it's bound to snap," said Pierre—much as everyone who has ever examined the actions of any government has said, since governments began. "I told them just one thing, in Petersburg."

"Why? Let him be," said Pierre, taking Nicholas by the arm and going on. "That's not enough, I told them. Something else is needed. When you're standing there expecting the overstretched string to snap at any moment, when everyone is expecting the inevitable catastrophe, then as many people as possible need to join hands, as tightly as they can, to stand against the general calamity. Everything young and strong is being lured away and corrupted. One man is drawn off by women, another by honors, a third by ambition or money, and off they go, over to that camp. There are no independent men left—men like you or me. What I'm saying is: widen the scope of our society, let the watchword be not virtue alone, but independence and action as well!"
Nicholas, who had left his nephew, irritably pulled up an armchair, sat down in it, and listened to Pierre, coughing with displeasure and frowning more and more.

"Why? Did the Tugendbund, which saved Europe" (they did not yet dare suggest that it was Russia that had saved Europe) "do any harm? The Tugendbund is an alliance of virtue: it's love, mutual aid... it's what Christ preached on the Cross."

"No, my fwiend! The Tugendbund's all vewy well for sausage eaters, but I don't understand it and can't even pwonounce it," Denisov broke in, loudly and firmly. "I agwee that evewything here is wotten and howwible, but the Tugendbund I don't understand. If we're not satisfied, let's have a wevolt of our own. That's all wight. Je suis vot'e homme—I'm your man!"

"I'll tell you this," he said, standing up and trying, with nervously twitching fingers, to prop his pipe up in a corner, then finally giving up the attempt. "I can't prove it to you. You say everything here is rotten, and that an overthrow is coming: I don't see it. But you also say our oath of allegiance is a conditional matter, and to that I reply: 'You are my best friend, as you well know, but if you formed a secret society and started working against the government—whatever government it may be—I know it's my duty to obey the government. And if Arakcheev ordered me to lead a squadron against you and cut you down, I wouldn't hesitate an instant, and I'd do it.' Argue about that all you like!"

Natasha and Pierre, alone together, began to talk the way only a husband and wife can: with remarkable clarity and speed, each understanding and finishing the other's thoughts in ways that violated every rule of logic — no premises, no chain of reasoning, no conclusions, and in a quite peculiar way. Natasha was so used to talking this way with her husband that for her the surest sign something was wrong between them was if Pierre started reasoning logically. When he began proving a point, arguing something out calmly, and she, following his lead, did the same, she knew they were on the edge of a quarrel.

From the moment they were alone, and Natasha came to him with her eyes wide open and happy, quickly grabbing his head and pressing it to her chest, saying, "Now you're all mine, mine! You won't get away!" — from that moment this conversation began, defying every law of logic, and defying it precisely because entirely different subjects were being discussed at the very same time. This simultaneous discussion of many topics didn't get in the way of clear understanding — on the contrary, it was the surest sign that they understood each other completely.

Natasha talked to Pierre about her brother's life and doings, about how she'd suffered and lacked life during his absence, about how she'd grown fonder than ever of Mary, and how Mary was better than her in every way. In saying this Natasha was sincere in acknowledging Mary's superiority, but at the same time, by saying it, she was making a demand on Pierre: that he should still, after all, prefer her to Mary and to every other woman, and that now, especially after seeing so many women in Petersburg, he should say so again.

"No, the main thing is that for Nicholas, ideas and arguments are a kind of amusement — almost a pastime," said Pierre. "For instance, he's building a library, and he's made it a rule never to buy a new book until he's read what he'd already bought — Sismondi and Rousseau and Montesquieu," he added with a smile. "You know how much I..." he began to soften what he'd said, but Natasha cut him off to show it wasn't necessary.

"Yes," Pierre replied, and went on with what was on his mind. "Nicholas says we ought not to think. But I can't help it. Besides, when I was in Petersburg I felt — I can say this to you — that the whole undertaking would fall apart without me, that everyone was pulling in his own direction. But I managed to bring them all together, and my idea is so clear and so simple. You see, I'm not saying we should oppose this or that. We could be wrong. What I say is: 'Join hands, all of you who love what is right, and let there be a single banner — that of active virtue.' Prince Sergey is a fine man, and clever."

Natasha would have had no doubt at all about the greatness of Pierre's idea, except that one thing unsettled her. "Can a man so important, so necessary to society, also be my husband? How did that happen?" She wanted to put this doubt to him. "Now who could really say whether he was cleverer than everyone else?" she asked herself, and ran through everyone Pierre most respected. Judging by what he'd said, there was no one he respected as highly as Platon Karataev.
"Platon Karataev?" he repeated, and thought about it, evidently sincerely trying to imagine what Karataev's opinion would be. "He wouldn't have understood... and yet maybe he would."
"I love you awfully!" Natasha suddenly said. "Awfully, awfully!"

"No, he wouldn't have approved," Pierre said after reflection. "What he would have approved of is our family life. He was always so eager to find seemliness, happiness, and peace in everything, and I would have been proud to have him see us. You know, you talk about my being away, but you wouldn't believe what a special feeling I have for you after a separation..."
"No, it's not that. I never stop loving you. And one couldn't love more — but this is something special... Yes, of course—" he didn't finish, because their eyes meeting said the rest.
"Don't say it! I can't bear it!" Natasha cried, and her eyes glittered coldly and vindictively. "Did you see her?" she added after a pause.

"Oh, do you know? While you were talking in the study I was watching you," Natasha began, clearly wanting to clear away the cloud that had settled over them. "You're as alike as two peas — like the boy." (She meant her little son.) "Oh, it's time to go to him... the milk's come... but I hate to leave you."

"Oh, it's nothing, just a trifle," said Natasha, smiling more brightly still. "I only wanted to tell you about Petya: today nurse came to take him from me, and he laughed, shut his eyes, and clung to me. I'm sure he thought he was hiding. Awfully sweet! There, now he's crying. Well, goodbye!" — and she left the room.

Meanwhile downstairs, in little Nicholas Bolkonski's bedroom, a small lamp burned as it always did. (The boy was afraid of the dark, and they hadn't been able to cure him of it.) Dessalles slept propped up on four pillows, his Roman nose giving off a steady, rhythmic snore. Little Nicholas, who had just woken up in a cold sweat, sat up in bed and stared ahead with wide-open eyes. He'd woken from a terrible dream. He'd dreamed that he and Uncle Pierre, wearing helmets like the ones pictured in his Plutarch, were leading a huge army. The army was made up of white slanting lines that filled the air like the strands of cobweb that drift about in autumn — the ones Dessalles called les fils de la Vierge, the Virgin's threads. Out in front was Glory, which looked like those threads, only thicker. He and Pierre were being carried forward, light and joyful, closer and closer to their goal. Then suddenly the threads carrying them began to go slack and tangle, and it grew hard to move. And Uncle Nicholas stood before them, stern and threatening.

"My father!" he thought. (Though there were two good portraits of Prince Andrew in the house, Nicholas never pictured him in human shape.) "My father was here with me, and he caressed me. He approved of me, and of Uncle Pierre. Whatever he tells me to do, I will do. The Roman Mucius Scaevola burned his hand. Why shouldn't something like that happen to me too? I know they want me to keep studying. And I will study. But someday I'll be finished, and then I'll do something. I only pray to God that something happens to me like what happened to Plutarch's men, and I'll act as they did. I'll do even better. Everyone will know me, love me, be delighted with me!" And suddenly his chest heaved with sobs and he began to cry.

"He's good and kind, and I'm fond of him!" he thought of Dessalles. "But Uncle Pierre! Oh, what an extraordinary man he is! And my father? Oh, Father, Father! Yes, I will do something that even he would be satisfied with..."

Historians who write biographies, or histories of a single nation, understand this force as a power built into heroes and rulers. In their telling, events happen purely by the will of a Napoleon, an Alexander, or whichever figure they are writing about. The answers this kind of historian gives to the question of what force makes events happen are satisfying only so long as a single historian is covering a single event. As soon as historians of different nationalities and different leanings start describing the same event, their answers immediately lose all meaning, because this force is understood by each of them not just differently, but often in quite contradictory ways. One historian says an event was produced by Napoleon's power, another that it was produced by Alexander's, a third that it came from the power of some other person. What's more, historians of this kind contradict one another even on the question of what a given person's authority was based on. The historian Thiers, a Bonapartist, says Napoleon's power rested on his virtue and his genius. The historian Lanfrey, a Republican, says it rested on his trickery and his deception of the people. So historians of this class, by tearing down each other's positions, tear down any understanding of the force that produces events, and give no answer to history's essential question.

Writers of universal history, who deal with all nations, seem to recognize how mistaken the specialist historians' view of the force producing events is. They do not treat it as a power built into heroes and rulers, but as the resultant of many differently directed forces. In describing a war, or the subjugation of a people, a general historian looks for the cause of the event not in the power of one man, but in the interaction of the many people connected to that event.

On this view, the power of historical figures—presented as the product of many forces—can no longer, it would seem, be treated as a force that itself produces events. And yet in most cases the universal historians still use the idea of power as a force that produces events in its own right, and treat it as a cause. In their accounts, a historical figure is first the product of his era, his power merely the resultant of various forces—and then his power is itself a force producing events. The historians Gervinus, Schlosser, and others, for instance, at one point prove that Napoleon was a product of the Revolution, of the ideas of 1789 and so on. At another point they plainly state that the campaign of 1812, and other things they disapprove of, were simply the product of Napoleon's misguided will, and that the very ideas of 1789 were stopped in their development by Napoleon's whim. The ideas of the Revolution and the general temper of the age produced Napoleon's power. But Napoleon's power suppressed the ideas of the Revolution and the general temper of the age.

This curious contradiction is not an accident. Not only does it turn up at every step, but the universal historians' accounts are made up, from end to end, of a chain of such contradictions. It happens because once the universal historians enter the field of analysis, they stop halfway.

To find component forces equal to a composite or resultant force (as in mechanics), the sum of the components must equal the resultant. The universal historians never observe this condition, and so, to explain the resultant forces, they are forced to bring in—alongside their insufficient components—some other, unexplained force acting on the outcome.

Specialist historians describing the campaign of 1813, or the restoration of the Bourbons, state plainly that these events were produced by Alexander's will. But the universal historian Gervinus, refuting this view of the specialist historians, tries to show that the campaign of 1813 and the restoration of the Bourbons came about because of other things besides Alexander's will—the activity of the statesmen and writers Stein, Metternich, Madame de Staël, Talleyrand, Fichte, Chateaubriand, and others. The historian, in effect, breaks Alexander's power down into its components: Talleyrand, Chateaubriand, and the rest. But the sum of those components—that is, the interactions among Chateaubriand, Talleyrand, Madame de Staël, and the others—plainly does not add up to the resultant: the fact of millions of Frenchmen submitting to the Bourbons. The fact that Chateaubriand, Madame de Staël, and the others said certain things to one another only affected their own mutual relations, but does not account for the submission of millions. And so, to explain how the submission of millions of people resulted from these relations of theirs—that is, how component forces adding up to some quantity A produced a resultant a thousand times greater than A—the historian is again forced to fall back on power. This is the force he had denied, and he now treats it as the resultant of the forces, which means admitting an unexplained force acting on the outcome. And that is exactly what the universal historians do, and as a result they contradict not only the specialist historians but themselves.

Peasants, who have no clear idea of what causes rain, say, depending on whether they want rain or fine weather: "The wind has blown the clouds away," or, "The wind has brought up the clouds." In the same way, the universal historians sometimes, when it suits them and fits their theory, say that power is the result of events, and sometimes, when they want to prove something else, say that power produces events.

A third class of historians—the so-called historians of culture—following the path laid down by the universal historians, who sometimes treat writers and society ladies as forces producing events, take that force to be something else again. They find it in what is called culture, in intellectual activity.

The historians of culture are quite consistent with their forerunners, the writers of universal history: if historical events can be explained by the fact that certain people treated one another in such and such ways, why not explain them by the fact that certain people wrote certain books? Out of the immense number of signs that accompany every living phenomenon, these historians pick out the sign of intellectual activity and declare that this sign is the cause. But despite all their efforts to prove that the cause of events lies in intellectual activity, one can admit any connection between intellectual activity and the movement of peoples only with a considerable stretch. And one can never admit that intellectual activity controls people's actions. This view is not confirmed by facts such as the extremely cruel murders of the French Revolution, which grew out of the doctrine of the equality of man, or the extremely cruel wars and executions that grew out of the preaching of love.

But even granting as valid every one of the cleverly constructed arguments these histories are full of—even granting that nations are governed by some undefined force called an idea—history's essential question still goes unanswered. To the old power of monarchs, and to the influence of advisers and other people brought in by the universal historians, a newer force is now added—the idea—whose connection to the masses still needs explaining. One can understand that Napoleon had power, and so events occurred. With some effort, one can even accept that Napoleon, together with other influences, was the cause of an event. But how a book, Rousseau's Le Contrat Social (The Social Contract), had the effect of making Frenchmen start drowning one another cannot be understood without an explanation of the causal chain linking this new force to the event.

Undoubtedly some relation exists among everyone who lives at the same time, and so it's possible to find some connection between men's intellectual activity and their historical movements, just as a connection can be found between the movements of humanity and commerce, handicraft, gardening, or anything else you like. But why intellectual activity should be treated by the historians of culture as the cause, or as the expression, of the whole historical movement is hard to understand. Only the following considerations can have led historians to such a conclusion. (1) History is written by learned men, and so it is natural and gratifying for them to think that the activity of their own class provides the basis for the movement of all humanity—just as the same belief comes naturally and agreeably to merchants, farmers, and soldiers. (If they do not say so, it is simply because merchants and soldiers do not write history.) (2) Spiritual activity, enlightenment, civilization, culture, ideas—these are all vague, indefinite notions, under whose banner it is very easy to use words with an even less definite meaning, and which can therefore be worked into any theory.

But setting aside the intrinsic worth of histories of this kind (which may perhaps even be useful to someone, for something), the histories of culture—which all general histories are increasingly coming to resemble—are revealing in this respect. After seriously and painstakingly examining various religious, philosophical, and political doctrines as the causes of events, the moment they have to describe an actual historical event, such as the campaign of 1812, they involuntarily describe it as the outcome of an exercise of power. They say plainly that it was the result of Napoleon's will. In saying this, the historians of culture unwittingly contradict themselves, and show that the new force they have invented does not account for what happens in history, and that history can only be explained by bringing in a power they apparently do not recognize.

History has given up the ancients' idea that a nation's will is divinely subordinated to some chosen man, and that this man's will in turn is subordinated to God. Without that idea, history cannot take a single step without contradicting itself, until it chooses one of two things: either return to the old belief in the direct intervention of God in human affairs, or arrive at a definite explanation of what is meant by that force which produces historical events and which we call "power."

Napoleon ordered an army raised and sent to war. We are so used to this idea, so accustomed to it, that the question of why six hundred thousand men went off to fight when Napoleon spoke certain words strikes us as senseless. He had the power, and so what he ordered was done.

It cannot be the direct physical power of a strong man over a weak one—a domination based on applying or threatening physical force, like the strength of Hercules; nor can it rest on moral force, as some historians naively suppose when they say that the great figures of history are heroes, meaning men gifted with a special strength of soul and mind called genius. This power cannot rest on a predominance of moral strength, because—setting aside heroes like Napoleon, whose moral qualities are a matter of sharp disagreement—history shows us that neither a Louis XI, the French king, nor a Metternich, the Austrian statesman—both of whom ruled over millions of people—possessed any particular moral qualities; but, on the contrary, they were generally morally weaker than any of the millions they ruled.

If the source of power lies neither in the physical nor in the moral qualities of the one who holds it, then it must evidently be sought elsewhere—in the relation between the man who wields power and the people over whom he wields it.
And that is exactly how power is understood by the science of jurisprudence—that exchange bank of history, offering to trade history's understanding of power for real gold.

The science of jurisprudence treats the state and power the way the ancients treated fire—as something that simply exists, absolutely. But for history, the state and power are merely phenomena, just as for modern physics fire is not an element but a phenomenon.

This basic difference between how history views the matter and how jurisprudence views it has a consequence. Jurisprudence can tell us, in detail, how power ought—in its opinion—to be constituted, and what power is when treated as something fixed outside of time. But to history's questions about how power actually changes over time, jurisprudence can give no answer at all.

If power is the collective will of the people transferred to their ruler, was Pugachev—the Cossack who led a peasant uprising—a representative of the people's will? If not, why was Napoleon I? Why was Napoleon III a criminal when he was captured at Boulogne, and why, later, were the people he himself arrested the criminals?

Do palace revolutions—in which sometimes only two or three people take part—transfer the people's will to a new ruler? In international relations, is the people's will also transferred to a conqueror? Was the will of the Confederation of the Rhine, the alliance of German states under Napoleon, transferred to Napoleon in 1806? Was the will of the Russian people transferred to Napoleon in 1809, when our army, allied with the French, went to fight the Austrians?

Three assumptions are possible. (1) We may assume that the will of the people is always transferred unconditionally to the ruler or rulers it has chosen, so that every emergence of a new power, every struggle against a power already appointed, must be regarded as a violation of the real power. (2) We may assume that the will of the people is transferred to rulers conditionally, under definite and known conditions, and show that every limitation on power, every conflict, even every destruction of power, results from the rulers' failure to observe the conditions under which their power was entrusted to them. (3) We may assume that the will of the people is delegated to rulers conditionally, but that the conditions are unknown and undefined, and that the rise of rival authorities, their struggles, and their falls, result simply from how well or badly the rulers fulfilled these unknown conditions under which the people's will passes from one person to another.

Some historians—the biographical and specialist historians already mentioned—fail, in their simplicity, to grasp the real question of what power means. They seem to consider that the collective will of the people is transferred unconditionally to historical figures. So, in describing any single state, they treat that state's particular power as the one absolute, real power, and treat any force opposing it not as a power at all but as a violation of power—sheer violence.

Their theory, well suited to primitive and peaceful periods of history, runs into trouble when applied to complex and turbulent periods in the life of nations, during which several powers arise at once and struggle against one another. A Legitimist historian—a supporter of the old monarchy—will prove that the National Convention and the Directory, the revolutionary governments that followed, and Bonaparte too, were nothing but usurpers of the true power. A Republican historian will prove that the Convention was the real power, and a Bonapartist—a supporter of Napoleon—that the Empire was, and that all the rest were violations of power. Since these explanations plainly contradict one another, they can satisfy no one but young children.

Recognizing the falseness of this view of history, another group of historians say that power rests on a conditional delegation of the people's will to its rulers, and that historical leaders hold power only on condition of carrying out the program that the people's will has, by tacit agreement, prescribed for them. But what this program actually consists of, these historians do not say—or if they do, they keep contradicting one another.

Each historian, depending on his own view of what constitutes a nation's progress, looks for these conditions in the greatness, wealth, freedom, or enlightenment of the citizens of France or some other country. But setting aside the historians' disagreements over the nature of this program—even granting that some single, general program of these conditions exists—the facts of history almost always contradict the theory. If the conditions under which power is entrusted consist in the wealth, freedom, and enlightenment of the people, how is it that Louis XIV and Ivan the Terrible end their reigns peacefully, while Louis XVI and Charles I are executed by their own people? To this, historians answer that Louis XIV's conduct, though it went against the program, reacted on Louis XVI. But why did it not react on Louis XIV himself, or on Louis XV—why did it have to react precisely on Louis XVI? And what is the time limit on such reactions? These questions have no answer, and can have none. Just as little does this view explain why, for several centuries, the collective will is never withdrawn from a given line of rulers and their heirs, and then, suddenly, over the course of fifty years, passes to the Convention, to the Directory, to Napoleon, to Alexander, to Louis XVIII, to Napoleon again, to Charles X, to Louis Philippe, to a Republican government, and to Napoleon III. Trying to explain these rapid transfers of the people's will from one person to another—especially once international relations, conquests, and alliances are factored in—historians are forced to admit that some of these transfers are not normal delegations of the people's will, but accidents resulting from cunning, from mistakes, from craft, or from the weakness of some diplomat, ruler, or party leader. So that the greater part of the events of history—civil wars, revolutions, conquests—end up being presented by these historians not as the outcome of free transfers of the people's will, but as the outcome of the misdirected will of one or a few individuals—that is, once again, as usurpations of power. And so these historians too end up seeing, and admitting, historical events that are exceptions to their own theory.

These historians resemble a botanist who, having noticed that some plants grow from seeds that produce two seed-leaves, insists that everything that grows must sprout in exactly that way, and that the palm, the mushroom, and even the oak—which grow into full maturity looking nothing like two leaves—are deviations from the theory.

But then the question arises whether the entire activity of the leaders serves as an expression of the people's will, or only some part of it. If the whole of a leader's activity counts as an expression of the people's will, as some historians suppose, then every detail of court scandal found in the biographies of a Napoleon or a Catherine must also express the life of the nation. That is obvious nonsense. But if only some particular side of a historical leader's activity expresses the people's life, as other, so-called "philosophical" historians believe, then, to know which side of a leader's activity expresses the nation's life, we would first have to know what the nation's life actually consists of.

Faced with this difficulty, historians of this class devise some highly obscure, intangible, and general abstraction, broad enough to cover any conceivable occurrence, and declare this abstraction to be the goal of humanity's movement. The most common generalizations adopted by nearly all historians are: freedom, equality, enlightenment, progress, civilization, culture. Having set up some such generalization as the goal of humanity's movement, historians go on to study the men who left behind the greatest number of monuments—kings, ministers, generals, authors, reformers, popes, journalists—according to how far, in the historian's opinion, these people advanced or hindered that abstraction. But it is nowhere proven that the goal of humanity actually consists in freedom, equality, enlightenment, or civilization. And the connection between the people and the rulers and enlighteners of humanity rests only on the arbitrary assumption that the collective will of the people is always transferred to the men we have noticed. So the activity of the millions who migrate, burn houses, abandon their fields, and destroy one another is never actually captured in the account of the activity of a dozen or so people who did none of that burning, farming, or killing.

History bears this out at every turn. Is the ferment among the peoples of the West at the end of the eighteenth century, and their surge eastward, explained by the activity of Louis XIV, XV, and XVI, their mistresses and their ministers, and by the lives of Napoleon, Rousseau, the philosopher Diderot, the playwright Beaumarchais, and the rest?
Is the movement of the Russian people eastward, toward Kazan and Siberia, captured in the details of Ivan the Terrible's disturbed character, or in his correspondence with the nobleman Kurbsky?

Is the movement of the peoples at the time of the Crusades explained by the lives and activities of the Godfreys—men like the Crusader Godfrey—and the Louis-es, the various kings named Louis, and their ladies? For us, that movement of peoples from west to east, leaderless, made up of a crowd of wanderers, and with Peter the Hermit, a preacher, among them, remains incomprehensible. And still more incomprehensible is the way that movement stopped once a rational and sacred goal for the Crusade—the liberation of Jerusalem—had been clearly spelled out by the historical leaders. Popes, kings, and knights urged the peoples on to free the Holy Land; but the people did not go, because the unknown cause that had earlier driven them to go no longer existed. The history of the Godfreys and the Minnesingers, the medieval poet-singers, plainly cannot cover the life of the peoples. And the history of the Godfreys and the Minnesingers has remained just that—the history of the Godfreys and the Minnesingers—while the history of the life of the peoples and their impulses has remained unknown.

The history of culture explains to us the impulses and living conditions and thoughts of a writer or a reformer. We learn that Luther had a hot temper and said such and such things; we learn that Rousseau was suspicious and wrote such and such books; but we do not learn why, after the Reformation, whole peoples massacred one another, or why, during the French Revolution, they guillotined one another.
If we combine both these kinds of history, as the newest historians do, we end up with a history of monarchs and writers—but not a history of the life of the peoples.

The life of nations is not contained in the lives of a handful of men, because the connection between those men and the nations has not been found. The theory that this connection rests on the transfer of the people's collective will to certain historical figures is a hypothesis unsupported by the experience of history.

The theory of the transfer of the people's collective will to historical figures may perhaps explain a great deal within the domain of jurisprudence, and be essential for its purposes; but applied to history, the moment revolutions, conquests, or civil wars occur—that is, the moment history actually begins—that theory explains nothing.
The theory looks irrefutable precisely because the act of transferring the people's will cannot be verified, since it never took place.
Whatever happens, and whoever may stand at the head of affairs, the theory can always claim that this person took the lead because the collective will was transferred to him.

"The herd is heading that way because the animal in front is leading it, and the collective will of all the other animals has been vested in that leader." This is what historians of the first class say—those who assume the people's will is transferred unconditionally.

"If the animals leading the herd keep changing, that's because the collective will of all the animals is transferred from one leader to another, depending on whether the animal is or isn't leading them in the direction the whole herd has chosen." That is the answer given by historians who assume that the collective will of the people is delegated to rulers under conditions they take to be known. (With this method of observation, it often happens that the observer, influenced by whichever direction he himself prefers, regards those as leaders who, owing to the people's change of direction, are no longer in front—they may be off to one side, or even at the back.)
The theory of the transfer of the people's will to historical figures is nothing but a paraphrase—a restatement of the question in different words.

What causes historical events? Power. What is power? Power is the collective will of the people transferred to one person. Under what condition is the people's will delegated to one person? On condition that this person expresses the will of the whole people. That is: power is power—in other words, power is a word whose meaning we do not understand.

If the realm of human knowledge were limited to abstract reasoning, then, having subjected to criticism the explanation of "power" that juridical science gives us, mankind would conclude that power is merely a word with no real existence behind it. But to understand phenomena, man has, besides abstract reasoning, experience, by which he tests his reasoning. And experience tells us that power is not merely a word, but a phenomenon that actually exists.

Not to speak of the fact that no description of the collective activity of men can do without the idea of power, the existence of power is proven both by history and by observing events happening around us now.

Whenever an event occurs, a man appears, or several men appear, by whose will the event seems to have taken place. Napoleon III issues a decree, and the French go to Mexico. The King of Prussia and the Prussian statesman Bismarck issue decrees, and an army enters Bohemia. Napoleon I issues a decree, and an army enters Russia. Alexander I gives a command, and the French submit to the Bourbons, France's former ruling dynasty. Experience shows us that, whatever the event, it is always tied to the will of one or several men who decreed it.

Historians, following the old habit of acknowledging divine intervention in human affairs, want to see the cause of events in the expressed will of someone who holds power—but that assumption is confirmed neither by reason nor by experience.

On one hand, reflection shows that the expression of a man's will—his words—is only part of the general activity expressed in an event, as in a war or a revolution, and so, without assuming some incomprehensible, supernatural force—a miracle—one cannot accept that words could be the immediate cause of the movements of millions of men. On the other hand, even granting that words could be the cause of events, history shows that the expressed will of historical figures does not, in most cases, produce any effect. Their commands are often not carried out, and sometimes the exact opposite of what they order happens instead.

If God issues a command, expresses His will, as ancient history tells us, then the expression of that will is independent of time and caused by nothing, since the Divine is not subject to events. But when we speak of commands that express the will of men acting in time and in relation to one another, to explain the connection between commands and events we must restore two things: (1) the condition underlying everything that happens—the continuity of movement in time, both of the events themselves and of the person giving the command; and (2) the inevitability of the connection between the person giving the command and those who carry it out.

When an event is taking place, people voice their opinions and wishes about it, and since the event results from the collective activity of many people, one of the opinions or wishes expressed is bound to come true, at least approximately. When one of these expressed opinions comes true, it gets linked to the event as a command that preceded it.

Some men are hauling a log. Each of them says how and where he thinks it should be hauled. They haul the log away, and it turns out to have been done the way one of them said. He gave the order. There we have command and power in their most basic form. The man who did the most physical work could hardly think much about what he was doing, or reflect on or command what the joint effort would produce; while the man who did more commanding would obviously work less with his hands, given how much more talking he was doing.

When a larger group of people direct their activity toward a shared goal, there is a still sharper division of those who, because their activity goes toward directing and commanding, take less part in the direct work.

For reasons known or unknown to us, the French began drowning and killing one another. And to match the event, its justification appeared: the belief that this was necessary for the welfare of France, for liberty, for equality. People stopped killing one another, and this event too came with its justification: the necessity of centralizing power, of resisting Europe, and so on. Men marched from west to east killing their fellow men, and the event was accompanied by phrases about the glory of France, the baseness of England, and so on. History shows us that these justifications make no sense at all and contradict one another—as when killing a man is the result of recognizing his rights, and the killing of millions in Russia is justified by the need to humiliate England. But in their own day, these justifications carry a very necessary meaning.

Without such justification, there would be no answer to the simplest question that comes up when examining any historical event: how is it that millions of men commit collective crimes—wage war, commit murder, and so on?

Whichever direction a ship is moving, the flow of the water it cuts will always be visible just ahead of it. To the people on board, the movement of that flow will seem like the only perceptible motion there is.

Only by watching closely, moment by moment, the movement of that flow, and comparing it with the movement of the ship, do we convince ourselves that every bit of it is caused by the ship moving forward, and that we were misled because we ourselves were moving without noticing it.

We see the same thing if we watch, moment by moment, the movement of historical figures—that is, if we restore the necessary condition of everything that happens, the continuity of movement in time—and if we never lose sight of the essential connection between historical figures and the masses.

Whatever happens, it always looks as though that very event had been foreseen and decreed. Wherever the ship goes, the rush of water ahead of it—which neither steers it nor speeds it up—foams out in front, and from a distance seems to us not merely to move on its own but to govern the ship's movement too.

By examining only those expressions of the will of historical figures which, as commands, were related to events, historians have assumed that events depended on those commands. But by examining the events themselves, and the connection historical figures actually had to the people, we have found that they, and their orders, were dependent on events. The undeniable proof of this conclusion is that, no matter how many commands are issued, the event does not happen unless other causes exist for it. But as soon as an event does happen, whatever it may be, some will always be found, out of all the continually expressed wishes of different people, which, by their meaning and their timing, are related as commands to the events.

In the last analysis, we arrive at the circle of infinity—the final boundary that human reason, in every field of thought, reaches whenever it is not merely toying with its subject. Electricity produces heat; heat produces electricity. Atoms attract one another; atoms repel one another.

Speaking of the interaction between heat and electricity, or between atoms, we cannot say why it happens; we simply say that it is so, because it is inconceivable otherwise, because it has to be so, and call it a law. The same applies to historical events. Why wars and revolutions happen, we do not know. We only know that to produce one action or the other, people combine into a certain formation in which they all take part, and we say this is so because it cannot be thought of otherwise—in other words, that it is a law.

If history dealt only with external phenomena, establishing this simple, obvious law would be enough, and we could consider the argument finished. But the law of history concerns man. A particle of matter cannot tell us that it doesn't feel the law of attraction or repulsion and that the law is false — but man, who is the subject of history, says plainly: I am free, and therefore not subject to the law.

In this contradiction lies the problem of free will, which since the most ancient times has occupied the best human minds, and since the most ancient times has been presented in its whole tremendous significance.

The problem is this: if we consider man as a subject of observation, from whatever standpoint — theological, historical, ethical, or philosophical — we find a general law of necessity to which he, like everything that exists, is subject. But if we look at him from within, as something we are directly conscious of, we feel ourselves to be free.

A whole series of experiments and arguments proves to every man that, as an object of observation, he is subject to certain laws, and man submits to them, and never resists the laws of gravity or impermeability once he has learned them. But that same series of experiments and arguments proves to him that the complete freedom he is conscious of in himself is impossible, that his every action depends on his makeup, his character, and the motives acting on him — and yet man never submits to the conclusions of these experiments and arguments. Having learned from experiment and argument that a stone falls downward, a man believes this without question, and always expects the law he has learned to hold.

However often experiment and reasoning may show a man that he will do the same thing as before, under the same conditions and with the same character, yet when he approaches, under those same conditions and with that same character, an action that always ends the same way — even for the thousandth time — he feels just as certain as he did before the experiment that he can act however he pleases. Every man, savage or sage, however irrefutably reason and experiment may prove to him that it is impossible to imagine two different courses of action under exactly the same conditions, feels that without this irrational notion — which is the very essence of freedom — he cannot imagine life. He feels that however impossible it may be, it is so, because without this idea of freedom he would not only be unable to understand life, he would be unable to live for even a single moment.

This consciousness of freedom is unshakeable and irrefutable. No experiment or argument can touch it. Every thinker has recognized it, and every person without exception has felt it. Without it, no conception of man is even possible. It makes up the other side of the question.

Only in our own self-confident age of popularized knowledge — thanks to that most powerful engine of ignorance, the diffusion of printed matter — has the question of free will been put on a level on which the question itself cannot exist. In our time, the majority of so-called advanced people — that is, the crowd of ignoramuses — have taken the work of naturalists, who deal with only one side of the question, for a solution to the whole problem.

They say, and write, and print, that the soul and free will do not exist, because man's life is expressed in muscular movements, and muscular movements are conditioned by the activity of the nerves. And they say the soul and free will do not exist because, at some unknown point in time, we descended from apes. They say this without the least suspicion that thousands of years ago this same law of necessity, which they are now trying so eagerly to prove through physiology and comparative zoology, was not merely acknowledged by every religion and every thinker, but has never been denied. They fail to see that the role of the natural sciences here is simply to serve as an instrument for illuminating one side of the question. The fact that, from the standpoint of observation, reason and will are merely secretions of the brain, and that man, following the general law, may have developed from lower animals at some unknown point in time — this only restates, from a new angle, a truth admitted thousands of years ago by every religious and philosophical system: that from the standpoint of reason, man is subject to the law of necessity. But it does not advance the solution of the question by a hair's breadth; the question has another side, the opposite side, grounded in the consciousness of freedom.

If men descended from apes at some unknown point in time, that is just as comprehensible as their having been made from a handful of earth at some fixed point in time. In the first case the unknown quantity is the time; in the second it is the origin. And the question of how man's consciousness of freedom can be reconciled with the law of necessity to which he is subject cannot be solved by comparative physiology and zoology. In a frog, a rabbit, or an ape we can observe only muscular and nervous activity; but in man we observe consciousness as well as muscular and nervous activity.

The naturalists, and their followers, who think they can settle this question, are like plasterers assigned to plaster one side of a church wall who, taking advantage of the head foreman's absence, get carried away and plaster right over the windows, the icons, the woodwork, and the walls that still have no buttresses — and are delighted that, from a plasterer's point of view, everything now looks so smooth and even.

In this way, our conception of free will and inevitability gradually shrinks or grows according to how closely or loosely a man is connected to the external world, how remote or recent the time is, and how dependent his life is on the causes in relation to which we consider it.

So that if we examine a man whose connection to the external world is well known, where a great deal of time separates the action from our examination of it, and where the causes of the action are most accessible to us, we arrive at the conception of a maximum of inevitability and a minimum of free will. If we examine a man who depends little on external conditions, whose action took place very recently, and the causes of whose action lie beyond our knowledge, we arrive at the conception of a minimum of inevitability and a maximum of freedom.

In neither case can we ever arrive at a conception of either complete freedom or complete necessity — no matter how much we shift our point of view: however clearly or however obscurely we make out the connection between the man and the external world, however long or short the interval of time, however comprehensible or incomprehensible the causes of the action.

(2) No matter how closely we bring the moment of judgment up against the moment of the deed, we never arrive at a conception of freedom in time. If I examine an action carried out a second ago, I still have to recognize it as unfree, because it is irrevocably tied to the instant at which it was performed. Can I lift my arm? I lift it — but then I ask myself: could I have refrained from lifting it at that moment, the one that has already passed? To convince myself, I don't lift it the next moment. But I am not now refraining from doing so at that first moment when I asked the question. Time has gone by, time I could not hold back; the arm I lifted then is not the same arm I am now refraining from lifting, nor is the air I lifted it in the same air that surrounds me now. The moment in which that first movement happened is irrevocable, and in that moment I could make only one movement, and whatever movement I made would be the only one. That I did not lift my arm a moment later does not prove that I could have refrained from lifting it then. And since at that single moment of time I could make only one movement, it could not have been any other. To imagine it as free, we would have to imagine it in the present, on the border between past and future — that is, outside of time, which is impossible.

But even granting that we could reduce this remaining element of inevitability to something infinitely small, equal to zero — by imagining a man wholly exempt from every influence, considering only his momentary action in the present, unprompted by any cause — we still would not have arrived at a conception of complete freedom in man, because a being uninfluenced by the external world, standing outside time and independent of cause, is no longer a man at all.

(1) However much we increase our knowledge of the spatial conditions in which a man is situated, that knowledge can never be complete, because the number of those conditions is as infinite as space itself. And so, as long as not every condition influencing a man has been identified, there is no complete inevitability, but a certain measure of freedom remains.

(2) However much we lengthen the period of time between the action we are examining and our judgment of it, that period will be finite, while time itself is infinite, and so here too there can never be absolute inevitability.

But beyond this: even granting that the remaining minimum of freedom equals zero, suppose we assumed a complete absence of freedom in some particular case — say, that of a dying man, an unborn child, or an idiot. Doing so would destroy the very conception of man in the case we are examining, because the moment there is no freedom, there is also no man. And so the conception of a man's action subject solely to the law of inevitability, with no element of freedom at all, is just as impossible as the conception of a man's completely free action.
Freedom limited by nothing is the essence of life, in man's consciousness. Inevitability without content is man's reason, in its three forms.

The undefinable essence of the force moving the heavenly bodies, the undefinable essence of the forces of heat and electricity, or of chemical affinity, or of the vital force — these form the content of astronomy, physics, chemistry, botany, zoology, and so on. In exactly the same way, the force of free will forms the content of history. But just as the subject of every science is the manifestation of this unknown essence of life, while that essence itself can only be the subject of metaphysics — so too the manifestation of the force of free will in human beings, in space, in time, and in dependence on cause, forms the subject of history, while free will itself is the subject of metaphysics.
